Title: Amazon Threat Intelligence observes threat actors running cybercrime campaigns with ARTEX AI agents
Context: MadPot telemetry allows Amazon Threat Intelligence to observe attacker behavior without exposing customer workloads
Full Text:
From Oct. 3 to Nov. 5, 2026, Amazon’s MadPot, a globally distributed network of decoy threat sensors, captured requests from AI agents that included operating memory from offensive campaigns that threat actors ran on ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework. The ARTEX agents sent these requests to MadPot sensors configured to present as popular large language model (LLM) inference APIs, and the requests carried the agents’ own records of their campaigns.

Amazon Threat Intelligence assessed threat activity referencing potentially affected AWS customers and notified them as appropriate. Because activity against other organizations could not be confirmed, this post shares the findings and indicators of compromise (IOCs) so that organizations that run the affected technologies can review their own environments.

The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting. Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection. In aggregate, the agent records show that agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention. This post describes how these campaigns operated based on the agents’ own descriptions of the campaigns.

Attribution and instructions

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that ARTEX was used for these campaigns due to prompt references to ARTEX tooling and other technical artifacts referencing ARTEX. Threat actors instructed ARTEX agents through standing instruction prompts that set the mission objectives, targeting rules, and operational constraints. Within those instructions, the agents handled the work themselves. In one credential theft campaign, operators told the agents to work through a fixed sequence of countries, prioritize enterprise production sites over personal projects, and grade every stolen credential by whether it worked and what it could reach. Agents were directed to treat credentials exposed publicly for more than 30 days as low-value inventory.

Amazon Threat Intelligence also assess with moderate confidence these are disparate Chinese-nexus threat groups due to use of simplified Chinese language in prompts, China time-zone configurations, targeting consistent with Chinese interests, and tooling predominantly used by Chinese-nexus threats. Sample instructions included setting red lines, such as excluding mainland China targets and government domains, and required all outbound traffic to go through proxies.

How MadPot saw inside these campaigns

MadPot presents controlled services to potential attackers and records how they discover, test, and attempt to compromise or abuse them. MadPot telemetry allows Amazon Threat Intelligence to observe attacker behavior without exposing customer workloads. In this case, the MadPot sensors presented popular LLM-compatible chat-completions interfaces on various ports. Agentic frameworks sent prompts to these interfaces as part of their offensive workflows, treating them as LLM inference backends.

The resulting telemetry contained the persistent task context, system prompts, tool histories, knowledge-graph state, and reported findings that these frameworks ordinarily send to an LLM to make operational decisions. Because agentic frameworks retain the history of past conversations, individual requests often contain the full operational history of a campaign. That history described activity that occurred before and between the captured requests, on systems MadPot does not monitor. Amazon Threat Intelligence did not observe that activity as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported, but the records show what the actors were pursuing.

Most of the activity used ARTEX to divide work among planner, worker, verification, and compression agents sharing a persistent knowledge graph. The knowledge graph acts as the operation’s shared memory: every agent reads from it, and writes its results back, so each agent picks up where the others left off. The agents’ records described reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, credential theft, cloud-privilege expansion, and cryptocurrency fraud attempts across hundreds of targets spanning AI application platforms and other workloads. These records show how threat actors are organizing persistent, financially motivated offensive operations using agentic AI frameworks.

Campaign 1: Stealing AI credentials at industrial scale

In this campaign, threat actors used AI agents to steal API keys and other credentials that grant access to AI models, most likely so they could use those models while someone else paid for them. The agents’ records show stolen keys being fed into the framework’s own model gateway, where they powered the agents searching for more keys. Beyond AI model access keys, cloud credentials were treated as a doorway to more access. Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities. They prioritized access to premium frontier models over general cloud permissions.

Agents recorded use of different AI gateways, keys, and models, but they all used a shared method: find internet-exposed AI applications, extract the upstream provider keys they hold, validate those keys, and store them in a managed pool. The agents focused on applications that aggregate provider keys, because one weak management interface can expose many downstream accounts. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. A codified vulnerability playbook mapped each fingerprinted product to its known attack chain, including uninitialized installs that could be claimed, anonymous management and provider-configuration endpoints, default administrator credentials, such as the LiteLLM default master key, CVE-2025-3248 (Langflow), CVE-2026-28797 (RAGFlow), an authentication bypass via the isCliRequest header in One API family systems, SSRF through URL-fetch features to cloud metadata services, and secrets left in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes, and environment files.

To find those keys, discovery drew on internet scanning services, certificate transparency, and public code and artifact sources: GitHub repositories and event archives (targeting secrets that fell outside automated revocation), npm and PyPI tarballs, container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels. One parallel operation worked through a fixed country sequence, prioritizing enterprise production sites, and graded every credential: L1 for a lead, L2 for a confirmed working API call, and L3 for quantified impact, such as readable data or spendable balance. Keys exposed publicly for more than 30 days were treated as low-value inventory.

Campaign 2: Defeating identity verification with deepfakes

In this campaign, threat actors used AI agents to defeat the identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges with deepfakes. The agents’ records show generating real-time deepfake video to pass live selfie checks and forged ID document photos to pass document checks.

The records describe a methodical approach to the liveness check, which is a security method that confirms a person interacting with a digital system is a real, living human being physically present at the time of capture. The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move. Their best recorded attempt completed the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target. Even so, the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt the agents recorded. In parallel, a separate session built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. By splitting the model and avoiding unnecessary memory copies on the GPU, it reached 11.5 frames per second, close to what a live video check expects.

The agents worked on the ID document as well. Verification vendors look for signs that a document photo was edited or is a picture of a screen rather than a camera capture. To get past those checks, the agents recorded building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that re-saving an edited image would normally replace. The result is an altered image that looks, at the file level, like an untouched camera photo.

This campaign also shows how ARTEX runs several workstreams toward one goal. At least four agent sessions ran at once: one searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass. They shared findings and handed off tasks through cross-session tools.

What this means for defenders

None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. What AI agents change is the speed and persistence of the attacker. The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software. Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.

Given the speed and persistence of the attackers, organizations should assume exposed secrets and misconfigurations will be found quickly and remediate accordingly. They should bring AI applications, model gateways, and inference endpoints under the same controls as other production systems, and they should watch for misuse of AI services through unexpected spend or unusual usage.

Title: How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks
Context: Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques in play even as abuse of AI tools has made attacks easier to mount and cheaper for even relatively...
Full Text:
AI may be helping cyberattackers increase the speed and scale of their operations, but it is not yet changing their core objectives or the techniques they employ as part of their attack chains.

Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques in play even as abuse of AI tools has made attacks easier to mount and cheaper for even relatively unskilled attackers, according to security experts.

“Attackers are still identifying targets, performing reconnaissance, establishing a foothold, moving laterally, achieving their objective, covering their tracks, and moving on to the next target,” says Ronald Lewis, director of cybersecurity governance at application security firm Black Duck. “What’s changed is the volume and velocity that AI allows this process to happen.”

Even in the most high-profile example of an AI powered attack to date, in which Claude Code was abused by Chinese state-sponsored actors to mount an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign in September 2025, conventional attack techniques and procedures laid the foundation, with AI abused as an enabler to support reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation, lateral movement, credential harvesting, data analysis, and exfiltration during the GTG-1002 campaign.

JadePuffer, a ransomware campaign disclosed in July 2026, witnessed an LLM-driven agent automating most of the intrusion chain. Initial exploitation was through CVE-2025-3248, a year-old missing-authentication flaw in Langflow, a popular open-source framework for building LLM applications and agent workflows.

Vulnerable internet-facing Langflow instances were looted for cloud credentials, API keys, and other secrets before lateral movement, privilege escalation, and ultimately destructive database encryption.

JadePuffer shows AI’s potential for automating conventional attack methods, but it also underscores how vulnerable software is where AI has been giving attackers the biggest edge to date. AI tools can readily find exploitable flaws in open-source code faster than defenders can patch them, a huge problem for the many enterprises carrying years of technical debt. And security experts see software flaws rising as a root cause of breaches as a result.

What AI enables

In addition to enhancing attackers’ flaw discovery prowess, AI is also enabling attackers to fail or succeed faster. Defenders are witnessing improvements in speed, scale, and operational ability from attackers that correlates strongly with increasing capabilities of AI tools.

“Adversaries are realizing the same gains in development velocity and operations that everyone else is getting from implementing AI,” says Darren Meyer, security research advocate at application security tools vendor Checkmarx.

Black Duck’s Lewis sees this expanding attackers’ reach and empowering more attack experimentation.

“An attacker can potentially investigate more opportunities, try more approaches, and move to the next target at a pace that would be difficult for a human team to match,” he says.

That in turn will increasingly alter a pivotal phase of conventional attack patterns that traditional favors defenders, notes Crystal Morin, senior cybersecurity strategist at cloud security firm Sysdig.“That dwell time, which was often weeks or months, was where detection happened,” she says.

Whereas attackers used to land, sit for a while, and poke around, AI-assisted attackers are showing signs of shortening detection windows. And AI agents won’t wait.

‘Agentic APT’ and AI attack phase specialization

By leveraging agentic AI in their operations, hackers can also draw on a deeper pool of domain expertise — database administration, CI/CD pipelines, etc. — compared to human attack teams where different people tend to specialize in different things such as web app security or malware development.

“Think of it as a database admin, a developer, an IT engineer, a DevOps specialist, a cloud architect, and a hacker combined into a single role,” says Nazar Tymoshyk, CEO and founder of agentic AI security vendor UnderDefense. “We call it agentic APT, and the critical shift is that it is no longer exclusive to nation-state actors.”

Tymoshyk adds: “A threat that previously required a coordinated team of specialists can be deployed by a single person with the right prompt and the right model.”

Security researchers, including UnderDefense, report that attackers favor Chinese models, specifically GLM and Kimi 3, which have significantly fewer content restrictions, rather than their more restricted Western alternatives as a platform to mount attacks.

“Attackers switch between models depending on what the task requires: one for reconnaissance, one for code generation, one for crafting social engineering content,” Tymoshyk says. “The modularity is part of the attack design.”

Attackers often prefer to use local models both because of operational security advantages and because some models may have weaker safeguards against malicious use.

Other experts cautioned that the abuse of particular models is difficult to determine and, in any case, a side issue to the main problem of defending against attacks.

“Attribution of particular attacks to particular models is generally pure speculation from very thin evidence on the ground,” says Checkmarx’s Meyer. “True attribution can only come from infiltration of threat groups or compromise of threat group infrastructure, both of which are rarely available to public researchers.”

The current baseline of attacks consists of AI-orchestrated operations where models surface, validate, and execute attack paths. Security researchers report a general shift from AI-assisted and AI-accelerated attacks toward fully autonomous attacks, with only minimal human roles remaining.

AI attack economics

The economics of mounting attacks is also changing — and is crucial in understanding attackers’ increasing use of AI.

“A human attacker builds a playbook per campaign and reuses it, so every new target costs engineering time to make adjustments,” says Sysdig’s Morin. “An agentic threat actor carries context about a whole class of applications and composes its plan live against whatever it finds. There, the only cost is inference budget. And as running a complex attack gets cheaper, the number of attempts will go up.”

Agentic attacks are still flawed, and breadth of expertise is a poor substitute for depth of knowledge.

“Agents hallucinate and are noisy, which is often why they’re catchable,” notes Sysdig’s Morin. “Jadepuffer had flaws in its ransom note, encryption, wallet, and data exfiltration. There are still many areas in which human analysis and skill still outperform agent memory.”

Countermeasures

“The core objectives of the threat actor haven’t really changed, but the timeframe for a successful attack has been compressed dramatically,” says Nathan Smolenski, CISO at vulnerability management and compliance firm Qualys. “Frontier AI tools accelerate vulnerability discovery and weaponization, shrinking the window between disclosure and exploitation to near zero.”

Smolenski adds: “Defenders can no longer rely on traditional, human-speed 30-day patch cadences or monthly static spreadsheets.”

AI significantly changes the entry dynamic by expanding the attack surface — particularly through end-user devices, API calls, and ungoverned AI agents.

In response, defending organizations must shift away from human-centric gatekeeping toward automated defences while still keeping on top of foundational security defenses such as patching and authentication controls.

“Implementing agentic workflows with human-in-the-loop guardrails enables security teams to automate lower-level triage efforts and focus human expertise on governing agents, validating outputs, and making more critical risk decisions,” Smolenski concludes.

Title: The Green Agent POV: Formulating the Fix for an Exposed Container with Sensitive Data Access
Context: A critical Issue was just discovered in an environment: an internet-facing container running an image with a known initial-access vulnerability, with a role attached that can...
Full Text:
A critical Issue was just discovered in an environment: an internet-facing container running an image with a known initial-access vulnerability, with a role attached that can reach sensitive data.

With AI speed reducing the time from discovery to exploitation, the pressure to fix it fast is intense. Yet remediation is never just about speed. Teams are forced to balance security urgency with business continuity, racing against the clock to answer three critical questions: what’s impacted, what the fix is, and who to send that fix to.

The Wiz Security Graph helps security teams answer the first question. It lays out the exact exposure path including the exposed endpoints, the deployment behind them, the image where the CVE sits, and the lateral movement path that carries an attacker from code execution to buckets holding PII.

Finding the fix and the owner, however, requires deeper investigation that security teams can’t spend hours on. They must rapidly contact the developer to deploy a fix, if it even exists, and apply mitigations in the meanwhile without disrupting production uptime.

That’s what we built Green Agent for. In this post, we’re excited to pull back the curtain and share how Green Agent investigates this exact Issue in minutes and determines the remediation strategies it recommends.

The Investigation

1. Understanding the Issue

Green Agent started by ingesting the Security Graph context to map the full attack path. This Issue represented a toxic combination centered on a single Kubernetes deployment in an AWS EKS cluster.

The Security Graph correlated five distinct risk types converging on this single workload:

External Exposure: A direct network path from the internet to the container.

Vulnerability: A known initial-access CVE-2026-111497 on the container image.

Insecure Kubernetes Cluster: A pod mounting a service account token to bridge into the cloud.

Unprotected Principal: An IAM role granting the workload access to cloud storage.

Unprotected data: Sensitive customer records residing in those accessible buckets.

Five risk types meant five distinct places where the attack chain could be broken - whether by removing the public exposure, patching the container image, unmounting the service account token, scoping down the IAM role, or purging the sensitive data.

Before it could recommend how to break the chain without disrupting production uptime, Green Agent needed to validate the ground truth behind each risk factor. It began investigating the attack path step-by-step, starting at the perimeter.

2. Validating Exposure: Is the Front Door Really Open?

Before recommending a fix, Green Agent needed to determine whether network containment was even an option. Many cloud workloads appear public in configuration tables but are actually shielded behind internal subnets, VPNs, or closed security groups.

Green Agent traced the full inbound route from 0.0.0.0/0:

The Ingress Route: Traffic flowed from the public internet through an AWS Internet Gateway, routed across an AWS Network Load Balancer, passed through the Traefik Ingress controller, and directly into the application's main container.

Unauthenticated Access: Both HTTP (port 80) and HTTPS (port 443) served public endpoints returning unauthenticated 2XX status codes.

No Perimeter Defense: Green Agent inspected the hops and confirmed no Web Application Firewall (WAF) or firewall rules were in place.

This established a critical operational boundary for remediation. Because this frontend was an intentionally public production service, simply pulling the network plug - like tearing down ingress or blocking the load balancer - would cause a total production outage. Any network-level remediation plan from Green Agent would need to preserve uptime, such as introducing authentication middleware rather than severing traffic entirely.

3. Assessing Exploitability: Is the Vulnerability Running in Memory?

With the front door confirmed open, Green Agent moved to the next link in the attack chain: the vulnerability risk factor, to evaluate whether the attack path could be severed at the application layer.

It investigated the container image flaw: CVE-2026-111497 ("Broccoli2Shell"), a critical RCE in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js and cataloged in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV).

It confirmed from the Wiz Sensor that the vulnerable Brotli libraries were actively loaded in memory by the running Node.js process, verifying that code execution was a live, viable threat.

Green Agent also checked upstream advisories and verified that vendor patches (including Node.js 22.23.4 and libbrotli 1.2.1) were already available, confirming a permanent code fix was viable.

However, organizational release processes mean that rolling out a new container image through testing and CI/CD pipelines takes time. Because the attack path can be broken at any of the five risk types, Green Agent turned to the remaining links - the Kubernetes configuration, IAM role, and sensitive data - to see if the toxic combination could be severed immediately in the cloud.

4. Evaluating Cloud Identity & Data: Can the Cloud Path be Severed?

Investigating the workload's connection to cloud storage, Green Agent evaluated the three remaining risk types:

The Cluster Remediation Lever (IRSA): Green Agent examined the Kubernetes service account and confirmed it projected cloud credentials via IRSA into the container. This revealed an immediate mitigation lever: disabling token automount on the pod spec to cut off cloud access.

The IAM Remediation Lever: Inspecting the assumed IAM role, Green Agent found overprivileged s3:GetObject and wildcard s3:* permissions across three S3 buckets. This surfaced a second lever: scoping the IAM policy down to least privilege.

The Data Remediation Lever: Querying the S3 buckets revealed over 5,000 unmasked records (credit cards and PII) in files, identifying a third remediation lever: purging or masking unprotected data at rest.

Investigating these layers proved that Green Agent didn't have to wait on a code deployment to neutralize the risk. Multiple zero-downtime levers were available in the cloud right now.

5. Code-to-Cloud Lineage: Finding the Source and Owners

Cloud mitigations can sever the attack path immediately and buy critical time, but permanent remediation requires fixing at the source. If changes aren't committed to code, the next CI/CD build or Terraform apply will simply overwrite your cloud tweaks and recreate the issue. Green Agent called its Code Subagent to bridge the runtime assets back to version control, tracing the container image to its source Dockerfile, the overprivileged IAM role to its Terraform definitions, and the workload to its GitOps deployment manifests.

By inspecting commit history and metadata, Green Agent connected each fix directly to the engineers who actually maintain the code: the application developer, service owner, and infrastructure lead so security teams didn’t have to go on a search for the right owner.

6. Determining a Verdict and Creating Remediation Plans

Within minutes, Green Agent analyzed organizational context to reach a verdict that this Issue needed to be remediated and is of Critical severity. Green Agent factored in real business impact: the workload belonged to High Business Impact (HBI) production projects, formed an active breach path to 5,000+ sensitive records, and aligned with historical remediation evidence showing 100% of similar sampled issues in the subscription were successfully remediated with a 0% rejection rate.

To break the toxic combination, Green Agent determined that Mitigate and Fix plans were most appropriate to break the risk types identified, balancing immediate protection against permanent resolution:

Mitigate Plans: Immediate actions security teams can deploy right now to reduce the risk, like disabling service account token automount to instantly sever cloud access while developers work on the code fix.

Fix Plans: Permanent root-cause resolutions, like updating the base image in the Dockerfile or scoping down Terraform IAM policies.

Just as importantly, Green Agent evaluated operational trade-offs to skip unviable strategies: it explicitly rejected deleting the ingress because severing an intentionally public frontend would cause a total production outage, and skipped long-term hardening where environment prerequisites weren't in place.

Finally, Green Agent turned planning into execution by assigning each plan directly to its verified owner, ready to resolve via a one-click pull request or by handing instructions straight to a coding agent.

Why this Matters

Green Agent brought two things to this remediation that are notoriously difficult to balance in security: addressing security urgency, and maintaining the context needed to protect business continuity.

First, speed. With risks and threats moving faster than ever, security urgency demands an immediate response. A human team investigating this toxic combination would spend hours or days context-switching: security analysts verifying the public endpoint, platform engineers checking if the Brotli library is actually in memory, cloud admins auditing IAM policies, and developers tracking down which Git repository built the image. Green Agent conducted this investigation in minutes, eliminating the friction and guesswork that typically stalls remediation.

Secondly, operational intelligence. Remediation isn’t only a security team problem, it’s an organizational decision that requires understanding real-world trade-offs. Green Agent knew better than to propose deleting the ingress and taking down a public service that would impact the business. Instead, it distinguished between immediate, zero-downtime cloud mitigations and permanent code fixes, found the exact files in version control, and assigned the work directly to the engineers who own them.

That balance is how organizations can move towards autonomous remediation. Trust has to be earned before teams hand over the keys to auto-execution. That trust is built on context: when engineers see that an agent genuinely understands business trade-offs and won't break production, they can safely evolve from reviewing every action (human-in-the-loop) to supervisory oversight (human-on-the-loop).

That progression is what finally enables teams to get on a path to self-healing, while giving engineers their time back to keep building.

Title: The Binance Aftershocks: Tracking the Nearly 130% Spike in Crypto Impersonation Scams
Context: Whenever an event of this scale hits, KnowBe4 Threat Labs routinely tracks an immediate surge in secondary attacks that exploit the chaos
Full Text:
Lead Analysts: Emily Hanlon, James Dyer

On October 29, 2026, cryptocurrency giant Binance lost approximately $6.34 billion in digital assets in under half an hour. The attack, attributed to the notorious Lazarus Group, stands as the largest crypto heist in history.

But how was an attack of this scale pulled off?

The entire compromise appeared to originate at the human and endpoint layer: a compromised engineer’s machine. Even in high-tech, cryptographically secured ecosystems, targeting humans and their admin permission remains the easiest way into an organisation.

Attacks of this magnitude trigger immediate fallout. In the days following the attack through November 2, KnowBe4 Threat Labs tracked a 128.9% surge in crypto currency impersonation threats. Cybercriminals specifically zeroed in on fake wallet transfers and withdrawal alerts.

The Aftershock: When the Phishing Fallout Hits Inboxes

Threat actors are notorious for riding the wave of major headlines. As we found for the Phishing Threat Trends Report Vol 8., attackers are 5.4 times faster responding to headlines in 2026 than they were in 2022. Whenever an event of this scale hits, KnowBe4 Threat Labs routinely tracks an immediate surge in secondary attacks that exploit the chaos. The sudden influx in cryptocurrency-related phishing is testament to this.

Fallout attacks following a major breach almost always fall across three main vectors:

Brand impersonation:

Impersonation was the main threat vector exploited by attackers following the Binance hijacking. In less than 48 hours, Binance rose from the 73rd most impersonated organization in Defend’s dataset to the 23rd.

High-profile attacks create prime conditions for cybercriminals. Threat actors exploit psychological fallout, specifically availability heuristics and salience bias. Constant media coverage pushes “Binance” to the front of everyone's minds and cuts through inbox noise. Even users who rarely check their accounts suddenly zero in on any message bearing the breached brand’s name. Fear does the rest: worried that their own accounts are compromised, recipients act on impulse. Scammers can ruthlessly capitalize on this anxiety, knowing urgency and fear crush skepticism.

Example:

This phish rolled out mainly to UK and U.S. inboxes, deliberately using the same font colors and styling as typical Binance mail. The attackers likely leveraged generative AI to mimic Binance’s standard email templates. By exploiting brand familiarity, they amplify the urgency and fear that the recipient's account is part of the compromise. The email included embedded hidden characters throughout the text, disrupting linguistic-based detection of Binance brand impersonation. When users click the link, they’re prompted to “login” to authorize the cancelled request, inevitably handing credentials over. This phish deployed only 13 hours after the initial attack.

Shown below is a legitimate email from Binance. The phishing campaign accurately replicates this template that end users are unlikely to spot any visual indicators of compromise:

These impersonation lures extended beyond just “Binance.” In fact, 8.9% of all phishing attacks on Friday, October 30, contained the word “bitcoin” in the email, primarily in the subject and display name.

Top subject lines:

“Bitcoin Deposit Confirmation”

“<name> Update Your Bitcoin Details Now”

“Funds added to your Bitcoin wallet”

“Secure your Bitcoin wallet fast”

Recovery scams

High-profile exchange breaches reliably trigger a predatory second wave: recovery scams. Cybercriminals understand that when news breaks, users scramble in fear. Fraudsters capitalize on this chaos in two ways: first, by blasting fake security alerts that prompt users to "secure" or "re-verify" their wallets, a common credential harvesting lure, and second, by promising users who have lost assets reimbursement or recovery for a fee.

This triggers a cruel cycle of double-victimization. Desperate to recover lost savings, panicked users lower their guard for spoofed "claims portals" and end up signing away whatever assets they had left. Recognizing this pattern is critical: once an attack goes public, assume any unsolicited outreach, no matter how verified or urgent it looks, is an attacker trying to profit from the wreckage.

This campaign has similarly tried to match Binance's branding, pretending to come from the company’s internal insurance or risk division. To slip past automated link scanners, the attackers drop a plain-text URL directly into the body and instruct the recipient to copy and paste it into their browser. The address mimics a legitimate Binance domain at first glance, but swaps the "i" for a "1" and uses a .net extension. Once pasted, the link requests the user pay a small upfront fee to unlock ‘security advice’.

Spear Phishing

Right after a major exchange breach, phishing gets much smarter. Attackers drop the generic spray-and-pray emails and start using the actual details of the incident as bait, knowing everyone is glued to the news waiting for updates.

One of the sharpest vectors targets third-party partners and contractors. Posing as internal incident response teams or forensic investigators, the attackers send emails dangling "Confidential Forensic Reports," "Urgent IoC Feeds," or "Emergency Security Questionnaires." Tucked inside is usually a password-protected ZIP, a poisoned PDF, or a malicious cloud link. The moment an engineer opens it, malware drops quietly onto the machine—setting up a foothold inside partner networks using the exact same playbook that started the breach in the first place.

This phish relied on techniques that work even against alert, well-trained employees. Attackers increasingly go beyond simply avoiding detection and instead they actively limit telemetry from the email itself so detection engines view the emails as “safe.” This email used CEO impersonation to exploit a user’s natural reluctance to question a senior leader, using a spoofed authority figure alongside real organizational stress, pressures staff into skipping normal verification for a payment, access request, or file. This email used PDF-based malware delivery which doesn't require clicking a link inside the document: a crafted PDF can run embedded scripts or exploit the reader itself the moment it's opened.

How Has this Impacted Different Countries and Industries?

In the days following the finance hit, the U.S. was the biggest target for cryptocurrency phish, taking nearly 70% of hits, with the UK behind holding 18%.

Top industry proportions:

Industry

Percentage of the cryptocurrency phish received by industry

Insurance

32.4%

19.4%

12.9%

Dominant attack techniques across industry:

📑 Insurance - 32.4%

They have an average of nearly three tactics per email, aimed to overwhelm both traditional defenses and the user. They blend executive impersonation, BEC, fear-driven extortion, and heavier technical tricks into multi-layered traps designed to slip past defenses. This is a typically aggressive and chaotic technique.

💸 Finance - 26.9%

Finance is completely dominated by brand impersonation, where scammers clone recognizable banking portals and software alerts to harvest login credentials. Because finance teams are conditioned to click through security dashboards and transaction notices all day, attackers simply mimic those routine tools instead of reinventing the wheel.

📜 Law - 19.4%

Legal practices see a lethal mix of personal extortion and high-stakes corporate wire fraud. Attackers know that attorneys deal in tight confidentiality and massive settlement transfers, so they skip fake login pages and go straight for the jugular: personal blackmail or hijacking actual payment chains. It’s less about mimicking big software brands and more about exploiting human panic and professional reputation

🔢 Education - 8.9%

The threat landscape here is about as blunt and generic as it gets, heavily skewed toward automated, copy-paste sextortion blasts. Scammers aren’t burning precious zero-days or drafting elaborate ruses — they're playing an untargeted numbers game across thousands of easily accessible university inboxes.

How To Defend Your Organization

Treat all "recovery" and "refund" outreach as a scam: Real exchanges and insurance divisions will never reach out unsolicited, ask you to pay an upfront fee for "investigation advice," or demand you connect your wallet to an external claims portal. Once an attack goes public, assume any offer to restore lost funds is a predatory second-wave trap.

Never verify accounts through links or copied URLs: Following a massive breach, scammers flood inboxes with fake security alerts using lookalike domains and plain-text URLs to bypass automated scanners. If you receive a warning about unauthorized activity, open a new browser window and navigate directly to your bookmarked login page.

Confirm urgent executive demands: Threat actors weaponize organizational stress and executive authority to rush staff into skipping protocol. If an email claims to come from a senior leader demanding urgent action, wire transfers, or sensitive file downloads, verify it through a separate channel, rather than replying to the email.

Remember, just because it looks real doesn’t mean it is. When major headlines break, always expect the phishing aftershocks to follow.

Full Text:
Two people shopping for the same product shouldn’t have to wonder whether one is paying more because a company knows more about them.

That’s the concern behind a bill passed by the New York City Council on November 12. The legislation targets surveillance pricing, defined as using personal data and algorithms to offer different people different prices for the same goods or services.

Introduction 891-A would prohibit these practices in transactions with consumers in New York City. It would also restrict collecting, selling, or sharing personal data to facilitate surveillance pricing. The bill is at the mayor’s desk and would take effect one year after becoming law.

For consumers, the issue goes beyond an unexpectedly expensive shopping cart. It’s about companies turning information about your life and online behavior into a tool for deciding what to charge you.

Learn more about surveillance pricing in this episode of our podcast Lock & Code:

Large-scale data collection also creates risks beyond pricing, including sensitive inferences about people and unauthorized disclosure of their information.

What exactly is surveillance pricing?

Surveillance pricing uses information about you, or a profile a company has built about you, to help determine the price you see for a specific product or service.

That information can include your location, browsing history, shopping habits, and demographic characteristics. In initial findings published in January 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said pricing tools could draw on surprisingly detailed behavior, including mouse movements and the products people leave unpurchased in their online shopping carts.

This is not some conspiracy theory. There is evidence that the tools and data pipelines exist. The FTC’s findings drew on documents from pricing and technology intermediaries. Staff reported that the intermediaries examined worked with at least 250 clients across sectors including groceries and apparel. The published examples were hypothetical to protect confidential business information.

Surveillance pricing should not be confused with dynamic pricing. Dynamic pricing can respond to changing market conditions, such as demand or availability. Surveillance pricing uses personal information to differentiate between customers. While the two can overlap, they aren’t interchangeable.

A personalized price isn’t automatically a higher price. Some shoppers might receive discounts. The concern is that an opaque pricing system gives sellers detailed insight into customers while those customers are unable to see how they’re being assessed.

Another form of unequal pricing that the bill allows is qualifying loyalty and other discounts. The bill preserves genuine discounts, including qualifying loyalty and rewards programs and discounts for clearly defined groups such as veterans, seniors, and teachers. But those exceptions come with conditions.

Surveillance pricing doesn’t necessarily charge wealthy shoppers more and give everyone else a break. Pricing tools can estimate what you’re willing to pay, which may have little to do with what you can comfortably afford. Perceived price sensitivity is a deciding factor, so a wealthy bargain hunter could receive a discount, while someone with less money but an urgent need or few alternatives could be judged willing to pay more.

For consumers, the underlying question about surveillance pricing is straightforward: How much does the price reflect what’s being sold, and how much does it reflect what a company thinks it can get out of you?

New York City’s bill aims to limit how companies use your personal information to make that calculation.

Your name, address, and phone number may already be for sale.

Title: Inside the loop: Five AI attack frameworks that never ask permission
Context: What agentic offensive frameworks change for detection and response Agentic attacks land effects in seconds Within a burst, an agentic loop issues steps seconds apart, and each...
Full Text:
Five agentic offensive frameworks install with a single script or Compose file and have drawn more than 60,000 GitHub stars between them: ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Cairn, PentAGI, and HexStrike. All five have already turned up in intrusions rather than only in red team engagements. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant have observed ARTEX, Cairn, HexStrike, and PentAGI in incident response engagements, and Microsoft has attributed ARTEX use to Storm-0940. We traced an AI-assisted AWS intrusion to a CyberStrikeAI server in One CyberStrikeAI Server, Eight AWS Identities.

An agentic offensive framework puts a large language model (LLM) in charge of the scanners, curl, shells, and cloud CLIs that red teams and threat actors already use. The tools are familiar, but the loop around them is new: a model plans each step, splits the work across agents, builds or installs what it lacks, and in ARTEX’s case moves on in bursts of two to 25 seconds. We read the source of all five, alongside the public incident reporting, to work out what reaches a defender’s telemetry when one of them runs. None of them enforces authorization in code, and every action they take still has to land in telemetry you already collect.

Key takeaways

Agentic frameworks such as ARTEX work in bursts of seconds, so the detections trusted to start containment have to be chosen before an incident begins.

None of the five frameworks enforces authorization in code by default. Three assert it in the prompt, and the only target restrictions active by default are blocklists for government and education domains.

The frameworks are loud by default and, in ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI, change route when blocked. They also change faster than signatures, but their actions do not. Every action that touches your environment reaches defenders as a process, a web request, an API call, or a sign-in, so detections anchored on behavior outlast those anchored on a source address, a User-Agent, or a framework's fingerprint.

How agentic offensive frameworks differ from Traditional C2 Frameworks

Cobalt Strike and Brute Ratel C4 put a human operator behind an implant, deciding what to run next. Agentic frameworks keep the tools and replace the operator's think time with a planning loop. GTIG observed ARTEX execution bursts of roughly two to 25 seconds, while NorForge, tracking exposed Cairn panels it assessed as malicious, found that one actor cluster's successful projects took just under 23 hours on average from start to goal. Individual bursts fit within a short detection window, but operations can run for hours, so connecting bursts into one operation requires a long lookback.

The agents and most of the tooling usually run on infrastructure the attacker controls, calling a hosted or self-run model. What reaches your environment is what the tools do to it, recorded as new processes on your hosts, API calls in your cloud audit logs, and sign-ins.

ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Cairn, PentAGI and HexStrike compared

The five frameworks share the same loop but differ in where the model runs and what starts each tool.

Autonomy is the default. CyberStrikeAI ships with approval mode off, PentAGI's Compose file sets ASK_USER to false, Cairn launches two of its three coding-agent worker types with their approval prompts disabled, and ARTEX runs its agents in a bypass permission mode, so none of the four waits for human approval by default.

Beyond the shared loop, each framework makes a distinctive design choice.

ARTEX pairs an event-driven planner with parallel workers and keeps the human to a chat agent that observes progress and steers by hints. Its bundled browser extension records an operator's authenticated session, with captchas and one-time codes solved once, and hands those requests to the agents as evidence. We reviewed a public English-translated copy of the original repository.

CyberStrikeAI is a complete operator console. It builds its own implants, runs C2 listeners and a WebShell manager, and connects to chat platforms such as Telegram, Slack, Discord, and DingTalk.

Cairn delegates the work to existing coding agents. Its workers are command-line tools running inside Kali containers, and its README describes its debut in an AI penetration testing competition.

PentAGI keeps its agents moving with a reflector agent. When an agent hesitates or answers in prose instead of acting, the reflector replies in the user's voice, and the exchange is recorded as a human message.

HexStrike has no model of its own. It exposes about 150 tool functions through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to whatever AI assistant the operator already uses.

What each framework ships differs as well. CyberStrikeAI builds its own implants, and three of the five bundle cloud tooling, which puts cloud accounts within reach as readily as hosts.

What agentic offensive frameworks change for detection and response

Agentic attacks land effects in seconds

Within a burst, an agentic loop issues steps seconds apart, and each step takes effect as soon as it is sent. At that pace, the decisions that matter are made before an incident begins, starting with which detections are trusted to start containment automatically.

Do agentic offensive frameworks check authorization?

Like conventional offensive tools, none of the five frameworks enforces authorization in code by default. Three of them go further and tell the model it is authorized. CyberStrikeAI tells its model that authorization was settled in advance and that it should never question it or wait for approval, PentAGI opens nine of its role prompts with a pre-authorization block, and ARTEX describes each agent as part of an authorized penetration testing system. Cairn instructs its workers never to reject a task, and when a model refuses anyway, its dispatcher sidelines that worker for five seconds and hands the task to another configured worker, or retries the same one if it is the only worker.

The only target restrictions active by default are blocklists for government domains in ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI, and for education domains in ARTEX. Beyond those blocklists, the safeguards that ship are narrow:

ARTEX blocks destructive commands such as rm -rf and mkfs, and can check a task’s assets against an allow list the operator writes, which is empty by default. A shell command can still reach any host.

ARTEX’s rules-of-engagement scope mechanism was removed, its source notes and assets its workers record are added to the task’s scope automatically.

HexStrike accepts an out-of-scope list and never consults it.

ARTEX labels its own blocks as platform controls because a bare denial reads to an agent like a target's defense to bypass. A model provider's refusal is not a control defenders can rely on, because a framework can route around it, as Cairn's dispatcher can.

How agentic offensive frameworks respond when you block them

As shipped, the five frameworks default to capability, autonomy, and speed. Their scanners run with stock settings, several defaults name the framework outright, and CyberStrikeAI's implant checks in every five seconds with no jitter. Stealth ships as skills the model can load. CyberStrikeAI's operational security skill covers rate limits, IP-ban workarounds, and anti-forensics.

The change comes when ARTEX or CyberStrikeAI is blocked. ARTEX tells its workers that a filtered payload or a 404 does not exhaust an intent, and GTIG, relaying Wiz Research's findings on a campaign it tracks as UNC7228, reports that the actor fell back to open proxies when its initial infrastructure was blocked. CyberStrikeAI's skills tell the agent to answer a block by switching proxies, User-Agents, and forwarding headers, falling back to free proxies in the target's own country and then Tor. After a block, expect the same requests to return from new addresses and User-Agents, so detections that key on what is requested hold up better than those keyed on source address. A block on the source address leaves the framework's access in place, so it should be paired with revoking the credentials the framework was using.

Why IOC-based detections go stale on agentic frameworks

Agentic offensive frameworks move quickly. ARTEX's developers logged about 390 commits, more than 450 counting merges, in the ten and a half weeks from July 26 to October 7, 2026, and after its creator took the original repository down in October 2026, public forks carried it on. CyberStrikeAI logged more than 2,400 commits in its first year, and several of the frameworks write or install new tools in the middle of a task. The strings, file names, and defaults that identify a framework today can disappear in its next release, while the behaviors it depends on, such as credential access, remote execution, and offensive tools started by a service, stay the same, so detections anchored on behavior age more slowly than those anchored on a framework's fingerprint.

Why revoking credentials does not stop an agent immediately

AWS and Google each document a propagation delay for access changes, and in Entra ID an access token issued before a user or service principal is deleted or disabled generally stays valid until it expires, typically 60 to 90 minutes, unless the resource and client support continuous access evaluation, which Microsoft documents for Exchange, Teams, and SharePoint and, for service principals, only Microsoft Graph. An acknowledged revocation may not stop the next request, and an agent operating at machine speed can act within that gap. AWS's role-session revocation also leaves IAM users' long-term keys alone and does not block sessions requested after its cutoff, so pair it with removing whatever can still assume the role.

How to detect agentic offensive frameworks

Detecting agentic tempo and sequence per identity

Behavioral rules are the foundation, and the reach of the tooling sets how broad they need to be. GTIG's catalog of ARTEX tradecraft includes SQL injection, Kerberoasting, and mapping of Azure and AWS permissions. Agentic tempo adds two signals that emerge between individual events.

Tempo per identity. Count distinct sensitive actions per identity and issuing role in short windows, so a burst stands out even when every action in it is routine.

Sequence across sessions. Join discovery, secret access, and remote execution under the issuing role or source address to link activity from several sessions into one operation.

Higher-order detection rules apply the same logic to alerts, correlating related alerts that share a host, user, or address into a higher-confidence finding, because each added signal makes a benign explanation less likely. We expect more signals like these to emerge as the frameworks change.

An ES|QL hunt for tool-family bursts

A loop works through its toolbox as the task demands, so one source address can use curl, a Python client, a browser User-Agent, and an AWS client within the same minute. The ES|QL hunt below normalizes User-Agents into tool families, counts families and requests per source address in one-minute windows, and returns windows with at least three families and a burst of requests. Because the loop runs on infrastructure the attacker controls, the hunt reads the logs that record its requests, such as web server, proxy, and cloud audit logs (point the index pattern at those sources), and it excludes private, loopback, link-local, carrier-grade NAT, and multicast source ranges.

Build systems, monitoring scripts, administrators working from the AWS CLI, and shared NAT or proxy addresses can also mix these clients, so baseline that automation and tune the thresholds of three families and 20 requests per minute before alerting on the results. The hunt keys on how many kinds of client one address uses in a minute, so it does not depend on any single string, but a framework that returns from a new address starts a new window. The family list can also take the framework User-Agents in the table below, and norma* already covers the norma/0.4 that ARTEX's web fetch tool sends.

What to watch for in ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Cairn, PentAGI and HexStrike

These defaults appear on the systems under attack and, where noted, on a host you monitor. They are worth hunting for today, though any of them can change in the next release.

Framework

What to watch for

ARTEX

Traffic from the scanners it ships, such as nuclei, httpx, katana, ffuf, and sqlmap, which three parallel workers per task run by default, requests with the User-Agent artex-enrich/1.0 or norma/0.4, and new accounts registered on your applications followed by sign-ins from several sessions, because its agents register and share their own test accounts.

CyberStrikeAI

Webshell requests that carry the User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; CyberStrikeAI-WebShell/1.0) and a pass form field, a web server process running echo :OSPROBE_%OS%:END, and implant persistence named SystemUpdate (a scheduled task or Run key) or com.apple.systemupdate (a LaunchAgent), a .bashrc line ending in # cs, or an @reboot cron entry that launches the implant binary and carries no marker of its own.

Cairn

Reverse shells and out-of-band callbacks to the operator host's own address, because its example configuration runs worker containers on the host's network. Where it runs on a host you monitor, two of its three worker adapters start their coding-agent command-line tools with approval prompts disabled and the full task prompt in the command line.

PentAGI

Connections from compromised hosts to TCP ports 28000 to 29999 on the PentAGI host (two per engagement by default), and each page it browses requested twice at once, once for content and once for a screenshot. An installation on your network also reports to update.pentagi.com every three hours.

HexStrike

The User-Agents HexStrike-HTTP-Framework/1.0 and HexStrike-BrowserAgent/1.0 and, when the browser agent's active tests run, the cross-site scripting marker <hexstrikeXSSTest123>. Where it runs on a host you monitor, a Python server listens on port 8888 by default on all interfaces and starts security tools through a shell, so a tool can show the Python server as its parent.

Beyond these defaults, the scanners run with stock settings, so on the network the frameworks largely resemble the tools they drive.

How to defend against agentic offensive frameworks

Decide in advance which high-confidence detections start containment. Connect them to automated response actions on endpoints and to Elastic Workflows to orchestrate the response, including calls to your own automation for cloud steps such as deactivating an access key or revoking a role's active sessions.

Combine any block on a source address with revoking the identity's sessions and tokens, because these frameworks return from new addresses, then confirm that the next request fails.

Measure tempo and sequence per identity over windows long enough to connect bursts, and baseline the automation that already behaves like an agent.

Scope assumed roles and app-only identities to the actions they need, because an agent inherits everything the identity allows.

Remove secrets from the places an agent can read, such as file shares, wikis, code repositories, and CI/CD variables, rotate any that were exposed, and prefer short-lived credentials. GTIG reports that operators hand ARTEX compromised credentials and that it harvests more through Kerberoasting, SQL injection, and DCSync, so each exposed secret lets an operation reach another platform and makes containment harder.

Act on threat intelligence about framework infrastructure. GTIG reports ARTEX and PentAGI used against multiple organizations, and exposed consoles such as Cairn's can be enumerated from the internet, so intelligence on their infrastructure is an early chance to block an intrusion. Block those addresses at the perimeter or proxy, and feed the same intelligence into Elastic's threat intelligence integrations so the prebuilt Threat Intel IP Address Indicator Match rule flags traffic to and from known consoles and C2 servers. Build an enrichment workflow, triggered by the alert, that runs a reputation lookup on the matched address. Consoles can sit behind shared hosting or CDN addresses, so the lookup helps separate a dedicated server from a shared address before a match drives a block, and behavioral detections still cover the infrastructure that changes.

Open questions about agentic offensive frameworks

These are worth answering now, before the next releases change the answers.

What changes when the agent extends itself? ARTEX's operator assistant can create new tools, MCP servers, and skills, and PentAGI keeps the code it writes in a store shared across engagements. A tool written for one target has no history to match, which favors detections on behavior and parentage over tool names.

Is the advantage pace or adaptation? Scripts can match an agent's pace, so the more meaningful test is how quickly a new finding or an unfamiliar error becomes a new action.

How many actors is a multi-agent run? ARTEX runs a planner and parallel workers under one task. Several sessions or agent names can look like several actors, but the identity and controller behind them is the unit that matters.

Conclusion: What this means for detection and response

Agentic offensive frameworks amount to a new kind of operator, a loop that plans, coordinates agents, extends its own tools, and moves at a tempo that changes what detection and response have to do. None of the five enforces authorization in code by default, which leaves defender telemetry and controls as the real boundary.

This analysis covers five frameworks, and more deserve tracking. Gambit Security reported a criminal campaign that used Strix for vulnerability discovery, Cairn for exploitation, and the general-purpose agent Hermes as its control console. Other open-source projects that use models for penetration testing include Shannon, PentestGPT, CAI (now archived), CyberStrike (not CyberStrikeAI), RedAmon, PentestAgent, hackingBuddyGPT, Nebula, and BugTraceAI. New ones will keep appearing, so track each by how it plans, what starts its tools, and what it leaves for defenders to see.

Elastic's behavioral rules key on the actions these frameworks take, such as credential access and remote execution, rather than on the framework or the model, and LLM-based triage rules can roll related alerts on one user or host into a single verdict. Elastic keeps adding AI-focused protections, and its rules are published in the open detection-rules and protections-artifacts repositories. Add tempo and sequence analysis per identity, confirm that revocation took effect, and contain through automated response actions and Elastic Workflows, so the response is decided before the operation starts.

One server read 56 EC2 user data scripts in 141 milliseconds. Then it went quiet for 14 days and came back. That gap did more damage than the burst, because fixed correlation windows cannot span two weeks.

Between September 30 and October 16, 2026, a CyberStrikeAI server worked through stolen AWS credentials in a familiar sequence: validate identities, harvest secrets from Secrets Manager, pull EC2 user data, decrypt an SSM parameter, send a remote command. Every one of those is a call a legitimate role makes every day. Nothing in CloudTrail looked urgent at the time.

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source platform that pairs LLM agents with offensive security tools. Will Thomas at Team Cymru counted 21 IPs running it in early 2026, all of them aimed at Fortinet edge devices. This is the first case we have seen of the same tooling turned on AWS.

We call this AI-assisted on the strength of the tool attribution and the machine-speed behavior in the logs. We cannot prove an LLM agent was making the decisions, and we do not know how the attacker obtained the credentials.

Key findings from the CyberStrikeAI AWS intrusion

Between Sep 30 and Oct 16, 2026, one CyberStrikeAI server (43[.]240[.]29[.]11) used credentials from eight AWS identities (five IAM users and three EC2 instance roles) across four accounts and generated 78 alerts.

app-role sent 56 user data requests in 141 milliseconds, part of 58 user data retrieval alerts (74% of the total), which points to automated tooling.

On Oct 2, container-role read an encrypted SSM parameter and issued an SSM SendCommand 29 seconds later. The audit log does not show what the command was or whether it succeeded.

43[.]240[.]29[.]28 and 43[.]240[.]29[.]33 serve a CyberStrikeAI page on port 8080 with the same self-signed certificate as 43[.]240[.]29[.]11, which ties the three servers together. As of November, none of the three is serving that interface, so treat the IPs as indicators for retrospective hunting.

All 78 alerts were medium or low severity and only made sense once correlated by source IP.

AI-assisted offense is often sporadic and fast, especially with compromised identities. Elastic Workflows can enable responders by making API calls to AWS services such as IAM to block the identity automatically.

How to respond if your AWS identities were exposed

Assume anything an affected role could read is compromised, and work outward from the credentials.

Rotate credentials for every identity that touched the indicator IP, and revoke active sessions, including those from temporary credentials.

For instance roles, rotate by replacing the instance profile or the instance, since stolen role credentials expire but can be reissued while the host stays compromised.

Treat all secrets in EC2 user data as exposed, and move them to the Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.

Review SSM command history for the window of any unexpected SendCommand call to see what ran. Check for abuse of AWS-managed documents, AWS-RunShellScript and AWS-RunPowerShellScript or custom documents.

Check non-production roles and secrets for overlap with production.

Block the indicator IP at the WAF, VPC, NaCL and security group level, but rely on the behavioral detections, since the infrastructure can change and network blockage is not effective at stolen credentials to API calls prevention.

Restrict ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute for userData to the roles that need it, using IAM policy or a service control policy.

Enable GuardDuty if it isn't already, and alert on credentials used from outside your expected IP ranges.

Hunt for how the instance credentials were obtained, starting with exposed web applications, SSRF, code repositories and IMDS.

Conclusion: What this intrusion means for alert correlation

AI-assisted attacks are driven by objectives, so they generate a lot of alerts. One CyberStrikeAI server produced 78 alerts across six rules in 16 days, and 65 of them came on the first day. Every alert was medium or low severity, and each one looked routine on its own: a first-time GetCallerIdentity, a GetSessionToken, an SSM SendCommand from a rare user. Only the shared source IP showed they belonged to one intrusion.

Defenders need high-signal detections to stop the damage early; low false positive behavior rules, such as the two bulk enumeration rules described above, that justify acting immediately. Medium and low severity alerts are good candidates for correlation, but only by source IP, and the correlation window needs to be flexible because AI-assisted activity is irregular. Here, 56 requests landed in 141 milliseconds, later steps came hours to days apart, and the operator returned after 14 days. A short fixed window would have split this intrusion into unrelated alerts.

High-signal detections can also drive remediation. Attached to a workflow, such as those in the Elastic Workflows library, a rule like this can disrupt the attack automatically, for example by blocking the source IP, while analysts investigate.

Title: New Mior and Skyfall Attacks Let Rogue Cloud Hosts Steal Secrets From AMD SEV-SNP VMs
Context: Two attacks made public this week allow a malicious host to read data inside AMD SEV-SNP-protected virtual machines (VMs), which are built to keep the server's operator out
Full Text:
Two attacks made public this week allow a malicious host to read data inside AMD SEV-SNP-protected virtual machines (VMs), which are built to keep the server's operator out.

One of them, Mior, can also modify a VM's memory and fake the signed report confirming which software it runs. Both need control of the server's hypervisor, and Mior also needs control of the server's BIOS. Researchers showed both in lab tests on AMD EPYC server processors.

AMD, which makes the processors, lists SEV firmware for Mior and microcode for Skyfall, both dated August 12. It plans to give server makers platform firmware in November for Skyfall and in December for Mior, and fixes for embedded chips later. Customers are told to get the BIOS update from their server maker.

SEV-SNP brings confidential computing to AMD EPYC server processors. It uses hardware-enforced memory encryption and access control to protect a VM, even from the host's hypervisor.

The ETH Zurich team behind Mior attacked SEV-SNP while it was starting up. During start-up, a security co-processor on the chip, the Platform Security Processor (PSP), fills in a table called the Reverse Map Table (RMP). The RMP records who owns each page of memory and what they may do with it.

The team redirected the PSP's writes to the memory of a graphics card it controlled, instead of to main memory. The team used a card because it believes the PSP reads the values back to check them, and the card could return them. Start-up then finished without errors, but part of the real RMP, including the entry that protects the table itself, stayed uninitialized.

That let the hypervisor rewrite the RMP's protections. The team then enabled debugging on a confidential VM that had it disabled and used the PSP's own debug commands to read and write the VM's memory. This worked in all 1,000 attempts across both test runs.

SEV-SNP also measures a VM's software image when the VM starts, and the PSP signs attestation reports that include this measurement. In a second test, the team copied a harmless VM's measurement into a malicious VM, so the malicious VM's attestation reports described the harmless image instead.

The attack needs control of the hypervisor and the BIOS (also called UEFI), plus a PCIe device such as a graphics card, the Mior paper says. For the tests, the team modified the BIOS to leave the chip's memory-routing settings unlocked.

"We operate in AMD’s threat model defined for SEV-SNP. AMD explicitly distrusts the UEFI, thus an attacker can modify the UEFI," the researchers say.

Ordinary VMs already trust their host and its firmware, so Mior gives an attacker nothing new against them, the team says.

The team ran Mior on one EPYC 9135, a Zen 5 chip. It considers Zen 3 and Zen 4 chips potentially affected but did not test them because it had no setup that allowed it to change their BIOS.

The debugging and attestation tests both worked with ciphertext hiding turned on. That optional SEV-SNP feature stops the hypervisor from even reading encrypted VM memory.

Two earlier attacks by some of the same researchers, the Fabricked attack and the RMPocalypse attack, also corrupted the RMP as SEV-SNP started up. Mior is a separate flaw, unrelated to Fabricked and to the fix for it, the team says. It also worked on older firmware from before that fix.

Skyfall comes from a team at ETH Zurich and Google. It builds on Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA), a group of flaws in AMD processors that can leak data through instruction timing. TSA was first disclosed on July 8, 2025.

The team found that when a hypervisor intentionally causes a VM to fail to start, the processor has already cached part of the VM's saved state. That data is left behind without the usual cleanup, and the hypervisor can read it through TSA.

This way, the team recovered a VM's saved register values and a disk-encryption key from a test VM. For the key, it changed the VM's kernel to pause at the moment the key sat in registers. In a real attack, the team says, a hypervisor can instead use a technique called SEV-Step to step through the VM until the key reaches the registers.

Skyfall can also read VM memory, but only three fixed cache lines in a page it targets, at offsets 0x0c0, 0x380 and 0x3c0. The rest of the page stays out of reach.

The attack needs a malicious host or hypervisor, but no tampering with the hardware. The team tested it on an EPYC 7313, a Zen 3 chip, and on EPYC 9124 and 9334 chips, which are Zen 4. It did not show the leak on Zen 5 chips.

Beyond VMs, the Skyfall team read decrypted microcode updates on all three test chips. It also recovered register values stored in System Management Mode (SMM) memory, which even the operating system kernel normally cannot read. Both of these attacks need privileged software on the machine.

The program committee of the IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, which accepted the Skyfall paper, said it overlooks what a realistic attack on VMs would need. That includes a processor core free of other activity, failing VM starts and performance-counter reads at high speed, and a VM that does not crash or time out during the attack.

Affected Processors and Fixes

AMD tracks Mior as CVE-2026-0462 and rates it 5.9 on the CVSS 4.0 scale in a security advisory. It tracks Skyfall's VM leak as CVE-2026-40671, rated 4.9, in a second advisory that describes the flaw as exposing VM register data.

For Mior, the company lists only SEV-SNP as affected, not the earlier SEV and SEV-ES versions.

It lists the same five EPYC server lines for both flaws, with these fixes:

The two advisories give the same TurinPI_1.0.0.C package different target months. Microcode for Skyfall is dated August 12 for each of these lines. The Instinct MI300A accelerator has a Skyfall patch dated September 21, and fixes for embedded EPYC models are due between January and April 2027.

The Mior team says updated firmware that mitigates the flaw is already out, and the Skyfall team says new microcode has been released. The advisories do not say whether those updates work on their own or only as part of the BIOS updates, and they list no workaround.

Supermicro, a server maker, has published a BIOS fix list covering flaws in dozens of its H12, H13, and H14 motherboards. The same pages say the boards also need a BMC firmware update and that the company is still testing affected products.

Because the fixes are implemented in the host's firmware, customers who rent confidential VMs depend on their cloud provider to install them. The advisory covering Mior also lists TCB (trusted computing base) values for SNP attestation next to each fixed firmware version. It does not say how VM owners should check them.

Neither advisory says whether the flaws have been used in attacks. Both teams have published code, and the Mior proof-of-concept code needs a BIOS patched to leave the memory-routing settings unlocked.

The EDK II project assigned Skyfall's SMM leak CVE-2026-18448 and rates it 5.6. AMD's EDK II bulletin traces it to missing TSA mitigations in EDK II firmware code.

The bulletin lists EPYC and Ryzen chips, including embedded models, and recommends the company's earlier TSA mitigations plus an EDK II patch when one is available.

For the five EPYC server lines listed above, the bulletin lists only that patch, due in November. Platform firmware with the fix is already available for other chips, including the EPYC 4004 and 4005 models. The EDK II project's own advisory lists no patched version as of today.
