A real cloud platform doesn’t always fit this matrix. A service can run in a separate virtual machine, in a pod in a shared cluster, or in a microVM. A hypervisor belongs to the Underlay, but its management API may be reachable from the Overlay. That’s why the layer a pentester is currently on (External, Overlay, or Underlay) depends not just on the IP address but on four attributes taken together:

Who controls the cloud infrastructure component.

Whose data and resources the component serves.

Which IAM service account is used for interaction.

How far its privileges extend.

Where the trust boundaries lie

When analyzing the network that supports a cloud’s internal infrastructure, it’s easy to wrongly assume there is only one trust boundary, between the tenant and the provider. But reaching the provider’s internal network may be only the first step. A real platform contains many zones with different trust levels, and compromising one component doesn’t necessarily give access to the whole infrastructure. For example, a user request may pass in sequence through the customer interface (the management console), then the tenant plane (a database), then the service runtime (the virtual machine that the database runs on), then the service management plane (an internal service that monitors database health), then the cloud control plane (an internal service that manages database resources). Only after that does it finally reach the infrastructure layer.

Each transition changes the trust zone, but it doesn’t necessarily mean reaching a new subnet or obtaining root privileges. It’s like passing through turnstiles inside the same building. We haven’t left the building (a new subnet) or gotten keys to every door (root privileges), but at each checkpoint we have our badge checked again, because different security rules apply on the other side. Sometimes the boundary lies between two roles in the same process, sometimes between an API and a worker, and sometimes between a guest virtual machine and a hypervisor. At the boundary between an API and a worker, a vulnerability can arise from differences in data handling. For example, an internal cloud API accepts a string containing a null byte (\x00) from a user, considers it valid, and passes it on. A background worker then blindly trusts this data and inserts it into a low-level query to a PostgreSQL database. In C libraries, \x00 terminates a string. As a result, the database handler truncates the text at the point where this byte was injected. This breaks the logic of the SQL query or permission check and resets the regular user’s context. The system is then forced to change the password of the main administrator (postgres), which leads to full database takeover.

Example 1. Strict isolation (managed database)

A customer rents a managed database in their tenant. The tenant is allowed to run SQL queries but not allowed to connect to the operating system the database runs on. Here, the trust boundary lies between the permissions of a database role and the runtime environment of the database process. If, through the permitted SQL queries, the pentester manages to reach code execution at the operating system level as the service process, the pentester gains full access to the host’s resources. This lets them do more than just collect information. They can actively interact with the host: read and modify files, analyze running processes, establish network connections to internal services, and extract credentials (for example, an IAM service account token) to attack other cloud components.

Example 2. Legitimate access (managed virtual machine)

In another implementation, the provider supports SSH key authentication by design, and the user connects to the resource like to any other virtual machine. Formally, the product is still called a “managed database”, but the actual trust boundary shifts deeper, to the level where the guest OS interacts with the host infrastructure. In this case, SSH access to the operating system is not a violation in itself, because the service model allows it. What we need to test is the next boundary, the one between the service virtual machine and the management agents, metadata, host, or control plane.

This leads to several practical rules:

Normal execution of user code does not, by itself, prove an isolation breach. In IT services such as interactive notebooks, continuous integration (CI) runners, or serverless systems, code execution is a product feature.

Gaining maximum privileges inside a pod does not mean gaining maximum privileges on the node. After crossing each trust boundary (for example, into a zone with different privileges or service accounts), you need to re-check what’s visible: processes, mount points, interfaces, devices, and IAM service accounts.

An IAM service account token that a researcher finds is not necessarily useful. What matters is who issued it and which systems accept it. The tenant or service the token is bound to, and the actions it permits there, also matter.

The fact that a tenant container can reach a provider’s internal IP address does not mean a compromise has occurred. In many clouds, some internal services are reachable over the network by design. For a real compromise, an attacker must either steal a service token or find an internal service that mistakenly accepts customer accounts or requires no authentication.

Remote code execution inside the environment where a service runs does not mean access to the control plane. This is only the initial zone, from which the researcher must look for the next trust boundary: service tokens, the provider’s internal APIs, and neighboring containers.

To tell a real trust boundary violation from a false positive, we use four sequential stages from the researcher’s perspective:

Network visibility. The researcher can see the provider’s internal service from the tenant plane. This is not a breach yet, but it is the first sign that isolation may be insufficient.

The researcher manages to authenticate to a service by presenting a token or certificate compromised at the previous step (for example, a service account token or a metadata token). This is serious, because the service treats the request as legitimate.

The target object grants specific permissions to the current context. This is not yet the execution of dangerous operations, but only a check that they are allowed.

Controlled action beyond the original trust boundary. The researcher performs the minimum safe action that confirms the previously obtained permissions work in practice. For example, they create a test record in a neighboring tenant (usually a second test tenant).

The first two stages only produce a hypothesis that the trust boundary has been violated. The object is visible on the network and accepts requests, but that does not mean the researcher can change anything in it. Confirmed impact appears only in the last two stages, when the researcher obtains authorization and performs a controlled action beyond the original boundary. For example, network reachability of a neighboring database indicates insufficient network isolation, but cross-tenant impact appears only when the researcher can use the original context to perform an action on another tenant’s resource that the cloud model doesn’t allow, such as reading data. To keep the test ethical, the researcher demonstrates such reading only between their own test accounts, so real users’ data stays confidential.

Attacker model and three research goals

Dividing the cloud infrastructure into three layers (External, Overlay, and Underlay) helps define the attacker model for each layer. In penetration testing, the researcher can focus on one layer and look for every possible way to violate the nearest trust boundary. Another approach is to build a full attack chain across all layers. The attacker model also defines the starting point: the access level and position from which the pentest begins. Below is a general list of attacker models that apply to most cloud infrastructures:

External attacker without an account. The test covers the public attack surface, registration, the login mechanism, externally accessible services, and the path to the first tenant context. Layer: External.

Attacker with legitimate tenant access. This is the key model for a multi-tenant cloud: the tenant is entitled to create their own resources and tries to go beyond the limits those resources impose. Layer: External.

Internal attacker with a compromised runtime. The starting point is a compromised process, pod, or virtual machine. This scenario is especially relevant for supply chain attacks. The researcher explores options for lateral movement in the network and host environment. Layer: Overlay or Underlay.

Internal attacker with a compromised IAM service account token or an operator account. This model involves testing IAM and the cloud platform management processes. Layer: Overlay or Underlay.

Regardless of the attacker model and the initial entry point, the research goals at the initial stage fall into three groups.

1. Code execution first

The goal of this approach is to execute arbitrary code inside a provider-managed environment. To do this, a pentester can attack a managed database, serverless function, CI/CD workload, PaaS application, tenant virtual machine, container, or virtual network gateway.

Example of an attack chain through a managed service The pentester interacts with the managed service interface and finds a vulnerability in it (for example, CVE-2026-19478 in the case of the GitLab web interface) or in add-on modules deployed by the cloud provider. The vulnerability allows the researcher to execute code remotely inside the runtime (operating system), find an IAM service account, and use it to gain access to the resource management service. The researcher can then look for vulnerabilities in that service and penetrate the provider overlay.

Example of an attack chain through a virtual environment The chain begins with the compromise of a tenant workload. The researcher plants malicious code in a popular OS or container image in advance. A cloud tenant downloads and runs the trojanized image, and the attacker gains access inside that specific container. Next, the attacker finds ways to escape the container (using CVE-2026-43284) into the runtime: the container runtime, hypervisor, or host agent. From there, they reach the host shared with other containers and can affect the provider’s management components.

2. Credentials first

Rather than gaining access to a runtime environment, the researcher may obtain credentials that cloud services accept as valid: a service account token, metadata access credentials, an mTLS certificate, a bootstrap token, or an object storage key.

In this scenario, the move into the provider overlay doesn’t come from breaking network isolation. It happens through legitimate platform functionality. The network may be well segmented, but an over-privileged IAM service account token that the attacker manages to extract (for example, from environment variables or metadata) can legitimately call an internal API through a standard gateway or token exchange service.

3. Administrative or service context

The goal of this scenario is to bypass technical restrictions by gaining legitimate access through channels intended for staff. The route often starts with targeting people (phishing, insiders, or leaked employee or contractor credentials). However, the final entry point into the internal environment is technical: a connection through the operator’s VPN, a support portal, a remote support tool, an administrative workstation, an SSH certificate, or a serial console. Although the route often starts with compromising a person, the resulting initial zone (the technical context with certain privileges and access to resources where the researcher ends up) can match the first scenario. For example, access to a managed database host (DBaaS host) can be obtained not by exploiting a vulnerability but through a legitimate administrative channel, which is then used for privilege escalation.

Sorting out the architectural zoo

After moving deeper into the cloud infrastructure and gaining access to a node, the pentester analyzes local artifacts. Completely different architectures can hide behind the same managed service.

OpenStack-like infrastructure

IaaS services based on OpenStack usually include a large set of components: an IAM service account, compute resources, networking, images and block storage, as well as API processes, workers, a message broker, and platform state databases. A managed service built on top of such an IaaS layer can use a separate virtual machine for each database instance, several instances on a shared virtual machine, a Kubernetes cluster on virtual workers, or even a dedicated tenant for a specific product.

A message broker such as RabbitMQ is typical for OpenStack, but finding one doesn’t prove that the target is a stock OpenStack deployment. The provider may have changed the trust model, added its own API, and replaced some of the components.

Kubernetes-based platforms

In clouds of this type, a central Kubernetes cluster controls the entire infrastructure: not only containers but also virtual machines, other tenant Kubernetes clusters, and managed services. At the service runtime level, a product can run as a pod in a shared namespace, an application inside a tenant, a KubeVirt virtual machine, or a worker node of a separate cluster. From the outside, they all look like the same product, but their trust boundaries and the attack surface behind them differ radically.

Because the platform is managed through a Kubernetes cluster, where the service account token is the main unit of authorization, it’s especially important to determine where the IAM service account you obtained during the pentest lives: in a tenant cluster, in a managed cluster, or with an operator that serves multiple tenants. Identical-looking tokens may have permissions for only one pod, or they may allow changing resources in several environments at once.

Custom control plane and configuration management systems

A provider may forgo off-the-shelf platforms altogether. For example, in this kind of architecture, a provider might build its public API in-house, deploy virtual machines through libvirt or a lightweight IaaS layer, automate networking with scripts around Open vSwitch (OVS), build object storage on Ceph, and distribute node configuration through SaltStack or another configuration management system.

In this architecture, a virtual machine management service might get its settings from an internal HTTP service, a script with shared credentials might run backups, billing might receive events from a queue, and an internal agent might talk to the control plane over mTLS. Almost every component here is specific to the provider. The main risk area is not vulnerabilities in well-known products, such as those built on open-source solutions, but logic errors at the junctions between internal systems.

Mixed-stack platform

In practice, the most common setup is a mix of approaches

The infrastructure core (IaaS layer) is built on OpenStack

Kubernetes runs the managed services

The storage system runs on Ceph

IAM, billing systems, and the internal API are custom-built.

Here are some clues that can help form initial hypotheses about the environment:

A Kubernetes token and cluster DNS in the runtime environment of the host under investigation suggest that the service is running in the context of a pod.

A running qemu-guest-agent process indicates that we are inside a virtual machine rather than on a physical server.

Attached Ceph/RBD volumes point to a separate storage plane in the platform architecture, implemented as distributed block storage.

A large number of CNI or Open vSwitch (OVS) network interfaces means that this is a shared Kubernetes node

However, any such clue needs additional verification tests.

Example of a mixed-stack cloud platform

How to choose the next trust boundary

After the pentester has examined the initial zone, the next route depends on a combination of two factors:

Network visibility: which segments, services, and tenants are reachable.

Available trust level: which credentials, certificates, and API methods are accepted as valid in those segments.

Sometimes the network has almost no restrictions, but all services require correct mTLS authentication. In other cases, the network is almost completely closed, but a discovered service account can create resources across the entire region through the standard API. Title: Maersk Reveals Data Breach as Extortion Group Demands $5m
Context: The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect...
Full Text:
Maersk has disclosed a data breach involving one of its IT systems after an extortion group claimed to have stolen 100GB of logistics-related data from the company.

The shipping and logistics giant said in a November 11 statement that it “identified unauthorized access and data extraction,” although it didn’t clarify when.

The incident affected one of its “local legacy systems from a previous acquisition,” it claimed.

“Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI [electronic data interchange],” the statement continued.

“We do not anticipate disruption to operations for customers at this time, and customers can continue to use Maersk platforms to book and manage their shipments as usual.”

Read more on Maersk: Cybersecurity Lessons from Maersk’s Former CISO

Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of BreachLock, explained that ownership of acquired systems often gets muddled during M&A activity, and pen tests should be carried out during due diligence to highlight any potential weaknesses.

“Acquired systems arrive with their own credentials, their own patch schedule, and connections into the parent network that were set up during integration and rarely revisited,” he added.

Darin Fredde, senior director and offensive security evangelist at Ridge Security, said that investigators must determine what the attackers accessed, how they gained entry, and whether the boundaries separating that legacy environment from other systems held.

“The lesson for organizations isn't simply to replace every legacy system,” he argued. “It's to know what you own, understand how inherited systems connect to the business, and continuously validate that the security controls protecting them work.”

WhiteArmor Ramps Up Attacks

A relatively new extortion group known as WhiteArmor claimed responsibility for the attack, according to screenshots of its leak site posted to X.

The group demanded $5m in Bitcoin, claiming it has 100GB of data linked to Maersk’s OCF/LF logistics platform, including driver records and plaintext passwords, staff accounts, delivery receipts, purchase orders, inventory rows, and mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses and IMEIs.

WhiteArmor is behind a string of extortion demands ranging from $140,000 to $20m over the past month, according to Nick Harris, CISO at cyber-insurance specialist Assured.

Citing publicly available information on the attacks, he noted that several were aimed at the logistics sector, with victims including J.B. Hunt, Ryder, and Echo Global Logistics.

“The group describes itself as focused on data-theft extortion, intending to expand into ransomware, and says its encryptor is nearly complete,” Harris said.

“The protections include cycling credentials, strong access controls, data loss alerts and validating third parties. If they aim to recruit insiders, treat security as “assumed compromise” and set controls and alerts accordingly.

Maersk hasn’t experienced a serious cyber incident since the NotPetya campaign in 2017, which it claimed at the time may have cost the firm as much as $300m.

Title: Can Agentic AI Investigate a Phishing Campaign? Evidence Walkthrough
Context: They make a good test case because the attack never needed a phishing email, so an inbox-only investigation would have missed most of it
Full Text:
Yes, with a human signing off.

An agentic AI can run most of a phishing investigation on its own. It can pull domain registration records, open the lure safely, pivot to related infrastructure, extract indicators and write up a verdict with the evidence attached. What it shouldn't do yet is act on that verdict unchecked, because attackers are already hiding instructions inside phishing emails meant for the AI doing the reading.

The evidence for both halves of that answer is now public. Microsoft's randomized trial of 167 security analysts found that its phishing triage agent made them faster and more accurate. Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that one phishing email can carry a lure for the human and a hidden prompt for the AI in the same message.

This post walks through what an agentic investigation of a real phishing campaign looks like, evidence item by evidence item, using the lookalike Microsoft Teams domains that researcher Steven Lim exposed in October. Then it covers where agents break, and what to ask before you trust one.

What is an agentic AI security investigation?

An agentic AI security investigation is one where an AI agent plans and runs the investigation itself. It decides which data sources to query, calls the tools, reads what comes back, chooses the next step and stops when it can support a verdict with evidence a human can check. The phrase "agentic AI security" also gets used for protecting AI agents from attack. This post is about the other direction: agents doing the investigating.

The difference from older automation is who picks the next step. A SOAR playbook runs the same steps every time. A chat assistant answers the question an analyst types. An agent sets its own path based on what it finds, which is exactly what makes it useful and exactly what makes it attackable.

SOAR playbook

AI chat assistant

AI investigation agent

Who picks the next step

The playbook author, in advance

The analyst, one prompt at a time

The agent, based on each result

What it produces

Enrichment fields and tickets

Answers and summaries

A verdict with an evidence trail

Typical failure

Breaks on anything off-script

Only as good as the questions asked

Can be steered by content it reads

What the evidence says so far

The best public data comes from Microsoft. In November 2025, Microsoft economist James Bono published a randomized controlled trial of the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent. Microsoft recruited 167 professional security analysts and split them into groups that triaged a 25-email queue of real, privacy-vetted user-reported emails, 20% of them malicious, with or without the agent.

Analysts working with the agent found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute and were up to 77% more accurate, measured by F1 score. They also spent 53% more time on the malicious emails. The paper found no sign they simply rubber-stamped the agent's calls.

Read the fine print before quoting those numbers in a budget meeting. Microsoft studied its own product. On the test corpus, the agent's precision and recall were both 100%, which no production deployment should expect, and the paper's own scenario with a less accurate agent and more malicious mail cut the accuracy gain to 48%. The trial also measured triage: one reported email, one verdict. Investigating a campaign means connecting dozens of artifacts across days, and no comparable trial covers that yet.

The skeptical data point comes from Gartner. In June 2025, Gartner predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 over costs, unclear value or weak risk controls. It estimated that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI offer real agentic capabilities, calling the rest "agent washing."

Put together: agents have measurable value on narrow, high-volume phishing work, and plenty of products wearing the label won't deliver it. The way to tell them apart is to watch one work a real case.

Evidence walkthrough: investigating the fake Teams portals

In October 2026, Microsoft Security MVP Steven Lim posted a series of lookalike Microsoft Teams domains on LinkedIn, with screenshots. They make a good test case because the attack never needed a phishing email, so an inbox-only investigation would have missed most of it.

Below is the evidence chain an investigation agent should build from that same starting point, one step at a time. It reconstructs the work from the artifacts Lim made public; it is not output from a specific product run. Each step names what the agent does, what it collects and where a human should check.

Step 1: Enrich the seed domain

The seed is teams-online[.]com. The agent pulls registration data and reputation in parallel. Lim's screenshot gives the answers: registered Oct. 4, 2026, through a privacy service attached to the registrar Global Domain Group, and no active verdict in Microsoft Defender threat intelligence.

A lazy agent stops here and calls the domain clean. A good one treats "no verdict" on a four-day-old domain as missing data, not a pass, and weighs what it does know: brand name in the domain, days old, owner hidden.

Human check: none yet. This is enrichment, and it's cheap to be wrong here.

Step 2: Render the page safely and compare it to the real thing

The agent opens the URL in an isolated browser and captures a screenshot, the page source and the assets it loads. The page is a near-copy of the Teams pre-join screen: camera preview, audio options, a "Meeting with the Design team" heading, Sign in and Need help links.

The evidence that matters is the comparison. The agent should record which brand assets appear, how closely the layout matches the real join page and whether the page asks for anything (a name, credentials, a download).

Human check: confirm the brand match. Visual similarity scoring can flag a legitimate partner page that embeds a Teams meeting.

Step 3: Pivot to sibling infrastructure

One domain is an incident. Several are a campaign. The agent searches for domains that share traits with the seed: the "teams-" plus generic-word naming pattern, the registrar, hosting, TLS certificates and page templates.

Lim's later posts surface two siblings. teams-livemeeting[.]com shared the registrar Global Domain Group, was about 15 days old and was flagged by 3 of 92 vendors in a domain scan. teams-cloud[.]live copied the same Teams join page and was five days old.

This is where agents most often overreach. A registrar serves many unrelated customers, so a shared registrar alone proves little. A careful agent links siblings on stronger evidence, such as shared IP addresses, certificate details, identical page code or tracking IDs, and labels each link with its confidence. Lim describes the domains as registered by the same organization; the agent should attribute that claim to him until its own evidence supports it.

Human check: review every link the agent marks as "same actor" before anyone writes that in a report.

Step 4: Trace how victims reach the pages

An email-centered workflow looks for the message that delivered the link. Here there may be no message. Lim reported that teams-livemeeting[.]com surfaced through sponsored search ads and an AI-generated answer, and his screenshot shows a search engine's AI overview citing it beside Microsoft's own links. A later post shows teams-cloud[.]live ranking second in ordinary results for "teams cloud live."

The agent should capture these delivery paths as evidence too: the search queries, the ad or result position and the date seen. For practitioners, this maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1583.001 (acquiring domains) and T1608.006 (SEO poisoning).

Human check: none for collection. The findings feed the response plan.

Step 5: Follow the payload path without detonating blindly

On teams-cloud[.]live, joining the meeting led to a fake "You need to update Microsoft Teams" prompt. The Update Teams button downloaded a file named realtek-demo.txt.

The agent records the filename, hash and file type, and notes that a text file can't execute on its own. The honest verdict is "staged lure, payload not yet weaponized or swapped per visitor," not "malware delivery." Overstating this step is how investigation reports lose credibility.

Human check: decide whether to detonate further, for example by revisiting from a different region or browser profile, since some kits serve payloads selectively.

Step 6: Write the verdict and the response plan

The output should be a verdict a person can audit in five minutes: three lookalike Teams domains, cloned join pages, delivery through search and ads, a staged fake update, and a confidence level for each claim.

The response plan follows from the evidence: block the domains in DNS and web filtering, which is what Lim advised; search proxy and DNS logs for any visits from your users; file takedown requests with the registrar and host; and add the naming pattern to watch lists.

Human check: approve every action that touches production or goes outside the company. Blocks are reversible. A takedown request filed under your company's name is not.

Where AI investigation agents break

The walkthrough has the agent reading attacker-controlled pages at every step. That is the core weakness, and attackers have already found it.

Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that phishing emails in one campaign carried a password-protected attachment for the human and hidden instructions for the AI assistant that summarizes the inbox. Sublime Security documented phishing emails stuffed with invisible text copied from real Adidas newsletters and romance novels, meant to push AI filters toward a benign verdict. StrongestLayer found a malicious file carrying an "LLM_IGNORE_START" comment aimed at AI scanners. Sublime's researchers put the hidden-text technique at under 1% of phishing traffic, so this is early. It is also exactly the input an investigation agent consumes.

Three other failure modes show up in practice:

Overconfident links. Step 3 is where agents turn a shared registrar into "the same threat actor." A claim without an evidence item behind it should never reach a report.

Missing business context. An agent doesn't know that your marketing team runs a microsite on a hyphenated domain, or which vendor portals your staff use.

Too much permission. An agent that can file takedowns or change firewall rules on its own turns one poisoned page into an outage or a legal letter.

The defenses are design choices you can ask about. Treat everything the agent fetches as data, never as instructions. Separate the permission to read from the permission to act. Require every claim in a verdict to point to an evidence item. Log every tool call so the investigation can be replayed. Keep a human approval step on anything that leaves the building.

Seven questions to ask before you trust an investigation agent

Gartner's agent-washing estimate means most demos will look impressive. These questions separate an agent that investigates from a chatbot with a playbook behind it.

Show me the evidence ledger for a real case. Every claim in the verdict should link to an artifact: a record, a screenshot, a log line.

What does it do with a domain that has no reputation yet? If the answer is "marks it clean," it would have passed teams-online[.]com.

Can it investigate beyond the inbox? Lookalike domain registrations, search results and ads are delivery channels now. An email-only agent sees part of the campaign.

How does it separate content from instructions? Ask what happens when a phishing page or email contains hidden text addressed to the AI.

What can it do without human approval? Get the list in writing. Read-only enrichment can be automatic. Blocks, takedowns and user notifications need a person.

Can we replay an investigation? You need every query and tool call logged, so an analyst or auditor can retrace the path.

What is its accuracy on our data? Vendor benchmarks are best cases; in Microsoft's trial, the agent was 100% accurate on the test corpus. Run a pilot on your own reported phishing and measure false positives and misses yourself.

Frequently asked questions

Can AI agents investigate phishing on their own?

AI agents can gather and correlate most of the evidence in a phishing investigation on their own, including domain records, page captures, related infrastructure and indicators. They should not take outward-facing actions such as takedowns or blocks without human approval, because attackers can plant instructions in the content agents read.

How accurate are AI phishing triage agents?

In Microsoft's randomized trial with 167 analysts, people working with the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent were up to 77% more accurate and found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute. The agent was 100% accurate on that test corpus, so expect lower numbers in production and measure on your own data.

Is agentic AI different from SOAR for phishing response?

Yes. A SOAR playbook runs fixed steps written in advance. An AI agent chooses its next step based on what it finds, so it can follow a lead like a sibling domain that no playbook anticipated. That flexibility is also why agents need evidence logging and approval controls.

What is the biggest risk of AI agents in security investigations?

Prompt injection. An investigation agent reads attacker-controlled emails and web pages, and researchers at Barracuda, Sublime Security and StrongestLayer have documented phishing content with hidden text aimed at AI systems. The fix is design: treat fetched content as data, limit what the agent can do without approval and log every step.

Will AI investigation agents replace SOC analysts?

The evidence points to a shift in analyst work rather than replacement. In Microsoft's trial, analysts with the agent spent 53% more time on the malicious emails, because the agent handled sorting and first-pass reasoning. Judgment calls on attribution, business context and response still sat with people.

Watch an agent work a real case

The fake Teams portals show where investigation work has moved. The evidence sat in domain registrations, cloned pages, search results and an AI answer. An agent that only reads the inbox would have seen a fraction of it, and an agent that can't show its evidence shouldn't be trusted with the rest.

The useful test is the one in this post: give it a seed, watch it build the evidence ledger and see where it asks a human to decide.

Enhanced AI Classification Engine in Cofense Triage learns from analyst decisions and enables automated processing of high-confidence email classifications

LEESBURG, Va., November 12, 2026 – Cofense, the leader in AI-driven post-perimeter phishing defense, today announced enhancements to its Phishing Defense Platform with an updated AI Classification Engine (AICE) within its Phishing Remediation solution. AICE uses customer-trained AI to classify reported emails based on an organization's unique categories and enables automated processing of high-confidence decisions. This helps security teams reduce manual triage, accelerate phishing response, and free analysts to focus on complex threats that require human expertise.

Unlike static AI models, Cofense’s enhanced AI combines the power of its globally trained phishing detection models with AI trained on an organization’s own analyst decisions and threat environment. Together, these capabilities enable faster, more accurate threat classification and unlock greater automation of phishing response, reducing manual effort while allowing security teams to focus on the threats that matter most. This advancement reinforces Cofense’s commitment to delivering intelligent, adaptive, and automated phishing defense.

“AI should help analysts spend less time on repetitive email handling and more time on the threats that need their expertise,” said Jason Meurer, Director of Product Management at Cofense. “That requires AI that adapts to how their organization works and unique profile of threats they see. By learning from analyst decisions, explaining its classifications and letting teams set their own automation thresholds, AICE gives security teams the confidence to automate more of the response process while staying in control.”

Available within Cofense Triage, the enhanced AI Classification Engine advances phishing response in three areas:

Greater automation and analyst efficiency. High-confidence AI classifications trigger automated email processing, reducing manual triage and helping teams focus their expertise on complex, high-risk threats.

Adaptive AI tailored to each organization. Customer-trained models learn from analyst decisions and can be retrained on demand, delivering more precise classifications and adapting to evolving threats and workflows.

Explainable AI with security teams in control. Transparent AI decisions and configurable confidence thresholds give teams control over automation, while data and processing remain securely within the customer’s Triage environment.

In testing and validation, high-confidence AI classifications automated at least 30% of email handling work, with accuracy exceeding 98%.

Triage also provides model performance metrics, automation coverage and estimates of analyst hours saved, helping organizations evaluate results and refine their use of automation.

“Our investment in AI is focused on helping security teams automate phishing defense without increasing manual work,” said Marc Olesen, Chief Executive Officer of Cofense. “Customer-trained AI models, explainable decisions and analyst-controlled automation give organizations a way to increase the speed and scale of response while keeping human expertise focused where it matters most.”

About Cofense

Cofense is the leader in post-perimeter phishing defense, built for the reality that phishing gets through. Cofense helps enterprises identify threats already in employee inboxes, remediate active attacks fast, and reduce future risk. The Cofense platform combines phishing-specific AI with expert validation, automation, and collective insight drawn from millions of real-world user interactions. Context: ConnectWise later released a security update to address a critical file-transfer vulnerability (CVE-2026-84869) that ranked 9
Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Tanner Filip, Tyler Marzen, Austin Worline, Ethan Williams, Sharon Martin, Ben Bernstein, Andrew Brandt, Jamie Levy, Max Rogers, and Aaron Deal for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Update: 11/11/26 @ 11:34pm ET

Huntress has learned that the activity seems to be related to one of the specific extensions that had already been disabled by ConnectWise, RMM+. ConnectWise has disabled this extension (and several other related plugins) on all hosted environments, and urged on-premises partners to do the same in their public advisory.

RMM+ is a third-party extension for ScreenConnect that lets another tool manage ScreenConnect sessions without a technician working through the console. Our analysis suggests that most RMM+ installations we encountered were legitimate, usually added for a project and left in place. But versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 contained a serious authentication flaw: if an administrator had never configured the extension's access key, RMM+ would accept a blank one.

RMM+ bypasses ScreenConnect's user accounts, roles, and MFA, and authenticates requests with a shared access key stored in the extension's settings. In versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, that key defaulted to blank, meaning the authentication check didn't reject an empty value and a caller could pass the check when no key had been configured.

The important part is the access key setting:

<Setting Name="RMMPlus.AccessKey" IsServerOnly="true">

<Description>This is like a password. This is required to be sent in the POST request to access the functions. Set to a strong key..</Description>

<DefaultValue></DefaultValue>

</Setting>

The description tells the admin to set a strong key, but if empty, will introduce the vulnerability.

This matched our observations in this incident. Commands reached endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances within minutes. There was no corresponding login activity and the commands appeared in the logs reviewed linked to RMM+.

A special thanks to Mendy Green for helping us validate these findings.

ORIGINAL POST

Background

On November 11, 2026, Huntress observed an operator using access to multiple cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push commands to groups of managed endpoints. The commands installed attacker-controlled ScreenConnect clients and an additional toolkit called SCKit. At least 288 hosts across 48 organizations that use Huntress have been affected.

In an advisory posted at 22:45 UTC on November 11, ConnectWise shared that they had identified five independent third-party extensions that may be associated with this activity; they said that they had not yet identified an initial access vector and full scope of the attack. They disabled the following extensions across 400 partner environments as a precaution:

Labtech Plus

RMM Plus

RMM+

RMM Plus Password Link

RMM+ Password Link

In September 2026, Huntress stood up a Rapid Response to similar worm-like activity that spawned rogue ScreenConnect clients across several customer environments. ConnectWise later released a security update to address a critical file-transfer vulnerability (CVE-2026-84869) that ranked 9.9 on the CVSS scale.

In analyzing this threat, we have reviewed the activity on two fronts. First, we examined what was observed in the incidents we've seen, where threat actors have used the ScreenConnect panel's Run command feature to deploy SCKit to multiple endpoints.

Then, we analyzed the kit's code to understand how it was built to spread from an infected endpoint to a technician's workstation, and then to other endpoints accessible through the technician's ScreenConnect session. We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far.

Huntress is continuing to respond to and track this November 11 incident; we are releasing further information below about the attacker's tradecraft, a breakdown of SCKit, and Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in an effort to help defenders responding to this attack.

Technical Details

At approximately 17:47 UTC on November 11, 2026, Huntress observed suspicious activity on endpoints associated with multiple ScreenConnect environments. In total, we saw all 288 hosts impacted over the course of 90 minutes; with about one third of those in the first 10 minutes.

The infection path works in two stages: from an infected endpoint to a technician who connects to it, and from a technician's workstation to every endpoint their panel can connect to. However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analysing the payloads.

Figure 1: Timeline of attack across multiple organizations

SCKit in detail

SCKit is the name of the toolkit used to carry this attack forward. This toolkit is a package of 16 files - PowerShell scripts, batch scripts, Windows command-line .cmd files and other configuration data - designed to spread the infection laterally, through a multi-stage process.

Figure 2: The content of the decrypted SCKit archive

The kit is delivered as an encrypted payload, but the infected machine provides the actual decryption key to extract the files from the SCKit package; when the worm sends the request to retrieve the kit from its infrastructure, it passes the UUID of the Windows system it is running on as a part of the URL's query string. The server returns header data that include an encryption key, initialization vector, and a salt value, which the script uses to decrypt the package into the target's %temp% folder.

Figure 3: GET request and server response

As seen in figure 3 above, the query string to retrieve the SCKit payload passes along the GUID for the Windows machine it is running on (top highlighted text). The server returns decryption values the script will use to unpack the payload into the %temp% folder on the same machine.

Observed activity

We initially observed the toolkit's deployment coming through ScreenConnect panels, as opposed to the toolkit's self-replicating behavior. It appears as though an operator used the consoles' Run command feature to send commands to multiple endpoints in one go, running as SYSTEM.

Figure 4: Overview of the attack chain

The command first checked for an existing ScreenConnect client, then downloaded an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect installer to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi and installed it silently. It then wrote a base64-encoded dropper to C:\Windows\Temp\sckit-run.bat.

The dropper then connects to attacker controlled infrastructure and downloads C:\Windows\Temp\sckit-decoder.ps1, and then fetches a keyed version of the SCKit toolkit for the specific system. Several of the components in the toolkit carry out further activity:

Panel-Lateral.ps1 attempts the console takeover (unsuccessfully)

sckit-loader.ps1 decrypts and launches the machine specific script k<32 Hex>.ps1

k[32 Hex].ps1 then extracts the toolkit to C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap

lab-trap-cleanup-embedded.ps1 cleans up the installation in the Temp folder

Figure 5: Install sequence on an endpoint

The trap, along with lockout policies, are then installed by C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\install.ps1 while CWInstall_<8 hex>-c1\

Installer.ps1 adds exclusions to Defender and installs a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client.

Finally, TrapWatch.ps1 is launched as SYSTEM, and compiles RelayTrap.cs into a host-specific copy of C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\trapbins\<client id>\RelayTrap.exe and creates a scheduled task named TrapWatch. The legitimate installation of ScreenConnect is then stopped, set to manual start, and the attacker controlled copy of ScreenConnect positioned to replace it.

Figure 6: The C# source code of the RelayTrap executable appears to have been generated by an LLM, based on the detailed source code references and comments that explain exactly what it is intended to do

Further functionality in the code

Going beyond what we've observed, we've reconstructed an additional functionality intended to spread from a technician's workstation to the ScreenConnect panel. This has been discovered from analysis of its scripts, configuration, and tools. To date we have not observed a successful jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation, or from that workstation to other endpoints.

Figure 7: Additional functionality, designed to spread from technician's workstations.

It appears as though this was designed to wait for when a technician connects to the relay and on to the compromised endpoint. A file transfer takes place 2.5 seconds after the connection is established, and retrieves a copy of the Run-Lateral-Full.bat dropper from the compromised endpoint with the action set to Run.

This dropper is built to connect to hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php and download a loader onto the compromised workstation. The loader gathers the workstation's unique ID, sends it back to the attacker's infrastructure, which returns a unique, encrypted kit for that specific workstation.

Panel-Lateral.ps1, with support from LabConfig.ps1, then steals the .aspxauth session cookie from the workstation and attempts to replay the cookie against the panel and obtain the tokens needed to enumerate any other sessions the technician can access.

Next, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe is engineered to use access gained to any other sessions to upload a payload, WithUninstall.ps1, to the panel's Shared Toolbox. A panel request tells every reachable session to run the toolbox item. This payload is designed to run as SYSTEM on those endpoints, installing the trap and extending the cycle. Roughly 60 seconds after the broadcast, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe deletes the Shared Toolbox item.

Mitigation Guidance

If you use ScreenConnect, review your environment now, even if you have not received an alert. Look for unexpected mass activity in ScreenConnect Run Command and Toolbox history, including commands or tools you did not initiate, and check for an unauthorized second ScreenConnect client on managed endpoints.

If you suspect a host is affected:

Do not connect to it through ScreenConnect. An interactive session can trigger the malware to spread to the technician's workstation and then to other ScreenConnect panels available to that technician. Use EDR live response, WinRM, or another out-of-band CLI tool. If a technician has already connected to a suspected host, treat that workstation as potentially exposed and investigate it from a clean device.

Isolate the host and keep it isolated until cleanup is complete. Isolation alone does not remove the persistence, and affected systems have been observed reinfecting shortly after isolation was lifted.

Remove the unauthorized ScreenConnect client and persistence mechanism. Look for and remove the rogue client service, the TrapWatch scheduled task, C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\, and the toolkit files under %TEMP% (including sckit-*, Panel-Lateral.ps1, runnew.cmd, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, and sqlite3.exe). Check for and remove the RelayTrapLiteAlert value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Verify the legitimate ScreenConnect client separately before removing anything.

Revoke access that may have been exposed. From a clean device, terminate active ScreenConnect web sessions and rotate affected ScreenConnect credentials. Because the toolkit can steal browser session tokens, revoke potentially exposed browser and identity-provider sessions as well.

Review and investigate panel activity. Audit ScreenConnect Run Command and Toolbox history for unrecognized executions, and use the instance audit logs to investigate panel access and determine which systems and technician workstations may be affected.

Use SIEM to hunt. If you use Huntress SIEM, ensure ScreenConnect is connected as a data source to help Huntress hunt for suspicious administrator activity across your environment at scale.

Do not return a host to service until the rogue client and its persistence mechanism have been removed, and the system has been checked for reinfection. Continue monitoring ScreenConnect panels and endpoints for suspicious activity.

Note that file hashes are weak indicators for this activity as the scripts are rebuilt with different embedded values, and the trap executable is compiled separately on every host.

Title: Zero Trust Doesn't End at Login. Neither Does the Attack. by Mark Wojtasiak
Context: Through the Netskope Cloud Threat Exchange integration, selected indicators of compromise (IoCs), such as IP addresses and domains derived from Vectra AI detections, can be...
Full Text:
I've got a question for anyone investing in Zero Trust: What happens after you grant access?

Not who authenticated. Not whether the device passed a check. Not whether policy allowed the connection. Those are important questions, and we should absolutely keep asking them. I'm asking a different one. Once a trusted user, device, or AI agent is inside an approved session, how do you know that trust is still deserved?

Because that's where a lot of modern attacks live. Not outside the front door, trying to smash their way in. Inside legitimate access paths, using credentials, applications, and services the business already trusts.

Access is a decision. Trust is a moving target.

Continuous evaluation is already a Zero Trust principle. The challenge is putting it into practice by connecting access decisions with evidence of attacker behavior throughout the session. Netskope does something essential. It helps organizations make and enforce context-aware access decisions across web, SaaS, cloud, and private applications. That control matters.

But a correct access decision at 9:00 a.m. doesn't guarantee legitimate behavior at 9:05.

A session can be authorized and still be abused. An identity can authenticate successfully and still be compromised. An approved application can carry command-and-control activity. A connection can be encrypted and still be part of an attack.

None of that means Zero Trust failed. It means we sometimes ask access controls to answer a question they weren't designed to answer. Access policy tells us whether a connection should be allowed. It doesn't, by itself, tell us whether everything happening through that connection continues to make sense.

That second question is behavioral. And behavior changes.

The attacker sees one environment. Why doesn't the SOC?

Picture a remote employee with legitimate access to a SaaS application and an internal service. An attacker compromises the employee's identity. They log in through an approved path, explore available systems, use an unfamiliar service, and begin moving toward more valuable resources.

Each step may look ordinary when viewed alone. A successful login. An HTTPS connection. A cloud API request. A new destination.

Now think about the analyst. Secure access has one piece of the story. Identity has another. Network detection has another. SaaS and cloud tools have the rest. The analyst becomes the integration layer, manually reconstructing what happened while the attacker keeps moving.

I call that getting attacker soundbites when what we need is the attack story. I'm less interested in alert counts than in how quickly defenders can answer three questions: Is this real? Does it matter? What do we do next?

‍What Netskope and Vectra AI change together‍

This is why the Netskope and Vectra AI integration matters to me. It's not about putting two logos next to each other or adding another feed to a SOC dashboard. It's about connecting the access decision to what attackers actually do after access is granted.

Netskope brings the secure access context and control. Vectra AI brings AI-native behavioral detection and Attack Signal Intelligence to identify suspicious activity, connect related behaviors, and prioritize the identities and hosts that warrant investigation.

With Netskope Cloud TAP, policy-selected web traffic traversing Netskope infrastructure can be copied into customer-managed cloud object storage. Netskope Stitcher retrieves and replays that traffic to a dedicated Vectra virtual sensor. The sensor processes it and sends enriched metadata to the Vectra platform for analysis. The integration can also associate observed remote-user activity with the corresponding Netskope user identity.

Why does that matter? Because Vectra AI's behavioral analytics can look for attacker signals in that traffic without requiring payload decryption. That includes the kinds of suspicious patterns attackers try to conceal inside otherwise routine, encrypted communications. That observation can then be assessed alongside behavior from other connected network, identity, cloud, and SaaS sources.

There is also a path back.

Through the Netskope Cloud Threat Exchange integration, selected indicators of compromise (IoCs), such as IP addresses and domains derived from Vectra AI detections, can be shared with Netskope, where configured policies can use them for enforcement.

Observe. Understand. Prioritize. Act. That's the workflow. The technology should make it easier, not make analysts learn another alphabet soup of consoles.

What continuous threat detection means for the defender

Start with the compromised remote user. The question isn't simply whether Netskope allowed the session. It should have, based on the information available at that moment. The question is whether subsequent behavior starts looking like reconnaissance, command and control, credential abuse, lateral movement, or other signs of attack progression.

And consider the SOC team's day. If analysts have to stitch access logs, network evidence, identity events, and cloud alerts together by hand, they're spending scarce time assembling context instead of making decisions. Correlated, prioritized attacker behavior gives them a place to start and a clearer reason to act.

This isn't a claim that one integration magically sees every packet or stops every attack. Cloud TAP coverage depends on the traffic Netskope captures and the deployment choices customers make. Nor is behavioral detection a replacement for secure access, endpoint protection, or policy enforcement. These controls do different jobs. The point is to make those jobs reinforce one another.

Make Zero Trust continuous

Here's my takeaway: A Zero Trust architecture has to support continuous evaluation long after a session is approved.

People, devices, workloads, service accounts, and AI agents all operate through trusted connections. Some will be compromised or misused. Attackers will keep making malicious activity resemble business as usual.

We can't solve that by denying every connection. We also can't solve it by trusting every connection forever.

We have to secure access and use continuous monitoring to assess the behavior that follows. Netskope helps determine who or what gets access to which applications and data. Vectra AI helps defenders recognize when activity after access starts telling an attacker story, then decide what deserves attention.

That's the opportunity I see in Netskope and Vectra AI together: less blind trust, fewer disconnected soundbites, faster clarity for the people defending the business.

Because getting through the door shouldn't give an attacker the benefit of the doubt for the rest of the day.

‍Secure access. Continuous attack defense. That's how Zero Trust becomes more than an access decision.

Title: Five Findings From the 2027 State of Threat Intelligence
Context: When I first saw the results of this year’s survey, a few findings stood out to me as especially relevant for anyone who runs, funds, or relies on a threat intelligence program...
Full Text:
The much anticipated State of Threat Intelligence report has just been published. The State of Threat Intelligence report is based on a survey Recorded Future conducted with UserEvidence of 768 cybersecurity professionals at enterprises with at least 1,000 employees. It’s the latest edition in our annual report series, where we gauge how threat intelligence is currently being used, funded, and measured. When I first saw the results of this year’s survey, a few findings stood out to me as especially relevant for anyone who runs, funds, or relies on a threat intelligence program and is planning for the year ahead. Here are my top five findings and why.

1. Cost is the least common reason to consolidate

A strong majority of respondents (79%) said they plan to consolidate threat intelligence vendors in the next year. That alone is no huge surprise, especially given that respondents reported using an average of five different vendors. Cost would be a reasonable guess for why, but reducing costs actually ranked last of five drivers, at 5%.

The drivers that ranked higher point to what teams want from consolidation:

Improving correlation across signals (34%): connecting intelligence across threat domains and internal telemetry into one view of risk.

Bringing siloed tools together (29%): ensuring different risk owners can efficiently act on intelligence.

Simplifying operations (22%): fewer interfaces and handoffs so teams can act on intelligence sooner.

Reducing vendor-management overhead (9%): fewer vendors to evaluate and renew.

Overall investment is still rising: 83% plan to increase threat intelligence spending in the next 12 months. Teams are consolidating to get better results from their intelligence, not to cut spend.

That puts the focus on outcomes. Jason Steer, CISO at Recorded Future, framed the risk well: consolidation only counts “if that provider has the same or better outcomes.” For anyone evaluating vendors this year, that’s the bar to consider.

Especially as teams expand the reach of their threat intelligence programs and support more stakeholders across the enterprise, they’re pursuing vendors that provide coverage across the risk domains that matter for those teams, but equally important that friction is not created in that pursuit of breadth, and that the organization is able to see how threats across disparate domains actually connect.

2. Only 25% have external intelligence and internal telemetry in one place

Correlation is the top consolidation driver, yet only a quarter of respondents say external intelligence and internal telemetry reside in one place. The rest break down as follows:

52% are partially integrated across some tools.

18% rely on manual correlation by analysts.

5% keep the two in separate workflows.

Poor integration with existing tools and workflows was also the most-cited pain point with current vendors.

This doesn’t mean every team needs to move everything into a single tool. What often matters is whether external intelligence can be correlated with internal signals across the tools a team already uses, without an analyst doing it by hand. Collective Insights® is built for this: it pulls detections from a team’s existing security tools and enriches them with Recorded Future intelligence.

For the 70% who are partially integrated or correlating manually, it’s worth identifying where that manual handoff still happens.

3. Confidence in ROI is high, but few measure cost savings

Nearly every respondent (99%) formally measures the value of their threat intelligence program, and 57% say they are very confident in their ability to quantify its ROI. But when asked how they measure value, more than half (58%) of that very confident group did not include cost savings. Across all respondents, 39% measure cost savings, and 31% measure whether triggered actions actually worked.

The most common metrics are operational:

Enhanced threat detection rates: 60%

Improved response times: 59%

Fewer incidents: 57%

Those matter to security teams, but ultimately fail to communicate the bottom-line impact of your threat intelligence program to the business. The Impact & Metrics dashboard in the Recorded Future platform helps here by showing the hours and dollars saved through use of the platform.

4. About one in four have already closed the loop

Closing that measurement gap depends on connecting intelligence to outcomes. That is what closed-loop operationalization does: intelligence is automatically shared with the relevant stakeholders, they take action based on it, and the efficacy of that action is validated and used to inform what intelligence is collected and shared with these teams.

Closed-loop programs can answer the questions stakeholders outside security ask: did the intelligence drive an action, and did that action work? Answering those questions also requires a clear definition of what intelligence should achieve. Most programs have that starting point: 68% say formally documented, regularly reviewed Priority Intelligence Requirements (PIRs) govern their program.

For teams building next year’s measurement plan, PIRs set the benchmark, and closed-loop validation should be the goal for how outcomes get measured against it.

5. Threat intelligence is now an input to AI, not only a beneficiary of it

98% of respondents use AI in their threat intelligence work. Less discussed is the other direction: 74% say threat intelligence already feeds their organization’s AI or automation initiatives.

44% describe this as established, with intelligence regularly feeding one or more AI or automation workflows.

30% describe it as advanced, with structured intelligence as a core input across their AI and agentic systems.

Only 4% don’t use threat intelligence to support AI at all.

Across all of the tasks where we assessed comfort with AI autonomy (summarization, alert triage, enrichment, false-positive reduction, detection rule generation, prioritization, and enforcement actions), at least 92% of respondents are comfortable giving AI some role. That makes the earlier findings more pressing. AI workflows inherit whatever gaps exist in the intelligence they draw on, including signals that aren’t correlated and actions that aren’t validated.

Looking ahead

Taken together, these findings describe programs that are still investing. Their focus is on connecting intelligence, proving its value, and extending it into new workflows, including AI. Most are partway through that work, and some are further along than expected.

The full 2027 State of Threat Intelligence report covers each of these areas in more depth. That includes which teams beyond the SOC rely on threat intelligence and how comfortable organizations are giving AI autonomy. Download the report.

Title: ARTEX and AI-Powered Red Teaming Tools: What Defenders Need to Know
Context: Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability
Full Text:
A rapidly expanding ecosystem of AI-enabled tools such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI — marketed for red teaming and penetration testing — are being used by attackers to execute offensive operations autonomously.

Their footprint is already substantial. Unit 42 has observed ARTEX used in intrusion attempts against multiple targets.

Our Incident Response team investigated multiple intrusions in which the attacker’s server hosted an ARTEX console or used infrastructure and user agents associated with ARTEX.

Separately, Unit 42 Managed Threat Hunting tracked a coordinated ARTEX campaign against customer cloud environments in sectors worldwide, including retail and consulting.

External scrutiny has already disrupted project lifecycles: the author of ARTEX recently made the repository closed-source and ceased public development to prevent misuse. Emerging alternatives are rapidly filling the void, introducing new capabilities that threat actors will inevitably co-opt.

Here, we share our observations of how attackers are using AI-powered red team tools, along with our recommendations for how defenders can mitigate.

Why Is ARTEX Such an Effective Tool for Attackers?

ARTEX and other red-teaming platforms are free, quick to deploy and need little more than access to a large language model (LLM).

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent AI penetration testing framework first published in mid-2026. It has been widely forked since.

Attackers can use ARTEX to evaluate responses, adapt when something fails and keep pursuing their objective. They can target the identity workflows and APIs that organizations expose to the internet, and then use the associated credentials and trust relationships to reach the cloud.

AI-Powered Red Teaming and Pentesting Ecosystem Infrastructure

As of October 2026, Unit 42 identified 1,323 internet-facing hosts running CyberStrikeAI and 609 running ARTEX. Notably, 21 hosts were running both at the same time.

Unit 42 analyzed 14 tools across the pentesting and red-teaming tool ecosystem, highlighting 12 emerging tools alongside CyberStrikeAI and ARTEX.

These tools can be broken down into four categories of AI assisted red team activities.

Category

Tools

Goal

Reconnaissance and attack-surface management

ARL, ARL-Next, Scope Sentry, Nemo, XingRin, OpenEASD

Identify what assets exist, what is exposed and what changes

Agent-led testing and vulnerability hunting

CyberStrikeAI, ARTEX, Cairn, PentAGI, AutoHunter

Manage what should be investigated and how the system can act on it

Source-code auditing and verification

DeepAudit, AIxVuln

Identify where source code might be vulnerable and what supports that finding

AI-system security assessment

AI-Infra-Guard

Identify if AI infrastructure, agents, tools and model interfaces are vulnerable or unreliable

Table 1. Tool categories.

Implications For Defenders

Defenders should be aware of the following implications of AI-powered red teaming platforms:

Lowered Skill Floor for Attackers

Adversaries no longer require specialized tradecraft to execute multi-stage, adaptive penetration testing.

Off-the-shelf tooling combined with LLMs like DeepSeek allows financially motivated actors to launch and manage dozens of complex, concurrent network intrusions for minimal compute cost.

Risk of Internet-Exposed Assets

Any internet-exposed asset, regardless of organizational size or sector, is equally likely to be impacted by automated, persistent intrusion attempts.

Attackers using the autonomous AI penetration testing framework ARTEX are turning public password reset pages and exposed APIs into a path to cloud access, sometimes in less than a day. Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability.

Because these autonomous platforms cannot target what they cannot find, continuous discovery and mitigation of exposed edge assets remains an effective barrier against automated campaigns.

Proactive AI Adoption Helps Defenders

Autonomous testing frameworks rely on foundational LLM reasoning patterns. Therefore, there is some predictability to AI-powered adversary tooling.

Security teams do not need to guess an agent's methodology; they can deploy identical open-weight offensive frameworks internally to surface, validate and remediate vulnerable exposure before external agents identify them.

Defenders Benefit From Tracking Ecosystem Shifts

The rapid adoption curve of tools in this ecosystem highlights how quickly operational trends can shift. Keeping an eye on these developments provides practical defensive advantages:

Observing emerging agent-led frameworks allows teams to test new capabilities early in controlled environments.

Monitoring the infrastructure hosting these tools makes it possible to update perimeter blocks before active targeting begins.

Current AI-Powered Frameworks Are Noisy

Current autonomous frameworks prioritize rapid trial-and-error over stealth. In our study of a tool called Cairn, it generated hundreds of thousands of noisy, high-frequency requests across multiple edge protocols from a single origin IP address.

Organizations with unified perimeter telemetry and centralized logging can readily distinguish this brute-force agentic traffic from legitimate users and block campaigns at the network edge before exploitation occurs.

Defensive Deception Could Help

LLM-driven testing tools use target responses as context for follow up actions.

Defenders may be able to take advantage of this to trick attackers using AI-powered red teaming tools into wasting resources.

When a target serves identical, generic error codes or enforces silent connection throttling, an AI agent lacks the contextual cues needed to adapt. Deprived of environmental feedback, autonomous loops burn context windows and compute budgets on dead ends.

Recognizing an AI-Driven Operator

ARTEX is forked and modified constantly. Furthermore, attackers rotate infrastructure quickly, so indicators lose value fast. How the operator behaves is more durable, and the behavior across our observations consistently pointed to an automated planner reacting to what it sees. Table 2 shows the hallmarks of this behavior.

Hallmark

What We Observed

Think-then-act cadence

Bursts of one to 14 requests about a second apart, then a pause of 25–31 seconds, consistent with an agent waiting on a model inference call

Machine speed

Pivots within about one minute of a credential download. More than 200 client secrets validated in about three minutes

Spec-driven targeting

Routes from downloaded OpenAPI specifications and source maps targeted almost immediately

Self-correction

Failed requests (HTTP 422) adjusted and retried successfully moments later

Checking its own work

A GET to the same path after almost every successful write. Write-then-delete tests on storage buckets.

Canary inputs

Bogus usernames before real ones, and placeholder values such as evil[.]com, test@example[.]com and deadbeefdeadbeefdeadbeef12

Parallel targeting

An application delivery controller, more than a dozen VPN appliances, a NAS device, workforce identity and cloud ports attacked within the same hour

Recheck loops

Polling every 48 seconds for three days, and attack sequences replayed identically about 30 seconds apart

Table 2. Behavioral hallmarks of ARTEX-driven activity observed by Unit 42.

Any one of these traits could come from an unusually configured tool or a person testing an API by hand. Seen together, they point to autonomous tooling.

Despite the autonomous tooling, humans were not entirely absent from the attacks we observed. In one engagement, the attacker switched from scripted clients to a desktop browser for the password reset and first token request. This suggests a human in the loop, or browser automation, for the most sensitive steps.

Conclusion and Mitigations for ARTEX Attacks

AI-driven tooling is not inventing new attacks. Self-service abuse, exposed APIs and stored credentials are long-standing weak points.

What has changed is the pace and the persistence. An ARTEX operator can test every exposed workflow in parallel and switch routes within minutes of being blocked. It can act on a stolen credential within a minute of finding it.

Because the framework is open source and widely forked, indicator-based detection will not keep up.

Defenders who remove machine-readable attack maps, require authentication everywhere and build detections around operator behavior will be best placed to stop an AI-assisted attacker.

Autonomous tooling probes faster than people can review alerts. Defenses need to block by default and remove the credentials these tools are looking for. Organizations should:

Remove public attack maps. Take OpenAPI specifications, source maps and configuration files containing tokens or client IDs off internet-facing applications.

Reduce and understand your organization’s public footprint. Certificate transparency can create target lists for threat actors. In cloud environments, it is vital to understand if host fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) are public knowledge. Consider private certificate authorities to limit information disclosure and locking origin traffic to content delivery network (CDN)-only ingress where possible.

Require authentication on every write endpoint, including development and staging APIs.

Harden self-service flows. Rate-limit and bot-protect registration, password reset and verification code endpoints. Remove unauthenticated account-existence checks.

Protect federated identities. Block local passwords for workforce accounts in customer and partner identity providers, and make sure a password reset can never unlink a federated identity.

Get credentials out of reach. Replace long-lived cloud keys with role-based access, keep administrator credentials out of provisioning records and move function secrets to a secrets manager.

Enforce least privilege for workload roles and any function that can create roles, keys or tokens.

Hunt for behavior, not just indicators. Look for:

Canary usernames in identity provider logs

First use of a cloud key from a new IP address

Write-then-delete storage tests

Early-phase probing that precedes a later intrusion
