Seed phrase, private key file, and system reconnaissance

The implant performs two regular expression patterns to search on the entire filesystem of the victim machine. These two regular expressions are designed to scan file names for sensitive cryptographic assets and credentials, functioning as case-insensitive patterns ?i. The first expression targets cryptocurrency recovery materials and wallet backups by matching keywords like "seed," "mnemonic," or "wallet" paired with common plain-text and data file extensions (.txt, .md, .csv, .dat), while the second seeks out asymmetric private keys and general secrets using terms like "private," "privkey," or "secret" paired with both text files and standard cryptographic key containers (.key, .pem). Because both patterns use unanchored, greedy matching (.*) without start (^) or end ($) boundary anchors, they capture any file where these sensitive terms precede the target extensions. Matched data are collected under the label of seed candidates and archived into “browserdata.zip”.

(?i)(seed|phrase|mnemonic|recovery|backup|wallet).*(\.txt|\.md|\.csv|\.dat) (?i)(private|privkey|secret).*(\.txt|\.md|\.key|\.pem)

The implant also performs victim machine reconnaissance by executing the following commands and uses chcp 65001 prefix to force the output in UTF-8 format.

chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & systeminfo chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & wmic os get lastbootuptime /value chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & wmic /namespace:\\root\SecurityCenter2 path AntiVirusProduct get displayName 2>nul chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & Get-Process | Select-Object Id, ProcessName | ConvertTo-Json -Compress

After all collection paths are complete, the implant assembles all collected data into a single document that looks like a formatted report with clearly labeled sections for each data category such as === CRYPTO ===, === WIFI ===, === BROWSER ===.

Keylogger: Keystrokes livestreamed to C2

The keylogger module of the implant uses a persistent background goroutine that polls all 256 Windows virtual key codes, detecting keypresses via dynamically resolved API calls, and transmits the captured input. When a compromised victim presses a valid key on the keyboard, it is simultaneously streamed live as an AES-256-GCM encrypted JSON payload over WebSocket to C2 and also appends to an in-memory buffer capped at 10,000 entries and halved when full to prevent memory leaks. On an actor's dump command, this buffer is concatenated into a single string and returned to C2 via WebSocket or HTTP fallback, ensuring complete data transfer even during network interruptions.

Stolen data exfiltration to C2

Once the archive is assembled, the entire result map is handed to the result transmission routine of the implant. That routine constructs a new JSON object containing five specific fields. It includes the command identifier echoed back from the original command. It also contains the agent's persistent identifier, formatted as ag_<16 hex chars>. The type field is set to the string quick_steal_response. Finally, the data field holds the complete result map.

Once constructed, this object is forwarded to the encryption routine. The routine serializes the object into JSON. It then generates 12 fresh random bytes to serve as a nonce. Next, it encrypts the serialized JSON using AES-256-GCM with a static key derived from a hardcoded seed. It concatenates the nonce, the ciphertext, and the 16-byte authentication tag and Base64-encodes the entire payload. The encrypted payload is placed in a wrapper object under the "e" key alongside the plain-text agent ID, and the wrapper is JSON marshaled into the final payload.

This encrypted payload is then delivered through an available transmission path. The sending routine first checks whether the WebSocket connection is live. If it is, the payload is written directly into a WebSocket text frame on the existing connection, reaching the actor's panel with minimal latency. If the WebSocket is not currently connected, the routine falls back to an HTTP POST request to the endpoint path /api/c2/result on the C2 server, using the same encrypted body format. This dual-path design ensures stolen data is delivered even during WebSocket interruptions, as the HTTP channel remains functional independently of the WebSocket state.

Implant’s C2 protocol

The implant C2 architecture is designed for two independent, simultaneously operating communication channels. The primary channel is a persistent WebSocket connection over TLS. The secondary channel is an HTTP polling loop that posts to a fixed API endpoint at regular intervals.

With the primary channel, the connection begins with a TCP dial to the C2 server address with an eight-second timeout. If the port is not explicitly present in the configured address, port 443 is appended automatically. Once the TCP socket is established, it is wrapped in a TLS session using a custom certificate configuration that pins to a specific certificate rather than validating against the system's certificate authority store. This prevents standard TLS interception proxies from observing traffic.

Immediately after a successful WebSocket handshake but before any command is received, the implant transmits a full system registration message. The implant collects victim data such as the machine hostname, the local LAN IP address, the Windows username from the environment, a user security identifier, the local reverse-proxy port number that was assigned when the embedded proxy server was started, and the detected upstream proxy configuration derived from the Windows registry proxy settings. All of this is assembled into a JSON object and encrypted and sent to the C2.

Figure 10. Snippet of NIK C2 IMPLANT’s C2 communication handler function.

The HTTP polling channel runs independently. Every approximately 250 milliseconds, the agent collects a fresh snapshot of victim state hostname, watchdog status, local IP, username, current timestamp, and system uptime encrypts it in the same wire format and posts it to the /api/c2/update endpoint on the C2 server.

Below table shows the C2 endpoints that the implant communicates:

Endpoint

Purpose

/api/c2/update

Reconnaissance beacon – victim system info

/api/c2/result

Command output exfiltration

/api/c2/screen

Screenshot upload

/api/c2/file_chunk

File exfiltration

/api/c2/rproxy_up

Reverse proxy upstream data

/api/c2/ws

Websocket – actor command channel

Every message on both channels, in both directions, uses the same symmetric encryption scheme. A hardcoded seed value stored in obfuscated form in the binary data section is decoded at startup and produces a 32-byte AES key.

Decoded AES seed: d791dd0ff3228ed29a8d7333d4567be829159c5632ea347780992006f91c5295 32-byte AES key: 4887AFC0A574E9419A9695EF083460F58E4EF9A1C40793523CE112251273BDF9

The C2 server then responds with an encrypted payload, whose inner map contains a command array identical in structure to those delivered over WebSocket. Commands received through HTTP are dispatched through the same logic. If the HTTP POST fails, the agent rotates to the next server address before retrying.

Figure 11. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s C2 communication handler function.

The result transmission to the C2 is performed by the implant when a command handler completes its operation, the result is packaged into a response envelope containing the original command's identifier, the implant's own identifier, a type string formed by appending _response to the command name, the result data payload, and a top-level type marker of "result". This object is encrypted and delivered through either directly over the WebSocket connection if it is active, or via an HTTP POST to /api/c2/result.

Implant’s defense evasion and anti-analysis techniques

The NIK C2 implant deploys a layered set of defense evasion measures that activate immediately at startup and operate across the full compromise session. On launch, It hides its console window via API ShowWindow, renames the binary to “csrss.exe” in the Windows temp directory to impersonate a legitimate system process, disables Windows Recent Documents telemetry through a registry write action, and applies a critical-process flag via API NtSetInformationProcess with the parameter value 0x1D for ProcessBreakOnTermination that causes a Blue Screen of Death if any attempt is made to terminate the process through Task Manager or taskkill actions.

Figure 12. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s evasion handler module.

Alongside these, two anti-debug checks IsDebuggerPresent and CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent run silently and call os.Exit(0) on detection, leaving no exception record or crash evidence. When directed by the C2, the implant can also escalate privileges without a UAC prompt using the fodhelper.exe COM hijack, which writes the implant path into HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command, triggers elevation, and cleans the registry key within two seconds.

The implant bypasses the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) by executing a hardcoded, embedded PowerShell script that patches memory inside “System.Management.Automation.dll”. Specifically, it overwrites the AmsiInitFailed field with a six-byte stub (MOV EAX, E_INVALIDARG; RET), forcing initialization to report failure and disabling content inspection for the remaining of the PowerShell session.

Figure 13. NIK C2 Implant’s AMSI bypass PowerShell script.

Conclusion

The emergence of NIK C2, an AI-enabled command-and-control framework, underscores a critical shift in modern malware design: the transition from static intrusion toolsets to dynamic, modular implants that adapt on demand. By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, the compromised host is no longer a passive foothold but an autonomous operational asset. Operators can dynamically generate context-aware lure material, execute localized deception, synthesize operational intelligence, and craft targeted payloads directly on the compromised hosts — all while lowering the technical barrier which was traditionally required for such sophisticated tradecraft.

Title: MR ROBOT Malware-as-a-Service Targets Indian Bank Customers
Context: Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand
Full Text:
A new Android malware-as-a-service (MaaS) operation has been found renting customized banking trojans to criminals targeting Indian bank customers, with one affiliate intercepting 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices.

The operation, branded MR ROBOT by its operators, was detailed in research published on October 28 by threat intelligence firm CloudSEK. Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand.

The lures are distributed through fake Play Store-style pages and messaging-app links, and impersonate banks as well as utility providers and government services.

MR ROBOT Turns Banking Malware into Subscription Service

CloudSEK said MR ROBOT is not a single actor’s campaign but a multi-tenant crimeware platform. Each affiliate receives its own application ID and can generate Android packages impersonating specific Indian banks.

The platform supports a tiered reseller model with sub-admin accounts, and licenses access for set periods through a control panel identified as version 7.0.

The malware intercepts text messages carrying one-time passwords (OTPs), shows fake screens to harvest banking credentials, card details, PINs and identity information, and can silently enable call forwarding. CloudSEK said this reroutes incoming calls, including banks’ fraud-check callbacks, to a number the attackers’ control.

The storefront, a Telegram bot called APK Shield, offered around 36 lure apps, including bank impersonations and fake apps for utility bills, telecom services, traffic fines and government services.

One Affiliate Intercepted More Than 5400 Text Messages

CloudSEK tracked two affiliates. One affiliate’s panel held around 154 enrolled devices and approximately 3270 intercepted messages, while an exposed Firebase database linked to a second held 153 devices and 5407 messages.

That data was collected between July 16 and 30, 2026, and around 4000 of the messages came from bank and telecommunications short codes. CloudSEK said call forwarding was active on 58% of the devices.

Each build receives a fresh signing certificate and can hide from the Android launcher after installation. CloudSEK said MR ROBOT shares call forwarding and per-customer builders with FatBoyPanel and RedWing, operations previously documented by Zimperium, but its kit, storefront and panel had not been publicly reported.

Read more on Android banking malware: Rokarolla Trojan Combines Banking Fraud With Device Surveillance

CloudSEK advised users never to install bank-branded apps from links sent by text, WhatsApp or Telegram, and urged banks to move customers from text-message OTPs toward app-based or Fast Identity Online (FIDO) authentication where feasible.

Title: Amatera: How the prolific infostealer works and spreads
Context: ESET detections jumped by more than 500% in the first half of 2025 compared with the previous six months, making it the second most common attack vector after phishing
Full Text:
Infostealers have become an established business, with developers who produce and maintain the product and paying customers who run their own campaigns with them. Amatera – which topped ESET’s infostealer detections in Latin America in the first half of 2026 but targets victims worldwide – shows what this professionalization looks like in practice.

Like many other infostealers, Amatera goes after a range of data spanning login credentials, session cookies, tokens, crypto wallet information, messaging data, files, and secrets from development environments. The sheer breadth of the loot shows why infostealers are a mainstay of cybercrime – a single compromise can lead to account hijacking, financial fraud and crypto theft, as well as open the door into the organization where the victim works.

Here’s more about where Amatera came from, along with its business model, capabilities, and distribution.

What is Amatera?

Detected by ESET products as Win/PSW.Amatera, Amatera is a Windows infostealer written in C++ that was first observed in 2024. Since it’s marketed under the malware-as-a-service (MaaS) model, its developers maintain the code, the control panel, and the support infrastructure, while affiliates pay a subscription to use the malware in their campaigns.

Given the similarities in their respective code, Amatera is very likely a rebrand of ACR Stealer. Indeed, the latter has a predecessor of its own: a Sekoia investigation in May 2024 described it as an updated version of the GrMsk stealer, offered as a service on underground forums.

Rebranding – or releasing an updated version of a piece of malware under a new name – is very common across the MaaS ecosystem, particularly among ransomware operators. They sometimes sell the source code when they shut down their operations to avoid being tracked, or they update and rename it as a ‘business strategy’. In some cases, they leak it so that other malicious actors can reuse it. At any rate, by the end of 2024, Amatera Stealer was already on offer for $199 a month, with support via Telegram..

Amatera’s capabilities

Amatera extracts credentials stored in web browsers, along with cookies, browsing histories, form data, and session tokens. It can also search for and grab sensitive documents and files synced with OneDrive or SharePoint – Microsoft reported a surge in attacks on its enterprise customers between late April and mid-June 2026. Separately, Straiker found that the malware also went after cryptocurrency wallet data by manipulating the clipboard.

The malware is also under constant development, and it turns up as the final payload in a wide variety of attack chains. That variety is also typical of MaaS: the developers sell the product, and each affiliate chooses their own way to deliver it.

Amatera has spread via compromised websites, search engine ads, targeted emails, fake documents, SVG files, and ClickFix via fake CAPTCHAs. Indeed, several recent analyses of Amatera campaigns worldwide show that one of its key delivery vectors is ClickFix, a social engineering technique that was first documented in 2024 and was quickly picked up by adversaries to distribute a wide range of malware families.

Often, the victim sees a message that mimics a CAPTCHA check or a browser error and warns them of supposed technical problems that can be fixed by copying a command and running it on their computer. The victim’s own keystrokes then set the compromise in motion. The technique has moved beyond fake CAPTCHAs, however, as adversaries kept the social engineering core of ClickFix with some tweaks:

· AI-fix: Attackers build pages that impersonate legitimate AI services, including Anthropic’s Artifacts, OpenAI’s Canvas, and Microsoft Copilot Pages. The pages contain fake troubleshooting content for non-existent problems.

· CrashFix: A fake ad blocker triggers fake browser crashes and warns of data loss, pushing victims toward a malicious “quick fix.”

· ConsentFix: This variant tricks the victims into handing over their OAuth authorization tokens that open their Microsoft accounts to attackers without any password being stolen.

ClickFix-based campaigns have also used legitimate but compromised WordPress sites, among other methods. Attackers gained access to these sites through weak or stolen administrative credentials or by exploiting vulnerabilities in WordPress themes and plugins.

In Latin America, Amatera topped ESET’s infostealer detections in the first half of 2026, ahead of Formbook, Vidar, Lumma Stealer, SnakeStealer, and Rhadamanthys. ClickFix’s recent growth globally hasn’t been a straight line, however. ESET detections jumped by more than 500% in the first half of 2025 compared with the previous six months, making it the second most common attack vector after phishing. Detections fell steeply in the second half of 2025, before more than doubling in the first half of 2026 as attackers adapted the technique to new environments.

Amatera’s affiliates also buy Google ads. The Straiker research mentioned above uncovered dozens of fake install pages that were promoted through paid ads and SEO poisoning and impersonated AI and developer tools, such as Claude Code, NotebookLM, JetBrains, Comet, and Snowflake, and specifically targeted developers who use AI tools. Like AI-fix, these pages piggyback off the credibility of AI brands and share the execution chain with ClickFix.

Risks and consequences of an Amatera compromise

Based on its capabilities, these are some of the potential consequences of falling victim to Amatera:

Compromise of personal or corporate accounts through stolen passwords, cookies, and tokens

Unauthorized access to email and cloud storage

Theft of crypto assets when wallets or recovery phrases are exposed

Infrastructure compromise through SSH keys, FTP credentials, or development secrets

Installation of additional malware

Use of a compromised account for fraud, internal phishing campaigns, or further intrusions

The risk spills over to employers when the victim mixes personal and work profiles in the same web browser. A home computer may hold corporate email sessions, cloud consoles, code repositories, or HR systems. The stolen information eventually becomes a gateway that another actor can buy or exploit days later.

How to prevent and respond to an Amatera compromise

Here are a few tips for staying out of harm’s way, especially in corporate environments:

Remember that no legitimate CAPTCHA, error message, or installation guide will ask you to copy commands from a web page into the Run dialog, PowerShell, or Terminal. A search engine ad is no guarantee that a site is official. That applies equally to pages that look like they belong to a well-known AI service.

Enforce application control rules and reduce the attack surface by limiting the use of system interpreters and binaries outside their normal context.

Monitor PowerShell, Rundll32, WebDAV, unusual scheduled tasks, and the clearing of PowerShell history.

Use phishing-resistant authentication and keep browser sessions as short as business needs allow.

Separate personal and work profiles, and avoid storing secrets in the browser when a managed alternative is available.

Filter newly created sites, cloned installation pages, and downloads initiated from ads when the context doesn’t justify them.

If a compromise is confirmed, isolating the device is only the first step. From a trusted device, revoke active sessions, reset passwords, and rotate API keys, tokens, SSH credentials, and any other secrets present on the system. Also, review access to email, cloud services, repositories, and financial applications. The response must track follow-on activity, rather than stop at the initial host – documented campaigns executed additional payloads, created scheduled tasks, covered their tracks, and used legitimate system tools.

Conclusion

Amatera shows how the infostealer market works today. A developer maintains the product, and other actors distribute it via compromised websites, ads, fake AI tools, emails, or ClickFix instructions. The threat can outlive the malicious file itself, however, as passwords, cookies, session tokens, and confidential documents remain valuable even after the device has been cleaned. Stolen data can fuel both immediate fraud or later intrusions, and the rise in detections in 2026 shows attackers adopting and adapting malicious toolsets at a rapid clip.

Title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief: eMudhra Certificate Compromise Highlights the Value of Protection Delivered by an AI-Native SASE Platform
Context: The post Cato CTRL Threat Brief: eMudhra Certificate Compromise Highlights the Value of Protection Delivered by an AI-Native SASE Platform appeared first on Cato Networks
Full Text:
Executive summary

Eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) private keys were compromised after being generated with insufficient randomness. Attackers could use these keys to forge certificates and impersonate legitimate websites or services to clients that still trust them. An attacker able to intercept a connection could potentially read or modify sensitive traffic.

We have deployed a certificate-trust update through our centrally managed PoP architecture, removing affected eMudhra certificates from the trust store used for TLS inspection. Delivering the update through the Cato Cloud removed the need for customers to patch security appliances at individual locations.

What happened?

Intermediate CAs sign certificates used to authenticate websites and services. Compromising their private keys can enable attackers to issue fraudulent certificates for domains they do not control. Organizations can therefore face exposure even when their legitimate certificates come from another provider.

Google and Mozilla received reports on October 17, 2026, and distributed emergency certificate blocks that day.

Mozilla also released updates associated with CVE-2026-113470. These include the certificate block list directly in Firefox and Thunderbird, protecting installations even when automatic block-list updates are disabled or unavailable.

Google found that no website certificates issued through the six affected TLS intermediates had appeared in Certificate Transparency (CT) logs before its emergency block took effect. CT logs are public records of certificates. Browsers that enforce CT, including Chrome, require valid proof that a certificate has been submitted to these logs before accepting it. Those browsers would therefore have rejected fraudulent certificates from the affected intermediates even before receiving the emergency blocks.

However, this protection does not extend to all software. Some applications, older browsers, or configurations without CT enforcement may have accepted unlogged fraudulent certificates if they still trusted the affected intermediates. The absence of certificates from those intermediates in CT logs before Google’s block therefore does not prove that no attacks occurred.

eMudhra says its root private keys and other intermediate CAs are unaffected. Its investigation remains ongoing.

Business risks

The exposure extends beyond employee browsers. Applications, API integrations, containers, and embedded devices may use independent trust stores or lack effective certificate-revocation checks.

Potential business consequences include:

Credential theft and data exposure: Intercepted connections could expose passwords, session tokens, and confidential information.

Transaction manipulation: Attackers impersonating trusted services could alter business communications or API responses.

Service disruption: Emergency trust removal can also reject legitimate certificates. Google announced a broader root-removal rollout expected on October 27, requiring affected website operators to replace their certificates.

Operational costs: Identifying and updating separate trust stores across applications and infrastructure creates work and opportunities for missed remediation.

These are potential impacts, not evidence of observed exploitation.

Our response: centralized control, global enforcement

The Cato AI-native SASE Platform converges networking and security in a cloud-native service delivered through globally distributed points of presence (PoPs). Our Single Pass Cloud Engine provides integrated security enforcement, while centralized management allows us to deliver updates across our cloud infrastructure. This reduces the coordination and maintenance work customers would otherwise undertake across distributed security appliances.

Centralized operations also support controlled deployment. Our established PoP change-management practices include phased rollouts, validation, monitoring, and rollback capabilities to manage operational risk as the platform evolves.

What this means for our customers

We have centrally deployed a certificate-trust update across our globally distributed PoPs, removing affected eMudhra certificates from the trust store used for TLS inspection. Customers do not need to make configuration changes to receive this update.

Analysis of our data lake showed that the certificate chains affected by this update appeared in only a very small proportion of the network flows examined. Based on this limited usage, we expect minimal connectivity impact for customers.

For details about the update and potential connectivity impact, see the security update.

For locations or connections that access the internet outside our platform, organizations should apply the relevant vendor updates or extend our platform’s coverage so those connections are subject to our certificate-validation controls.

Title: Would Your Employees Join a Fake Anthropic AI Preview?
Context: In other campaigns, threat actors have abused non-AI, trusted services like link shorteners or cloud collaboration platforms as the first link in a phishing campaign to avoid...
Full Text:
By: Intelligence Team, Jacob Malimban

Since September 2026, threat actors have been sending emails that appear to be an invitation to a private Anthropic AI meeting, but are actually attempts to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials. Exclusive access to new AI technology is valuable to many organizations, which is why threat actors use it as a lure in their phishing emails.

Risks to the organization from this campaign include threat actors compromising a sensitive account, accessing the account’s sensitive documents (e.g. proprietary marketing material), and using the compromised account as an initial vector to further infiltrate the organization. Employees must stay vigilant, as these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies due to the abuse of legitimate tools like URL shorteners and CAPTCHAs.

Cofense Intelligence consolidates campaign data, including indicators of compromise (IOCs) such as malicious web addresses, phishing email content, and broader campaign context, into Active Threat Reports (ATRs), providing a comprehensive view of identified threats. ATRs contain the full infection chain from the initial phishing link to the final malware file or credential phishing resource. If one ATR IOC appears in the organization, cybersecurity professionals can read the ATR to understand the phishing attack’s impact and mitigations. Each ATR has been curated by a human analyst. This human-vetted intelligence provides context and the campaign information necessary to mitigate future phishing attacks. For this private Anthropic AI preview campaign, actionable intelligence can be found in ATRs 423868, 423866, and 423475.

Key Points

The campaign contains a tantalizing, private offer to preview Anthropic AI technology, which may be enough for employees to click before inspecting the email.

The video teleconference software GoTo Webinar, which is used to send legitimate meeting emails and is usually not blocked by email security technologies, was abused to send a threat actor’s URL instead.

The URL shortener zpr[.]io, which turns long URLs into short links, has been abused to help these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies.

CAPTCHAs, which are tests that confirm a real human is visiting the website, are similarly abused to prevent automated analysis.

Threat actors use subdomains and dashes (-) to obfuscate the malicious URL.

Step 1: The Invitation Email

Figure 1: Anthropic meeting invitation email used in credential phishing (ATR 423475).

Emails in this campaign claim to be an exclusive invitation to see Anthropic’s new AI tool. Many organizations are deciding how AI fits into their business, so a private preview would be very valuable if the email were real. As developments in AI continue to dominate the news cycle, getting a private preview of advancements in Anthropic’s AI is an effective phishing lure.

The phishing email appears to be an abuse of the legitimate GoTo Webinar service. The email sender address appears to be customercare@gotowebinar[.]com. Threat actors have previously abused that email address and GoTo Webinar’s free trial in 2020. The email also contains a footer with GoTo Webinar branding.

The text in the email contains no obvious spelling errors. The email sender name, however, reads “Austin from nthropic” with the “A” missing from Anthropic. Although this is a small misspelling, it is still a useful warning sign.

The link in the email appears to be generated by Zapier’s URL shortener service. Zapier is a legitimate business process automation company, and their URL Shortener is designed to work with Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible AI. Unfortunately, this tool has been abused by threat actors during this Anthropic AI Preview campaign. In other campaigns, threat actors have abused non-AI, trusted services like link shorteners or cloud collaboration platforms as the first link in a phishing campaign to avoid being blocked by email security technologies.

Step 2: The First Checkpoint

Figure 2: Cloudflare CAPTCHA page to hinder automated analysis (ATR 423868).

If the phishing email link is clicked, a CAPTCHA page appears. This Cloudflare CAPTCHA must be completed before the phishing content is shown. This CAPTCHA is the first of two checkpoints that help threat actors block automated scans of their website. Because CAPTCHAs are common on legitimate websites, phishing recipients may believe all is well and everything is secure because of the CAPTCHA.

Step 3: The Fake Meeting Page

Figure 3: Zoom-spoofing page with Anthropic meeting information (ATR 423475).

After completing the CAPTCHA, a Zoom-spoofing meeting invitation page appears. This brand does not match the GoTo Webinar branding from the email. The page’s Zoom branding is consistent with the “zoom” in the malicious domain, us968web-zoom[.]us.

If the phishing recipient wants to attend the “meeting”, they need to register for the event. They are prompted to register with their work email. Credential phishing occurs when the user clicks on either “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft”.

Step 4: The Second Checkpoint

Figure 4: Custom CAPTCHA page to further hinder automated analysis (ATR 423475).

After clicking “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft”, another CAPTCHA page appears. This CAPTCHA requires a sliding motion to “unlock” the page. This report covers the private Anthropic AI Preview campaign that uses a fake invitation lure, multiple CAPTCHAs, and Google and Microsoft login page replicas. Once the employee has reached the credential phishing page, they may not be looking for warning signs anymore. The Google credential phishing page only targets usernames, whereas the Microsoft credential phishing page asks for both the username and password. Remind employees that both the URL and domain determine whether a login page is legitimate. Context: Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Since the spring of 2026, Insikt Group has observed multiple Russian-language traffer teams that have quickly adapted affiliate-fraud models to capitalize on growing public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi. The platforms offered by three such teams — AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team — provide websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance. This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims. The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds. These mechanisms include controlled trading outcomes, fabricated market activity, artificial withdrawal restrictions and fees, and the collection of sensitive identity and payment information.

Artificial intelligence (AI) further accelerates this opportunism by reducing the time, cost, and expertise required to adapt campaigns to emerging events. Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim engagement.

The rapid adoption of prediction markets by multiple traffer teams illustrates a broader threat from mature fraud ecosystems that can pivot toward emerging technologies, financial products, and cultural trends without having to develop entirely new criminal capabilities. Prediction markets are particularly well-suited to this model because legitimate platforms already combine cryptocurrency, speculative financial activity, rapidly changing news events, and social media discussion. Fraud actors can imitate these characteristics to establish credibility and manufacture urgency. As the fraudulent prediction markets gain visibility, additional traffer teams may experiment with the prediction market theme or reuse the underlying tooling for adjacent fraud schemes.

Key Findings

AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team supply affiliates with simulated prediction-market websites, administrative panels, payment infrastructure, and promotional support. Advertised compensation includes 70% to 80% of net profits for AtlasCore affiliates, a minimum 60% revenue share for PolyFucked affiliates, and a base 70% share of victim deposits for Magnetic Team affiliates.

AtlasCore’s Telegram posts recorded approximately $10.97 million in claimed deposits across its scam offerings between May 2 and September 18, 2026, with the deposits predominantly associated with prediction markets. PolyFucked separately advertises approximately $2.4 million in quarterly turnover. Both figures rely on threat actor reporting and remain unverified.

Magnetic Team advertises more than 3,000 simulated traders across more than 5,000 markets to fabricate convincing trading activity. Its code exposes configurable withdrawal-blocking pretexts, forced-loss controls, and pools of up to 20,000 deposit wallets per blockchain. AtlasCore similarly exposes settings to force wins or losses and impose individualized withdrawal restrictions.

All three traffer teams advertise or provide AI-assisted victim support. AtlasCore and PolyFucked also supply guidance for AI-generated promotional content, including synthetic influencers and branding, respectively. Magnetic Team’s source code contains indicators of likely AI-assisted development, suggesting AI use may extend to building and maintaining the underlying fraud platforms, although that assessment remains unconfirmed.

Insikt Group identified over 100 unique domains and subdomains associated with AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team, including administrative infrastructure and scam websites likely operated by the teams or their affiliates.

Threat Analysis

AtlasCore

In August 2026, Insikt Group identified a post on a low-tier cybercriminal forum seeking affiliates to join the traffer team “AtlasCore”. The thread was first created on May 15, 2026, by the user “AtlasCore”. The affiliate program was also advertised on a top-tier cybercriminal forum by the user “AtlasCorp” on May 28, 2026. The program includes an offering for prediction markets, as well as more typical traffer scams such as cryptocurrency exchanges and casinos.

Title: Inside KeyDrift: Analyzing historical UAT-11473 activity on Cisco SD-WAN

Full Text:
Cisco Talos has identified UAT-11473, a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) actor, who exploited CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco SD-WAN Catalyst Controller instances to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to affected systems.

UAT-11473 then installed a custom malware framework we track as “KeyDrift” consisting of multiple components geared towards collecting sensitive keying information, acting as backdoors and intermediate command-and-control (C2) hosts.

Observed targeting spans across space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research.

Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-11473’s operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” covert access network.

KeyDrift is a custom malware framework that is designed to operate in Cisco SD-WAN controller environments. Talos assesses with high confidence that the framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material. KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records.

The framework's primary component is PolyFlame, a memory-resident module deployed through modified runit service paths. PolyFlame is injected into legitimate running vdaemon processes, and it can also masquerade as a packed “aaamgrd” loader variant. Once resident, PolyFlame interposes socket, DTLS, and runtime-linker behavior through functions such as recvfrom, sendto, getpeername, dlopen, dlsym, mprotect, and “/proc/%d/maps” parsing. This gives KeyDrift access to SD-WAN control-plane traffic from inside legitimate controller daemon execution rather than through a conventional endpoint beacon.

LittleFilch, another component of the KeyDrift framework, provides the collection and exfiltration capability identified in the framework. The module hooks “SSL_read” inside vdaemon, inspects decrypted control-plane buffers, extracts keying material for a list of predefined edge nodes, and stages the data locally in encrypted format for exfiltration.

Talos assesses with high confidence that KeyDrift's intended operational purpose is Cisco SD-WAN control-plane collection: persistent controller residence, in-band traffic access, key-material extraction from decrypted control messages, and encrypted staging or exfiltration of the recovered material. Observed variations of the KeyDrift modules and deployment mechanisms suggest active development of the framework’s capabilities.

KeyDrift analysis

KeyDrift uses Cisco SD-WAN runit service paths as its primary execution anchor. In the PolyFlame sshd deployment, the actor modifies the service run script, remounts /rootfs.rw executable, launches a malicious script “conf_sshd” in the background, and then starts the legitimate sshd service. The loader script enumerates running vdaemon PIDs, records them in “/tmp/system-vdaemon”, and invokes the injector component “rsshd” to inject PolyFlame (“libdssl.so”) into each process.

Recovered conf_sshd logic uses the same control flow across reviewed samples:

Figure 1. conf_sshd control flow logic.

Runit launchers

The observed sshd runit launcher preserves normal Cisco SD-WAN sshd startup logic while adding two malicious lines before service execution, which remount “/rootfs.rw” executable and background execution of conf_sshd, which then drives rsshd injection into vdaemon.

Figure 2. conf_sshd execution logic.

The recovered aaamgr runit launcher from an affected vBond appliance uses a parallel service-wrapper pattern, but it executes the packed aaamgrd PolyFlame loader directly. The deletion of the writable-overlay PAM configurations for sshd and login before remounting “/rootfs.rw” executable if part of the legitimate script, along with the invocation of the aaamgrd daemon via Python:

Figure 3. aamgrd daemon launch.

PolyFlame

PolyFlame is the primary operational module in the KeyDrift framework. PolyFlame operates at the socket and DTLS control-plane layer. PolyFlame serves two primary purposes:

Command execution via a TinyShell-styled backdoor

Intermediate C2 that can forward commands to and from the C2 to other peers

PolyFlame is primarily injected into the vdaemon process, providing operational obfuscation and access to all in-process state: DTLS session keys, vEdge topology, OMP routes, and policy tables. No hardcoded IPv4 addresses, binding ports, callback domains, URLs, host headers, or polling interval were recovered from the analyzed PolyFlame samples. PolyFlame is designed for in-band control or tasking over Cisco SD-WAN control-plane traffic rather than a conventional fixed external beacon.

This implant is meant to serve as a hook of the recvfrom() API call. The original recvfrom is replaced by a malicious subroutine in the vdaemon process. When recvfrom is called in the vdaemon process, the malicious subroutine will first execute the real/legitimate recvfrom() API to obtain the C2 IP address info for communicating with it in the future.

PolyFlame’s time check

The recvd data from the C2 consists of the MD5 value of a specific DATE. PolyFlame will calculate the local time on the device in format “%Y-%m-%d" and calculate its MD5 hash. If the MD5 calculated by the device does not match with the one sent by the C2, the implant will stop further execution. Otherwise, the implant then uses an “administrative code” from the C2 and performs an action.

PolyFlame’s tasking

PolyFlame contains an administrative mode that processes the admin code sent by the C2, that defines operations — it's one of the first flags checked in the backdoor:

Code = 1: Generate random bytes and send to C2. This is likely a check-in beacon or heartbeat for the C2.

Code = 2: Set implant type to backdoor (TinyShell) or intermediate C2.

Code = 3: Set up the command handler for the intermediate C2.

Any other code value: Check the implant type flag currently set. Based on the implant type flag, either send the accompanying data to TinyShell or the intermediate C2 component for processing.

PolyFlame’s command execution

PolyFlame contains a backdoor that matches the capabilities of TinyShell: file read, file write, and arbitrary command execution, but not interactive shell. This backdoor component’s implementation is quite similar to TinyShell, but the command codes differ. PolyFlame handles the following command codes:

Code = 0x100: Execute command using “/bin/sh -c <command>”

Code = 0x200: Write file to disk.

Code = 0x300: Read file from disk and send to the C2.

PolyFlame as an intermediate C2 component

The intermediate C2 component is a one-to-many handler (somewhat like a one-to-many multiplexer) — meaning the implant can connect to only one C2 but can connect to many peers who can be served by the intermediate C2 component. Similar to the TinyShell-backdoor component, the intermediate C2 component also accepts and processes specific command codes from the C2:

Code = 0x403: Create a thread to connect to the specified peer IP. Make a new connection and keep socket alive until specified.

Code = 0x404: Send data recvd from the C2 to a connected peer.

Code = 0x405: Remove a peer from the list of active connections.

Code = 0x407: Send a response recvd from a peer, back to the C2.

Code = 0x408: Set a specific value in memory.

PolyFlame variant: aaamgrd

Talos has observed a distinct PolyFlame variant that masquerades as the aaamgr service. The legitimate Cisco aaamgr component is a Python package; it does not normally appear as a compiled ELF runit service. This PolyFlame variant is executed by a malicious runit service under “/etc/sv/aaamgr/” with aaamgrd and a modified run launcher.

aaamgrd is a statically linked ELF64 executable with no section headers, a single RWE loader segment, and an RC4-encrypted embedded ELF payload. The loader uses direct syscalls including ptrace, fork, wait4, kill, tgkill, mmap, and mprotect. It performs an anti-debug check by deobfuscating /proc/%d/status and TracerPid: and exits if a tracer is present.

The observed staging sequence was:

Figure 4. PolyFlame staging sequence.

Note that in addition to the implant execution staging, there are also indications of timestomping.

LittleFilch: libcommon.so TLS interception module

LittleFilch is a control-session interception module positioned to collect data-plane keying material from control sessions visible to the injected vSmart process.

LittleFilch installs an SSL_read hook inside vdaemon. The hook calls the original SSL_read, then processes returned buffers only when the returned size is greater than 0x18F, the first decrypted byte is 0x07, and three marker patterns are checked for presence. These marker bytes are followed by the actual artifacts that LittleFilch aims to record:

LittleFilch records the extracted keying material and RSA-encrypts it before writing the output to “/var/tmp/vdaemon.bin”. It can then send the encrypted content over UDP in a DTLS 1.2 application-data style record.

Figure 5. Keying material recording format used by LittleFilch.

LittleFilch expects its configuration file — located at “/var/tmp/vdaemon.conf” — to contain two host port lines: one local bind IP/port and one remote destination IP/port. It deletes “/var/tmp/vdaemon.conf” after reading it. Talos has not been able to recover the “vdaemon.conf” file.

Title: Unwrapping Retail Peak Season Cyber Threats
Context: This includes the SolarWinds software supply chain compromise in December 2020 and the exploitation of a Log4j zero-day vulnerability in December 2021
Full Text:
Introduction

During the 2025 peak holiday shopping season, the National Retail Federation predicted that retail sales would surpass $1 trillion USD for the first time, with Salesforce later reporting that online sales equated to $1.3 trillion globally. This included $294 billion in the United States and $262 billion influenced by AI and agents. Cybercriminals are highly aware that the holiday season is generally the most profitable for retailers, and look to capitalize on it for their own financial gain.

This blog explores the main cyber threats that retail organizations need to be aware of and prepared to defend against as we approach peak shopping season in 2026. We highlight notable security events that occurred in prior years during this time period. We also examine relevant threats from both an enterprise and guest point of view and provide examples of the evolving trend of autonomous attacks that could impact retailers.

Background

Since 2020, there have been several notable security events disclosed toward the end of peak shopping season. This includes the SolarWinds software supply chain compromise in December 2020 and the exploitation of a Log4j zero-day vulnerability in December 2021. Both events posed complexities for retail security teams as they occurred during a period where code freezes were likely in place. This limited the ability for organizations to make changes to critical technology systems to prevent any operational disruption to core technology infrastructure.

In addition to these broader threat landscape events, retailers typically face an increase in many types of financially-motivated attacks during this time period. This includes tactics and techniques designed to target both enterprises and guests alike.

Based on years of previous activity against Fortune 100 retailers from cyber threats during peak shopping season, these are the types of attacks that retailers should be primarily focused on detecting and responding to this time of year.

Enterprise-Focused Threats

Ransomware

Ransomware continues to pose a major risk for retail organizations heading into peak shopping season due to potential for operational disruption that could negatively impact the guest experience (in-store and online) and supply chain requirements (inventory).

As of Sept. 30, 2026, ransomware operators have claimed 565 retail organizations as victims this year, with the median company revenue hovering around $22 million. The top three ransomware operators that claimed retail victims are TGR-CRI-1173 (aka The Gentlemen), Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Howling Scorpius (aka Akira).

One example of a ransomware incident that impacted a retailer during peak shopping season occurred in December 2023, when Ambitious Scorpius (aka ALPHV) stole millions of customer records from a victim and caused significant operational disruption in terms of delayed order fulfillment, canceled e-commerce orders and slowed inventory replenishment.

To mitigate ransomware risks that jeopardize uptime, retailers need to deploy automated containment mechanisms alongside robust network segmentation strategies. Security teams should:

Leverage advanced endpoint protection featuring real-time behavioral analysis to rapidly isolate compromised assets

Enforce zero trust access across the enterprise to limit lateral movement

Utilize inline sandboxing capabilities to inspect suspicious binaries and stop zero-day exploits before execution

Data Theft and Extortion

Data theft and extortion attacks continue to rise in volume as cybercriminals like Bling Libra (aka ShinyHunters) and Hazy Scorpius (aka CL0P) forgo ransomware to accelerate their attack lifecycles without compromising their actions on objectives.

The 2026 Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report found that extortion incidents without the use of encryption (78%) in 2025 dropped below the 90% range for the first time in several years. Consumers put a lot of trust in retailers safeguarding their personal data, and such extortion incidents this time of year severely damage it.

One notable example occurred in December 2021, when Bling Libra stole hundreds of gigabytes of data from a victim. This included customer email addresses, hashed passwords, customer payment invoices and internal employee files containing salaries and tax IDs.

To mitigate data theft and extortion risks threatening customer personal information and transactional records, organizations must deploy comprehensive enterprise data loss prevention (DLP) controls across their enterprise environments to identify and restrict illicit data exfiltration. Security teams should combine DLP capabilities with continuous attack surface management (ASM) to identify and remediate publicly accessible systems, while implementing zero trust access to strictly limit access privileges based on the principle of least privilege.

Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)

DDoS also poses a major risk for retailers during peak shopping season because these attacks severely impact the operational uptime for e-commerce platforms if successful.

During the December 2025 holiday rush, the pro-Russian hacktivist group Noname057(16) used the DDoSia botnet to launch coordinated TCP SYN and HTTP GET request floods targeting the victim's web-facing portals and API endpoints. This DDoS attack knocked its central systems offline, paralyzed package tracking tools, disrupted e-commerce merchant payment services and delayed parcel processing across their retail distribution networks.

To mitigate DDoS risks threatening e-commerce and payment processing platforms, organizations must combine inline application-layer protections. Security teams should:

Deploy dynamic rate-limiting controls to protect against web site request floods

Implement automated mitigation to filter malicious connections

Utilize distributed edge networks to absorb large-scale traffic spikes before impacting critical systems

Digital Skimming

Although carding shops are not as prevalent as they were in prior years, digital skimming continues to be a popular technique used by cybercriminals to steal and monetize payment card information.

One example of a digital skimming incident that impacted retailers during peak shopping season occurred in October 2024, when unspecified threat actors exploited the CosmicSting vulnerability (CVE-2024-34102) to execute remote code on unpatched servers. This led to the installation of persistent backdoors and the injection of payment skimming scripts into checkout flows, affecting roughly 5% of all online stores running on prominent e-commerce platforms worldwide leading into Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

To mitigate digital skimming risks threatening payment processing workflows, organizations must implement web application and API protection (WAAP) solutions to monitor web traffic, intercept remote code execution attempts and prevent unauthorized client-side script manipulation. Security teams should:

Leverage cloud security posture management (CSPM) alongside application security posture management (ASPM) to continuously identify server vulnerabilities

Remediate unpatched flaws

Correct security configuration drift prior to holiday code freezes

Guest-Focused Threats

Account Takeover

Credential stuffing attacks are a major concern for retailers during peak shopping season as they directly impact the trust of their customers if an account is compromised. This is even more damaging if the customer has payment card information saved in their account.

One key example occurred in December 2022, when unspecified threat actors used automated scripts targeting the victim’s mobile app and web login APIs. They used large databases of stolen credentials to conduct the attack, which ultimately led to the compromise of thousands of loyalty accounts. The actors were able to drain stored gift card balances, steal mobile payment funds and collect rewards points before advertising access to the compromised accounts on dark web forums.

To mitigate account takeover risks threatening mobile applications and authentication APIs, organizations must implement WAAP solutions with advanced bot mitigation capabilities to effectively distinguish credential stuffing campaigns from legitimate customer access without friction. Security teams should complement this by deploying advanced security to identify and block traffic attempting to communicate with malicious command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used to orchestrate automated login attempts.

Gift Card Fraud

Retail customers typically increase their purchase of gift cards during holiday periods. Cybercriminals are aware of this trend and typically ramp up their targeting of this form of digital currency during peak shopping season.

Unit 42 reported on the credit card fraud-based Jingle Thief campaign in October 2025. We continue to track this activity as CL‑CRI‑1032 (aka Storm-0539).

These threat actors send phishing and smishing messages to socially engineer employees at targeted retailers to obtain credentials for initial access. From there, they typically exploit cloud-based infrastructure, gain unauthorized access to sensitive data and issue unauthorized gift cards to monetize them at scale for financial gain.

AI-Powered Attacks

Back in May 2026, we predicted that threat actors would weaponize frontier AI models within 3–5 months. That prediction has already come true. Unit 42 recently disclosed an incident where a human attacker used frontier AI models to autonomously conduct various aspects of their intrusion to condense the timespan of their attack to under 10 hours. This typically would’ve taken multiple human operators at least two weeks to accomplish.

Since our report, several other security vendors have disclosed similar findings that directly relate to the types of threat that retailers are likely to face this peak shopping season. This includes Anthropic's reporting on Bling Libra using Claude to accelerate reconnaissance and exfiltration activities. Gambit Security has reported on an attacker using multiple open source harnesses to steal more than 600,000 payment card records from retailers using JavaScript-based web skimmers. NorForge also published their own findings related to Gambit Security's report on the usage of the Cairn autonomous penetration testing agent by a threat actor to infiltrate retail e-commerce sites, POS infrastructure, and web applications across the globe.

To defend against autonomous AI threats capable of compressing intrusion timelines to less than 10 hours, retailers must unify endpoint, network, cloud and identity data into an automated security operations infrastructure. Integrating centralized visibility with machine-learning triage and real-time automation orchestration enables security teams to:

Swiftly isolate affected systems

Invalidate compromised accounts

Drastically reduce mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR) from hours to minutes.

Conclusion

Peak shopping season is the most critical time of the year for retailers to ensure consistent operational uptime and maintenance of customer trust. The types of enterprise and guest-facing threats listed in this blog pose a clear and present risk to disrupting the core tenants of the retail shopping experience.

The ability for cyber defenders at retailers to reduce their MTTD and MTTR from hours to minutes is even more critical given the adoption of frontier AI models by financially-motivated actors.

To achieve this level of operational resilience, retail security teams can leverage the Palo Alto Networks security platform for an integrated, AI-driven security architecture that unifies enterprise-wide telemetry into automated response. Integrating Cortex XSIAM and XDR for real-time threat containment alongside Zero Trust network defense allows organizations to stop complex intrusions before they disrupt peak holiday operations. Furthermore, deploying Cortex Cloud will safeguard e-commerce platforms, protecting critical transaction paths from high-impact threat vectors.

If your retail organization experiences a cyber attack during peak shopping season, the Unit 42 Incident Response team is here and ready to support as needed.

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

Full Text:
Every enterprise has identity debt: over-privileged accounts, insecure credential storage, and poor control of account lifecycle are just a few weaknesses we see all the time. But what if that debt could be turned into a strategic advantage against attackers?

CISA recently described decoys, tripwires, breadcrumbs, and honeytokens as practical mechanisms for detecting post-compromise activity. It got me thinking about how we can apply this defensive concept at the identity layer, where an attempted authentication can become both a detection signal and an inline containment decision. In other words, is there a world where we can weaponize Identity Security controls as a set of simple but effective tripwires across enterprise environments?

I think there is—and, even better, I think it has potential to turn any environment into the kind of classic laser hallway you see in heist movies, with red beams criss-crossing the route to the goal, ready to alert and ready to stop the latest threats.

So, in this blog, we’re going to look at how organizations can turn the same weaknesses attackers target into opportunities to generate rapid, high-fidelity signals with minimal operational risk.

But first: What are cyber decoys?

Cyber decoys are legitimate-looking systems, accounts, and data designed to distract and detect adversaries or facilitate collection of threat intelligence.

When operationalized with monitoring and alerting, they can become tripwires to provide high-fidelity signals to defenders. CISA also recommends mapping decoy coverage to MITRE ATT&CK and MITRE Engage, continuously testing the controls, and refining them based on observed adversary behaviour.

Why does this matter now?

The Hugging Face attack alone generated 17,000 unique events to analyse and correlate in a matter of a few days. As we prepare for a reality where attacks like these are commonplace, generating signal from noise to drive effective detection, response and containment has never been more important.

The focus is primarily on enhancing correlation. Hugging Face recommended that organizations focus on this in their post-incident call, having used an open-source model successfully—evidently a good investment. However, even the world’s most effective correlation engine will remain subject to data pipeline and ingestion constraints, some of which are owned by platform providers and cannot be optimized directly.

Generating high-fidelity signals as events unfold complements runtime controls that contain the threat, providing deeper visibility into attacker activity while enabling more informed defensive actions in real time.

Safe deception in the age of machine-speed threats

The aim of a deception strategy is to expose attackers and increase the cost and difficulty of attacks by creating a misleading picture of the environment and its resources (i.e., identities).

In agentic terms, the goal is to increase the compute/token cost of attack, use up context window, and buy time. In the future, it’ll be to funnel agentic attackers towards pre-designed traps to cause the agent to loop without escape.

Deception relies on something—for example, an identity with high privileges and easily-acquired credentials—appearing significantly less monitored, controlled, and secure than it actually is.

Without this differential between appearance and security, and supported by traditional detection and response alone, adding designed ‘honey tokens’ in the age of machine-speed threats may not generate a response fast enough to prevent exploitation of the token itself. Decoys and tripwires must therefore be safe. In other words, they must not have possible negative security implications in and of themselves.

Importantly, a safe tripwire turns the traditional detect > contain methodology, and reliance on response-time, on its head: the containment action that took place is the detection that arms your SOC with a signal, with full context of what happened.

Finally, given the rise of machine-speed threats, tripwires must not provide additional information as to the defensive posture of the organization when triggered. Transparency of the tripwire—which must not be able to be enumerated or discovered directly will become key to identifying and defeating machine-speed threats.

Identity is where the attack becomes the control point

AI attacks do not move through an environment in neat, human-sized steps. They enumerate identities, test permissions, reuse valid credentials and tokens, and pivot across trust boundaries until they find a path that works.

As we’ve already seen, the Hugging Face investigation reconstructed more than 17,000 attacker actions, grouped into approximately 6,280 clusters. The important lesson is not only the volume of activity, but the repeated identity pivots hidden inside it: credential theft, workload impersonation, token reuse, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.

That makes identity a powerful place to deploy tripwires. The tripwire should not only sit on a file, share, or endpoint. It should sit on the attempted identity path itself:

An identity requests access to an unexpected resource, in an unexpected protocol, or in a way that deviates from its baseline.

The request is evaluated using identity, source, destination, protocol, behaviour, and context.

The access is denied or fenced inline.

The same event generates a high-fidelity signal for the SOC.

Related identities and adjacent attack paths can be investigated or contained.

The attacker sees a normal access denial. The SOC sees the identity, attempted destination, protocol, source, sequence of activity, and potential attack path.

Silverfort sits inside the authentication path, where it can enforce identity-based deny and segmentation before an attacker completes lateral movement or privilege escalation.

For a machine-speed attack, detection alone often arrives too late. An identity tripwire functions as a control-flow interrupt: it breaks the sequence between authentication and the next step in the attack chain.

Instead of allowing the attacker to authenticate, discover, pivot, and escalate while defenders correlate events after the fact, the control can deny the risky authentication attempt at the point where the path is exercised. This changes the operating model from detect → correlate → respond to deny → detect → contain, resulting in a synchronous control that limits blast radius while preserving the evidence needed for investigation.

How can we leverage identity debt for this?

Identity is ripe for deception. Traditional identity debt such as over-privileged accounts, shadow admins, insecure credential storage, use of legacy protocols, and loose account lifecycle management is common—maybe even ubiquitous. These do not need to be designed and created because they already exist!

I want to be clear here: hygiene is still really important. Just because it’s possible to weaponize these existing issues, doesn’t mean good hygiene practices can be neglected.

The real question is how do we create safe tripwires?

There are three key premises to creating effective, safe tripwires:

A differential exists between the outward appearance of the account (utility to attackers), and the security state (monitored, controlled).

Usage of the tripwire does not have security implications (i.e., it does not make our security position worse).

Tripping the tripwire must not provide additional defensive context to the attacker to learn from; it must be to the attacker.

Inline identity controls allow for us to meet these three conditions. For example, deny policies create the tripwire alert to the SOC team, while denying the attacker information about why the containment activity occurred. Likewise, service accounts can be ‘fenced’ down to their standard, accepted, recorded usage behaviour and deny anomalies so, should anomalous usage be detected, we can both directly deny the usage of the account, and notify the SOC with a high-fidelity, rapid alert with full context for further action and wider correlation. All of this can happen without the agent seeing anything except ‘access denied’.

Some other cases where we can weaponize identity as tripwires (you can read more in the appendix below):

If connections to Tier 0/1 must be via bastions or PAW and are not

If dormant accounts become active

If admin accounts are used in a highly unusual way

If a legacy protocol is being used to access a sensitive server

If a low-privilege identity is attempting to reach a Tier 0 system

When one of these edges is exercised, the response should combine three actions: deny or restrict the attempted access, generate a high-confidence alert, and expose the surrounding identity relationships for investigation. This is specifically a control against AI attacks and their speed, persistence, and ability to test many paths in parallel.

What this means for security in the age of machine-speed threats

As we move into the next phase of threats—autonomously driven by AI models with the capacity to enumerate and hold your full environment and its vulnerabilities in their context window—two challenges emerge:

How do we generate signal amongst the massive volume of noise?

How do we do this in a way that does not require a loop of detect > correlate > respond, dependent on replication and processing times and humans in the loop?

CISA defines tripwires as decoys where interaction generates an alert. Silverfort extends that idea into the authentication path, where identity-based deny and segmentation can block access before lateral movement or privilege escalation completes. While a conventional tripwire detects interaction, an identity tripwire can detect, deny, and contain the attempted path in the same control loop.

Rethinking how we weaponize identity against attackers—by leveraging the identity debt that already exists—allows us to generate high-quality signal to cut through the noise, while having containment built-in. The containment activity generates the signal, rather than the signal requiring containment activity.

Doing this allows for more rapid threat detection, safely, while denying any information to the model that may help it progress its attack—and gives us a pathway to active defense in the future by funnelling agents to useless traps in an endless loop.

Tripwire

Suspicious interaction

Recommended response

Decoy service account

Authentication from any source or destination outside its tightly defined baseline

Generate an alert and apply a virtual fence

Dormant privileged account

Tier-0 access edge

Title: Managed for Malice: How Attackers Turn MDM into Remote Access
Context: Background Huntress has observed several incidents recently where threat actors have leveraged mobile device management (MDM) applications to carry out attacks
Full Text:
Acknowledgements: Special thanks to Lindsey Welch, Anton Ovrutsky, and Harlan Carvey for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Huntress has observed several incidents recently where threat actors have leveraged mobile device management (MDM) applications to carry out attacks. In these cases, legitimate management tools are being weaponized for malicious purposes, as opposed to threat actors taking advantage of inherent weaknesses in the applications themselves, such as vulnerabilities.

MDM platforms are legitimate tools that organizations use to manage employee laptops, phones, and other devices. These tools help IT teams to enroll and configure company devices remotely, enforce security policies, and deploy approved applications. However, these applications' centralized control and trusted level of access can create an entry point for threat actors if the tools are misused.

These incidents often begin with social engineering—users falling subject to business-themed lures that arrive through messaging applications and email. While not a definitive list of MDMs that could be used in such attacks, we have seen threat actors recently using well-known applications from Hexnode and Rippling.

Once registered with the MDM application, the attacker gains a trusted and privileged management path on the system. In both cases described here, Huntress observed the threat actors installing unauthorized RMM (remote monitoring and management) tools in order to further their attacks.

Mystery of the reappearing ScreenConnect

Imagine receiving an alert for an unauthorized ScreenConnect installation. Naturally, given the severity of such an alert, you prioritize it and remove the ScreenConnect agent immediately. However, several hours later, you receive another alert—same unauthorized installation. Something's clearly going on behind the scenes.

A recurring ScreenConnect installation is the first clue that this is more than an isolated, rogue RMM deployment. If both installations connected to the same destination relay, this would suggest the same threat actor was involved both times.

So how are they managing to get back in after being removed once?

We observed this activity in a recent incident, where two Huntress alerts for unauthorized ScreenConnect activity on the same device, separated by several hours, connected to the same relay.

As it happened, a threat actor had previously managed to install an MDM client from Hexnode on the system that ScreenConnect kept appearing on. Removing the RMM did little to deter them. They simply staged and installed the RMM software again.

The attack began with a phishing email. The target received several emails with proposal-related subjects like "ATTN: Official Invitation to Submit Proposal" and "Review Required" that mentioned an organization that the target likely had a business relationship with.

Clicking a link contained within the email downloaded a file from https://webdocusign.viewportal[.]es/Windows/download/index.php

which was saved to the Microsoft Edge temporary downloads folder as eD0cuSign_Installer.msi.

While the file had been named to mimic a DocuSign installer, it actually contained an installation package for a Hexnode MDM, a legitimate device management application. The package included Hexnode Gateway, the Hexnode agent, and supporting PostgreSQL components, all of which were installed on the system.

Figure 1: Execution of the Hexnode MSI, designed to resemble a (fake) DocuSign installer.

The threat actor followed up by installing ScreenConnect shortly thereafter and connecting to the attacker-controlled relay, relay.bobdthjau[.]com:8041. This resulted in a Huntress alert for an unauthorized ScreenConnect installation, and the MSP removed the RMM from the compromised computer shortly thereafter.

However, several hours later another instance of ScreenConnect was installed and reconnected to the relay. This triggered another alert, which led Huntress to isolate the endpoint, and a thorough remediation began.

Enrollment from a link

Not all incidents involve phishing techniques that trick a user into running an MSI installer. In another instance, a receptionist opened an email titled "Re: Tax Planning and Preparation Inquiry." The email included a link to what appeared to be a Microsoft Teams meeting invitation.

Clicking the link brought the target to a page titled "Calendar." While the site was taken down shortly after the attempt, it likely impersonated a Teams scheduling calendar. This page redirected to a .php file that appears to have helped facilitate enrollment into an attacker-controlled Rippling MDM tenant. All three links resided on the following domain (see the IoCs section for full URLs):

https://teams-microsoftcom5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592.kiratham[.]com

About a minute after clicking the link, a Rippling enrollment registry key appeared on the compromised system, which is consistent with registration in the MDM platform. An installation MSI for the Rippling agent was subsequently downloaded to C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\mdm\{GUID}.msi. The agent was then installed with SYSTEM-level permissions as C:\Rippling\daemon.exe.

Further investigation by Huntress determined that this activity originated from the online Rippling management agent, suggesting that the threat actor had previously created an account to carry out the attack.

Approximately 35 minutes after installation, the attackers used the MDM to stage and run a ScreenConnect installer as SYSTEM, connecting back to an attacker-controlled domain relay.pronconetydesire[.]online:8041, triggering a Huntress alert for a malicious ScreenConnect instance.

Tradecraft patterns & motivations

These instances, and the abuse of MDM applications in general, highlights a frustrating situation for security practitioners. The challenge is that more tools designed to help organizations manage endpoints are becoming mechanisms to compromise them. Similar to the illegitimate use of RMMs, this further complicates what we can safely consider trusted software, because reputation alone is just not sufficient to determine intent. Neither Hexnode nor Rippling are at fault here—users are simply being socially engineered into installing their software.

So where does this leave us? MDM enrollment should be treated as security-sensitive activity as opposed to a routine administrative task. An unexpected enrollment can establish persistence, provide a privileged deployment path, and allow an attacker to introduce additional tooling without relying on conspicuous payloads like known malware.

These incidents also demonstrate how detection cannot treat RMM installation as an isolated event. While the RMM client, and its subsequent activity, may have been the most visible part of the intrusion, removing it does not remove the unauthorized management architecture that delivered it.

The sequence of events observed makes for a stronger signal—social engineering -> a new MDM enrollment -> RMM installation -> outbound communication with an unfamiliar relay. Because the chain can vary, correlation across identity, MDM, endpoint, and network telemetry is our best hope in providing the resiliency needed to defend against these attacks.

Mitigation Guidance

Organizations can reduce the risk faced by these techniques by controlling both the enrollment path and the applications that MDM platforms are allowed to deploy.

Maintain an inventory of authorized MDM products, tenants, agents, and RMM instances. Treat any unexpected enrollment, management agent, or RMM instance as a security event.

Train users to verify unexpected meeting, document-signing, and proposal-review requests. Email and web controls should also scrutinize business-themed lures.

If a compromise is suspected, isolate the endpoint, remove the endpoint from the unauthorized MDM tenant, disable attacker-created accounts, revoke active sessions or tokens, reset affected credentials, and reimage the endpoint if its integrity cannot be confirmed.
