Full Text:
Executive Summary

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 to fix two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2. The two flaws are known together as PHP2Shell. They were disclosed by the security firms Calif and Wiz and by OpenAI, working with the PHP security team, after AI-assisted auditing turned an out-of-memory weakness that a 2024 audit had flagged but could not prove exploitable into working remote code execution.

Both vulnerabilities sit in PHP's memory management and error handling, code that nearly every request touches, and the earliest affected path dates to PHP 5.4.0. An unauthenticated attacker can execute code on the web server or read its process memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys belonging to other requests. On Apache with mod_php, the attack runs before any application code executes, which means an application with no bugs of its own is still exposed. As of October 21, 2026, no verified proof-of-concept code is available publicly. Attack attempts have been observed by Cloudflare after the leak, but no confirmed in-the-wild compromise has yet been reported.

While upgrading every PHP runtime remains the primary control, SentinelOne agent detects attackers’ post-exploitation activities. Once an attacker has code execution on the web server process, the behavior that follows web server flaws: execute shell commands, drop and invoke webshells, download and execute custom payloads and outbound connections. On managed hosts, the Singularity™ agent and Singularity AI SIEM detection content look for such behaviors, and Purple AI® can be used to hunt for it during the patching window. The separate memory-disclosure path runs no code on the host, so it leaves no process behavior to detect; that path is instead surfaced through web server, WAF, and CDN telemetry forwarded into AI SIEM.

This report details PHP2Shell's mechanism, affected versions, and confirmed activity, and outlines how SentinelOne customers can strengthen their defenses.

Key Highlights

The flaw is in PHP itself, not in any application. WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, Laravel, and other web applications are all exposed on an affected PHP version, because the vulnerable code is in the runtime beneath them.

The patch is the only complete fix. PHP states plainly that no configuration change fully closes the vulnerability. Every interim mitigation reduces one attack path and leaves others open.

The unauthenticated path runs before your code does. On Apache with mod_php, a single crafted HTTP request triggers the flaw during request startup, so application-level controls never see it. PHP assesses the risk as highest for mod_php.

Memory disclosure leaks secrets without a shell. One path reads live worker memory and returns passwords, tokens, API keys, and certificates with no code execution, which makes it quieter than a shell and harder to catch with execution-focused tooling.

End of Life PHP will not get a patch. Organizations running PHP 8.1 and prior will not receive an official release. Source-only backports exist for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, and distribution or LTS vendors may offer fixed packages.

Leverage SentinelOne platform post-exploitation coverage. The detection by the agent is agnostic to the vulnerability and exploit chain and focuses on attackers activity following the exploit, including but not limited to, installation and usage of webshells, command executions and outbound connection behavior that follows the code execution.

Organizations should take the following steps immediately:

Update every PHP runtime to a fixed version and restart Apache, PHP-FPM, and any long-running workers.

Inventory internet-facing PHP, including the copies bundled inside appliances, control panels, and vendor software.

Isolate end-of-life PHP (8.1 and older) from the internet until it can be upgraded.

Rotate credentials, tokens, and keys that a PHP worker could hold in memory on any exposed, unpatched system.

Monitor the official PHP changelog for relevant updates

What is PHP2SHELL

PHP2Shell is a family of memory-safety vulnerabilities in core PHP, grouped under two CVEs that share one root cause. When PHP hits a fatal condition such as exhausting its configured memory limit, it does not unwind cleanly. It abandons the current operation with a “longjmp” out of the C call stack, so no cleanup runs and nothing records that a data structure was left half-built. A later cleanup routine, or a later request, then trusts that state.

CVE-2026-109618 is the out-of-memory case. PHP marks request data as valid before allocating memory for it. If that allocation hits the memory limit and fails, the entry is left pointing to uninitialized heap memory. When the failed request runs its cleanup routine, it processes these stale bytes, leading to corruption..

CVE-2026-109619 is the stale-state case. When a fatal error occurs, PHP fails to clean up properly, leaving a global pointer pointing to memory that has already been freed. Because worker processes handle multiple requests, a subsequent request on the same worker can interact with this freed memory before initialization resets it – resulting in a use-after-free condition. Session upload progress (enabled by default) is a confirmed trigger for this behavior.

Both flaws were discovered through AI-assisted auditing under OpenAI's “Patch the Planet” program. Calif and OpenAI independently reported the root cause to the PHP security team on August 11, 2026, and Wiz reported additional attack vectors on August 24, 2026. PHP first saw signs of the underlying out-of-memory problem during a 2024 audit by OSTIF and Quarkslab, but no exploitation path was proven at the time and the fix stalled. The PHP Foundation has since described that delay as a structural failure in its security process.

On October 20, the two CVE identifiers leaked on social media. PHP released a patch on October 21, 2026.

Am I Affected?

Assume exposure for any PHP runtime below the fixed version for its branch. Check the version the web server actually loads, which can differ from the command-line version, using php --version for the CLI and the equivalent for PHP-FPM or the Apache module. Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patch in advance, and a packaged build may carry the fix under an older version number, so confirm against your vendor's advisory rather than the version string alone.

PHP states that all installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, and rates the risk highest for mod_php. Do not use configuration to rule out exposure. PHP validated mod_php code execution with default input and memory limits, and states that no configuration change is a complete mitigation. OpenAI has published a PHP version checker, which should be reviewed before you run it.

Why This Matters

A flaw in PHP itself reaches far further than a flaw in any one application. PHP is widely used across the internet, and it is embedded in content management systems, control panels such as cPanel and Plesk, and a variety of vendor applications. The hard part of this response is not applying the patch. It is finding every runtime that needs it.

The patch is also the only complete fix, and a large share of PHP cannot receive it. PHP 8.1 and older are at end of life, and Talos estimates from open-source data that around half of internet-facing PHP runs on branches with no official update. Those systems need to be upgraded to a supported branch or taken off the internet, not merely reconfigured.

Exploitation is also hard to see. The memory-disclosure path returns secrets from live worker memory without running code at all, which Wiz notes makes it harder to catch with tools focused on malicious code execution. Because the flaws execute below the application layer, Wiz also reports that application logs may contain little context, and the clearest traces are in web server and PHP error logs rather than in application telemetry.

Attack Chain

Stage 1: Reaching the Flaw Over an Unauthenticated Request

The attacker sends a crafted multipart HTTP request that places PHP's memory under pressure or forces a fatal error during request startup. A chunked or lengthless request slips past the post_max_size check, and empty file controls with deeply nested field names expand a small request body into large internal allocations.

Stage 2: Corrupting Worker State

The forced out-of-memory condition or fatal error interrupts PHP in a context that does not account for the early exit. For CVE-2026-109618, Apache with mod_php runs its request shutdown unconditionally and processes the partially initialized state as if it were valid. For CVE-2026-109619, a global pointer is left referring to freed request memory, and a later request on the same worker consumes it.

Stage 3: Code Execution or Memory Disclosure

With the heap arranged to reclaim the freed or invalid memory with attacker-controlled bytes, the corrupted state becomes a memory-corruption primitive that yields code execution as the web worker. PHP confirmed complete remote code execution against mod_php with default input and memory limits. On a separate path, the attacker instead reads live worker memory and extracts passwords, tokens, API keys, and certificates belonging to other requests, returned through the PHPSESSID response cookie, with no code execution at all.

Stage 4: Post-Exploitation

Code runs with the privileges of the web server worker, commonly www-data. From there, operators drop a web shell into the web root, spawn shells and tooling such as sh, bash, python, curl, and wget, and move laterally using any credentials recovered through memory disclosure.

Hardening Recommendations

These steps apply to any PHP estate, independent of security vendor. Patching is the only complete remediation. Everything else reduces exposure during the window before every runtime is updated.

Patch Every PHP Runtime and Restart Workers

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or to the fixed package from your Linux distribution or hosting provider.

Restart Apache, PHP-FPM, and every long-running PHP worker after updating. The running process keeps the vulnerable code until it is restarted.

Remember that updating an application, CMS, or framework does not update the PHP runtime beneath it.

Assess Your Exposure

Inventory every PHP runtime: web servers first, then vendor appliances, Windows software that bundles php.exe or php-cgi.exe, control panels such as cPanel and Plesk, and any WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, or Magento install.

Isolate end-of-life PHP (8.1 and older) behind a VPN or take it off the internet until it is upgraded to a supported branch.

Apply Interim Settings Only as a Bridge

For CVE-2026-109618, set memory_limit=-1 administratively so applications cannot override it, and keep post_max_size low. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can trigger the vulnerable path.

For CVE-2026-109619, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0, and on PHP 8.5 set fatal_error_backtraces=0, applied before request parsing and followed by a worker restart.

Treat all of these as partial. PHP confirms there is no complete configuration mitigation, and hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors, or the @ operator does not help.

Constrain the Request at the Edge

At the proxy or web application firewall, enforce limits on decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count per part, and nesting depth, including requests that arrive without a usable Content-Length.

Enable your WAF or reverse proxy vendor's managed rules for PHP2Shell, which several vendors published on October 21, and test first because rules can block legitimate traffic.

Treat the WAF as a layer, not a fix: Cloudflare saw attackers mutating payloads to bypass its rules.

If an application does not use multipart form data, block multipart requests to it before they reach PHP.

Limit Worker Reuse and Blast Radius

Lower PHP-FPM pm.max_requests so workers recycle more often, reducing how long the corrupted state can persist.

Use a cgroup memory.max as an availability boundary that kills only the affected worker, not the whole pool.

Apply SELinux or AppArmor policies to restrict what a web worker can execute.

Rotate Secrets Reachable in Process Memory

Assume any credential, session token, API key, or certificate held by a PHP worker on an exposed, unpatched system may have been disclosed.

Rotate them now rather than after confirmed compromise, because memory disclosure leaves little trace.

Hunt for Post-Exploitation

Review the web root for newly created files and web shells, and watch for new cron jobs, scheduled tasks, and accounts.

Alert on PHP worker processes (php-fpm, php-cgi, httpd, apache2, w3wp) spawning shells, interpreters, or download tools, including cmd.exe and powershell.exe on Windows.

In web server and PHP error logs, look for unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit fatal errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, and for unexplained PHP worker churn (Wiz).

Check response headers for unexpectedly large or malformed PHPSESSID cookies, which Wiz identifies as a sign of the memory-disclosure path.

Enable log_errors, a working error_log, and error_reporting=E_ALL in startup configuration for an isolated audit, as PHP recommends, and treat a clean log as supporting evidence rather than proof of safety.

Treat these signals as leads, not verdicts. They come from public research rather than confirmed attack traffic, and memory-limit errors and HTTP 500s also occur on healthy systems.

How SentinelOne Protects You

PHP2Shell executes inside the web server worker process, below the application. SentinelOne’s visibility begins where that worker runs on a host with the agent installed. The agent cannot see internal application activity which doesn’t interact with the OS or other processes as the memory-disclosure path. What SentinelOne can address is the behavior of the code executed by the attacker.

The Behavior After Exploitation

Code execution through a web server worker process has the worker’s privileges. From there the sequence is familiar. The attacker runs host and user discovery, pulls a second-stage payload with a built-in download utility, writes a web shell into the document root so a fragile memory bug does not have to be triggered twice, opens an outbound connection to attacker infrastructure, and reads application configuration files for database credentials.

Detection on the Host

The Singularity agent builds a storyline of every process group activity on a host, including the web server workers PHP2Shell targets. These workers have a predictable life: they answer HTTP requests. They do not normally start /bin/sh, run reconnaissance commands, download executables into /tmp, write new .php files into the web root, or open outbound connections to arbitrary hosts. Behavioral detection looks for that deviation from the worker’s normal behavior. With the policy mode set to protect, the agent can terminate the process tree and quarantine dropped artifacts.

Visibility at the Edge

The memory-disclosure path never starts a process, so host telemetry alone will not see it. It can leave traces in web server, WAF, and CDN logs: unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or bursts of HTTP 500s, malformed or oversized PHPSESSID cookies, and unexplained worker churn. Singularity AI SIEM can ingest those sources alongside endpoint data if you forward them. Existing content covers allowed web shell uploads, successful POSTs to server-side scripts that have never received them before, and web shell command execution at the network layer.

Hunt with Purple AI While You Patch

Patching is the only complete fix, and the Hardening section covers interim settings. While that work runs, analysts can ask Purple AI questions such as:

The 500-response question depends on web server logs being ingested.

Confirm Agent Saturation on Web-Facing Servers

Confirm the agent is deployed, healthy, and in protect mode on every server that serves PHP, including internet-facing Linux hosts.

Conclusion

The exploitation picture for PHP2Shell is moving quickly. As of October 21, 2026, no verified proof-of-concept code is available publicly. Attack attempts have been observed by Cloudflare after the leak, but no confirmed in-the-wild compromise has yet been reported. SentinelOne is monitoring PHP2Shell activity and will update this report as exploitation evidence, vendor guidance, and detection content change.

SentinelOne recommends customers follow vendor guidance and prioritize patching as the primary defensive tactic. Interim settings, WAF rules, and detection reduce risk while it is deployed. Update every PHP runtime to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, restart the workers, and confirm the fix is running on the version the web server actually loads. Move PHP 8.1 and older to a supported branch or off the internet, and rotate any secrets that a worker on an unpatched, exposed system could have held in memory.

Title: New PhaaS Platform Uses AI to Craft Phishing Lures and Mask Malicious Activity
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Abnormal AI noted that the AI Studio gives threat actors another way to prepare phishing content without writing every lure from scratch or relying exclusively on ready-made materials. They can instead request content tailored to different pretexts and audiences.

AI Studio is integrated into Athena StealthRoute's broader offering, which also combines domain and link management, a marketplace for campaign materials, visitor monitoring and cloaking controls.

Athena StealthRoute still relies on external infrastructure for credential and token harvesting, but much of the preparation and delivery workflow can be managed through a single console, the researchers noted.

Five of the six offerings in the AI Studio focus on the creation of phishing lures and related materials. However, the sixth option extends to decoy content intended to conceal the phishing attempts. The White Page option produces structured, benign-looking content that could be used as a cover when Athena StealthRoute's cloaking layer directs scanners and other unwanted visitors away from malicious destinations.

How to Detect and Defend Against Athena StealthRoute

Abnormal AI said that for defenders, the platform’s combination of cloaking and customizable content reinforces the limitations of relying on individual messages or link inspections to detect phishing attempts.

“Security scanners may encounter benign content where intended victims would reach malicious destinations, while variations in lure copy can make exact wording less useful for linking-related attacks,” the researchers said in their analysis.

Shared backend infrastructure, matching operator-console code and recognizable link structures offer additional signals for identifying Athena StealthRoute-associated activity even as individual domains and lures change.

Finally, because credential and token harvesting occur through separate downstream services, investigations must also account for the particular theft mechanism involved.

Title: Symantec Uncovers AI Agent Hijacking Models for Autonomous Cyber-Attacks
Context: Researchers from the Symantec Threat Hunter Team found the malicious agent using an AI honeypot – a system that impersonates an unprotected, internet-facing AI service in order...
Full Text:
A new AI agent developed to run a full cyber-attack without human intervention has been uncovered by security researchers.

The agent was designed to use hijacked AI models to autonomously run up to 100,000 malicious actions without human approval, including scanning for targets, exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, deploying cryptocurrency miners and reinfecting compromised systems.

Researchers from the Symantec Threat Hunter Team found the malicious agent using an AI honeypot – a system that impersonates an unprotected, internet-facing AI service in order to attract and study attacks against AI infrastructure.

They captured the agent's full instruction set in the summer of 2026, revealing how it was designed to operate autonomously, although the honeypot did not execute the attacker's tools. They described it in more details in a report published on October 21.

AI Honeypot Exposes LLMjacking

The AI honeypot recorded over 127,000 external requests from tens of thousands of unique addresses between its setup and the publication of the report.

Upon analyzing this activity, Symantec researchers discovered that the agent searches for exposed endpoints linked to large language models (LLMs), including self-hosted models, AI gateways and model context protocol (MCP) servers, to use their computing power without paying for it. This technique is sometimes called ‘LLMjacking.’

“Running a model always costs someone money, either in processing time for a self-hosted model or in per-token fees for a commercial one. By routing its work through a stranger's endpoint or a stolen key, the operators shift that cost onto the victim,” Symantec researchers noted.

With this technique, the attackers also gain anonymity and avoid potential account bans the AI model provider would issue for abuse.

The captured instructions included about 74 tools for internet-wide reconnaissance, exploiting common web frameworks, stealing databases, harvesting credentials and managing botnets.

Notably, the attackers used layered instructions designed to override commercial AI models' safety controls, disguising credential theft as legitimate development work.

A separate request also contained an obfuscated script designed to install Monero-mining software, conceal its presence and erase logs.

Self-Directed AI Agent Lowers Barrier to Cybercrime

While Symantec researchers said none of the techniques used by the attackers in this campaign are novel, their combination into a single, self-directed agent lowers the skill required for other attackers to run a broad exploitation campaign.

“An operator can hand the model a goal and let it work,” they added.

They concluded that the activity “marks a shift in how attackers are using AI,” explaining that operators have embedded AI into offensive tools rather than trying to trick public chatbots into misbehaving.

They described the model as “a reasoning engine that plans and drives the attack,” while the tool’s own modules carry out scanning, exploitation and mining against separate victims.

Title: LiteLLM Compromised, Steals Credentials
Context: We have not yet confirmed how the attacker gained access to our internal deployment, but currently suspect it was through a recently patched vulnerability
Full Text:
LiteLLM Compromised

At 11:39 UTC on October 21, a malicious version (1.107.0) of the LiteLLM package was uploaded to PyPI. This version was quarantined on PyPI as of 13:20 UTC. According to ClickPy data, the malicious version received approximately 49,000 downloads.

LiteLLM Docker containers on GHCR and Docker hub also included the trojanized version of LiteLLM. These included the v1.107.0 , latest, main-latest and main-stable tags. These were removed ~13:53 UTC.

The most recent safe version is v1.106.2.

When the malicious package is installed, three files are extracted directly into the site-packages root: cook.pth, cook.py and sitecustomize.py. These packages are designed to be executed whenever a python interpreter is started.

Per LiteLLM developer BerriAI:

malicious actions were taken through three engineers' GitHub accounts, appearing to be by way of stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens. The threat actor used one user's account triggered the project-releaser run, and another user's account to approve it. All tokens which were involved in this attack have been revoked.

And in a followup:

GitHub CLI OAuth token exposure After a thorough investigation, we have observed specific situations in which Claude Code will embed a user’s GitHub CLI OAuth token into a response body, and in situations where response bodies are logged, these tokens may appear in LiteLLM logs. Access to our internal LiteLLM deployment We identified an unexpected, innocuously named user account in our internal LiteLLM deployment, which was exposed to the public internet. We believe the attacker gained access to this deployment, obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from its logs, and subsequently used those credentials to compromise our release workflow. We have not yet confirmed how the attacker gained access to our internal deployment, but currently suspect it was through a recently patched vulnerability.

UPDATES

14:05 UTC - added IOC table

14:15 UTC - added Attack Commits details

14:40 UTC - added Credential Stealer details, noted Docker takedown

15:20 UTC - clarified dual-technique approach novelty and LLM-aided development

16:40 UTC - added diagram of payload flow

16:55 UTC - added LiteLLM statement on root cause

18:35 UTC - LiteLLM has released a blog post

19:05 UTC - added observed post-exploitation activity

21:45 UTC - updated LiteLLM details on root cause

October 22 12:55 UTC - added PyPi download stats

Payload

The payload has strong indications of LLM-aided development, including verbose variable names (encrypted_private_key_output), overly defensive error handling with generic try/except blocks, platform-specific code paths that fail silently on untested platforms (Windows marker path /tmp/ doesn't exist, fcntl/fork calls crash the remote loader), and a dead code module (exec_py) that was defined but never called. The structure suggests iterative prompting: functional on the happy path but brittle at the edges and untested.

Upon startup, the interpreter processes cook.pth, which includes a command to import cook, which loads cook.py. cook.py deobfuscates itself, runs a stealer routine and writes a maker to /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb (note this fails on Windows, as the /tmp/ path often does not exist). The stealer routine gathers system, browser, developer, cloud and AI tool secrets, encrypts them and exfiltrates to www.litellm.dev/healthcheck via a post request. This domain is attacker controlled, impersonating LiteLLM infrastructure.

Python interpreters will also attempt to execute sitecustomize.py - however, it will only run on Linux & MacOS machines. This script attempts to fetch domain.txt from a GitHub dead drop (letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt). If it receives a response, it will attempt to download a second stage python script from http://<domain>/codepy and run it. As of the time of analysis, the domain.txt file was never populated beyond initial test values. The repo has been taken down by GitHub as of 1:30 PM UTC.

The dual-technique approach, using both .pth files and sitecustomize.py simultaneously, appears to be the first documented case in the wild.

Credential Stealer

The embedded credential stealer, internally named privcollect, harvests sensitive data across 16 modules targeting browsers, cloud providers, and AI services. It extracts:

browser credentials and cookies from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari

AWS credentials from ~/.aws/, environment variables, and EC2/ECS instance metadata (IMDS)

GCP service account keys and application default credentials

Azure tokens from the CLI cache

In terms of AI-specific theft, it targets API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, and other LLM providers stored in environment variables or config files. It also collects SSH private keys, GPG keys, and shell history files.

LiteLLM Proxy stores upstream API keys in a PostgreSQL database. The stealer queries this database directly (SELECT * FROM "LiteLLM_CredentialsTable" LIMIT 500) to extract all configured provider credentials.

Harvested data is encrypted with AES-256-CBC (key wrapped with RSA-4096) and exfiltrated over HTTP to www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck using the hardcoded X-Token header and an Internet Explorer 7 user-agent string.

Attacker Commits

The payload originates with malicious commits made on github.com/Berri-AI/litellm. Note, this is a hyphenated variant of the legitimate BerriAI organization. This repository, not visible on GitHub, was used to inject the payload into the release pipeline.

Between 08:56 and 10:46 UTC on October 21, the attacker pushed 10 commits using the author email ckdi82fkoos@proton.me. The first nine commits were created on GitHub.com and therefore signed with GitHub's verified signature.

The first three (within 2 minutes) added the persistence files: cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py. Four more commits bumped version numbers to 1.107.0.

After a 39-minute gap, two commits refined the payload and added the critical data = "cook" directive to pyproject.toml, which instructed the build tool to bundle the malware into the wheel.

A final commit, made 58 minutes later with a different email (Berri-AI@users.noreply.github.com) and unsigned (suggesting a different environment), added COPY cook ./cook to the Dockerfiles.

Although the Berri-AI repository is unavailable, all commits remain accessible through the parent repository due to Git's fork object sharing. The full diff is available at: github.com/BerriAI/litellm/compare/a8113b0d...20535d8f

Post-Exploitation Activity

Wiz Research has observed abuse of stolen credentials, starting approximately 4.5 hours post-exfiltration. Between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, the attacker validated AWS instance role credentials harvested from compromised CI runners and Kubernetes nodes across multiple environments, from the following IP addresses:

168.100.8[.]57

165.227.201[.]8

Each credential was checked with sts:GetCallerIdentity, followed by bedrock:ListFoundationModels and a ListModels call, consistent with LLMjacking.

In a small number of environments, the attacker also enumerated IAM (ListRoles, ListUsers, ListAccessKeys) and performed general discovery (ListAccounts, DescribeTrails, etc.).

Recommendations

Wiz customers should review our Threat Intel Center advisory: Supply Chain Attack Targeting LiteLLM .

Title: Amazon-Themed ClickFix Campaign Serves Up Finger-Licking Malware
Context: Introduction Attackers often exploit trusted brands in their initial access lures, either by spoofing their logos or by abusing legitimate features
Full Text:
Introduction

Attackers often exploit trusted brands in their initial access lures, either by spoofing their logos or by abusing legitimate features. In the past few months, Huntress investigated incidents that began with ClickFix lures using ChatGPT, Google Docs, and many more trusted tools. In an attack method that has already struck at least three Huntress customers, a threat actor using paid search results led victims into ClickFix-style social engineering that, as is usually the case, prompts the victims to run a command in their terminal.

But the command used in this lure unusually leverages a decades-old (and infrequently used) network utility, finger, to initiate a convoluted and elaborately obfuscated sequence of attack scripts that, eventually, led to the victim's computer being infected with at least three completely different forms of infostealer and remote access malware. Threat actors have been abusing the finger utility, which (although present on most modern computers) is not well understood by most computer users, in ClickFix attacks for at least a year.

In the course of the investigation, Huntress Labs' Adversary Tactics observed a full infection chain, captured and reverse-engineered the components, and analyzed network traffic sent and received by the various payloads, in order to build a complete picture of the attack method.

A Google search, a spoofed Amazon login, and a fake CAPTCHA

Figure 1: The sponsored Google search result that led to a fake Amazon login page

The attack started with a simple search. The top sponsored result at the time of the attacks for the keyword "amazon business" (shown above) was hosted on a deceptive-looking subdomain of an attacker-controlled domain: orders-amazon[.]com[.]advancedfences[.]com.

The malicious link redirected to a fake Amazon login page, hosted in a private Google Sites cloud storage location, sites.google[.]com/view/ch-pc/sign-in. The page prompted the user to enter their email or phone number.

Figure 2: Spoofed Amazon login page

After the user hits "submit," the page pops up a fake CAPTCHA dialog. Clicking a button labeled "I'm not a robot" saves a pastejacked command to the user's clipboard, and a pop-up window instructs the user to run the command in the Windows Run box.

Figure 3: The ClickFix attack prompts the user to paste a command into their Run dialog on Windows computers

Although the following analysis covers Windows-specific payloads, the attack was cross-platform: Users who visited the page with a browser User-Agent that references macOS received alternate instructions to run a script in the Mac Terminal application, but the destination URL in that instance—hxxp[://]ashevilleroofingcontractor[.]com/curl/bc9e2dac08fb4f83dddb44f89bf7082bb4134697fbf6a99ad8ce30c634e9fe8a—was offline at the time Huntress conducted this research.

Stage 1: Literally giving users the finger

The entered commands launch the built-in utility finger.exe to communicate with a specific user account on the attacker-controlled domain grillrecipespro[.]com.

The finger command is ancient, by internet standards, predating the existence of the web itself by nearly two decades. In its halcyon heyday, people who used the internet would interact directly with Unix shell accounts on remote servers; finger offered a way for someone who owned an account to publish their contact information, a clever quotation or two, even ASCII art to what was essentially a personal bulletin board posted to their virtual office door, inside a file named .plan, stored in the root of the user's shell account directory. But for most of the past year, finger has developed a new life as a LOLbin abused in ClickFix attacks.

In this attack, the threat actor has placed a Windows script in a .plan file tied to a user account. The ClickFix command that invokes finger is, itself, obfuscated (in a rudimentary way) by breaking up the characters that make up the command with a comma, caret (^), hyphen, and underscore characters, which the Windows command interface helpfully ignores. The command, pasted into a text editor, looks like this:

Figure 4: The ClickFix command text

The command itself is not readily visible in the Run dialog because the threat actors have crafted the command line with a suffix that uses extra spaces and hyphen characters to trail the actual command. To an end user, the effect is that the content of the Run dialog seems to say, simply, "Push the Enter key."

Figure 5: The Run dialog conceals the command

The effect of the command line, however, is far from benign. It instructs the Windows command interface to execute the content contained within the .plan file at the other end of the command finger DLVBUCeFfF@grillrecipespro[.]com.

Figure 6: The top of the adversary-controlled user account's .plan file

The script content inside the remote .plan file is "hidden" with the use of 68 extra carriage-returns that put the weaponized content beyond the screen height of a typical terminal console. (Finger commands transmit plaintext over port 79/tcp by default, which should make them easy to detect or block, but since nobody uses finger anymore, most networks don't block this content.)

Well below the top of the screen, the .plan file contains a script with instructions to trigger the first stage of the attack, which requires an executable Python interpreter named ipyw32.exe that is included in a Python distribution called IronPython. So the script spawns curl to download and unpack IronPython.3.4.2.zip from its repository location, github[.]com/IronLanguages/ironpython3/releases/download/v3.4.2/IronPython.3.4.2.zip.

Figure 7: Don't you love it when a .plan comes together?

"The script places the IronPython ZIP file in the user's Temp directory, as a file with a .pdf extension." It then uses the tar command (which is now a part of modern Windows installations) to unpack the .zip; The script then navigates to the \net462 folder inside the nested structure of the unzipped archive, and passes a Base64-encoded, zlib-compressed Python script data blob directly to the ipyw32.exe program as a command flag.

The end result of this process retrieves and executes the content from hxxp://grillmasterchef[.]com/90e4a147-1234-505c-a024-062e543b5df8/timer6, and this is where it gets interesting.

Stage 2: Begin the barbeque

The timer6 file is a Python script that has been encoded in Base64, which has then had some of the latin alphabet characters substituted with cyrillic letters. Since the Base64 encoding scheme doesn't interpret cyrillic characters, a straight decode won't work. The script reverses the substitution of these alternate letters back to ASCII characters, then decodes the Base64 blob.

Figure 8: The top of the still-encoded timer6 Base64 (cyrillic lowercase letter "Yo" highlighted), with the script's cyrillic character/latin character substitution rules (inset)

Several cybersecurity vendors appear to believe that timer6 leverages a now-deprecated adversary simulation framework called Veil, which was designed to obfuscate Metasploit Meterpreter Python scripts to make them less easily detectable during penetration testing. That's arguably accurate, but not entirely correct: In reviewing the timer6 script, it appears to leverage some aspects of Veil's Python shellcode_inject/flat.py—in particular, it contains the same HeapCreate flag, HeapAlloc flag, buffer-copy pattern, and native API sequence. Veil explicitly describes this module as designed for inline shellcode injection, which is one thing that timer6 does. But there are other aspects of timer6's behavior that stray from what the full Veil package does by default.

The content of timer6, after decoding, is another Python script.

Figure 9: The second layer of timer6, a Python script decoded from Base64, which contains another decoding layer for XORed data that has been Base64 encoded

This shellcode layer is protected with a 19-byte XOR key (Hex: 84 0d ff da 80 29 b6 1b 52 9b 42 40 5d 55 aa 80 a5 7e 7c) that is embedded within the script as a separate Base64 blob.

Figure 10: The XOR key is in the house with you right now

When unpacked and decoded, the output of this script is a Windows PE malware loader, which executes as soon as the script decodes it. This malware loader searches the disk for a specific .ini file that contains a URL. If it finds the URL in the .ini file, it downloads whatever is at the other end (using the User-Agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36), then performs RC4 decryption of the downloaded file.

In this instance, the loader connected to another barbeque-themed URL, hxxps://grillmasterchef[.]com/90e4a147-1234-505c-a024-062e543b5df8/v6, and decrypted the contents, which was another malware executable. The RC4 decryption key is prepended as the first 64 bytes of this v6 file.

The v6 malware, once decrypted, is automatically injected into memory by the script. The security vendor consensus is that this is a malware called Doina, which can serve as a delivery mechanism for other malware. In 2024, security vendor Halcyon reported that Doina was implicated as a precursor step to ransomware attacks, but Doina has multiple features and a modular architecture that make it useful as a general-purpose RAT, infostealer, and profiler tool.

Immediately after Doina began running, it began to communicate with the same grillmasterchef server from which it originated, sending a series of HTTPS POST communications, then retrieving a ZIP file from the URL hxxps://kiriosyka[.]com/KsxmmKiN5N0j/sqr-viewertr6: a 52MB compressed file that contains a full, portable instance of the Node.js code interpreter, and a malicious, heavily obfuscated index.js script. The malware unpacks this to the location C:\ProgramData\NodeView, then runs the (non-malicious) node.exe interpreter, passing it the index.js file as an argument.

Figure 11: Unzipped contents of the sqr-viewertr6 file

It's also notable that other elements of this attack deploy their various payloads, logs, and related files to both the root of the C:\ProgramData\ path, and to folders beneath that directory.

Stage 3: Cranking up the heat with more malware

While the index.js is a form of malware in its own right, it is also designed with a modular architecture that can download, decrypt, and inject various kinds of encrypted malicious payloads into memory as fileless malware.

In this investigation, the Node component pulled down two additional files, which then began beaconing and performing malware-esque activities. The two files were given randomized names that resemble GUIDs; One is only about 17KB in size, the other greater than 19MB in size. Neither has a discernible PE header, and both have high entropy. So what's going on here?

All three files are part of a package. The index.js component decrypts both files using AES-256-GCM, in which the first 12 bytes of each file is the nonce value, and the next 16 bytes are the key. It then executes the smaller file.

It turns out that the smaller of the two files is a shellcode reflective DLL injector (or sRDI), essentially a loader for the larger file. The larger file is an infostealer malware, allegedly Lumma Stealer. The sRDI component injects the stealer into memory through process hollowing, and the malware immediately begins beaconing.

As part of its initial check-in with its C2, the stealer malware transmits the hostname, username, and other profiling information as part of an initial HTTPS POST connection. It then switches gears and communicates over the websocket protocol for continuous monitoring.

Figure 12: Packet capture of websocket session traffic generated by the malware, receiving file name conventions to search for from the C2 server (red), and sending a unique identifier and "heartbeat" during idle time (blue).

The websocket connection included the URL pointing to the suspected Lumma Stealer download package, as well as filenames and other strings indicating software targets of interest to the stealer:

Browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera)

Cryptocurrency wallet apps (Ledger, Electrum, Atomic Wallet)

Password managers (LastPass, Dashlane, 1Password, NordPass, RoboForm)

Email clients

Command processors like PowerShell

As with many of the other elements of this attacker infrastructure, the C2 addresses the malware communicates with are all themed around barbeque: thegrilljournal[.]com and homelygrill[.]com are used for exfil after an initial check-in to perfectgrillrecipes[.]com. The malware originates from the domain liokida[.]com (which, as far as we can tell, is not a barbeque term), and the stealer contains this domain embedded inside itself as a string. An earlier version of the attack also linked to the stealer payload from kiriosyka[.]com.

Interestingly, there are two forms of periodic updates that the Node malware, index.js performs: It can call for an update file that contains both the stealer and the reflective loader executable payloads and the Node.js interpreter files (which total at roughly 58MB in size), or it can retrieve just the payload files (index.js and the two .tmp files, at just under 20MB). To get the smaller-sized update, the malware calls the same URL with the query string ?exclude_bins=true at the end.

Every file retrieval request returns an archive with a unique hash, because the server hosting these payloads appends a random amount of null bytes to the archive at the time of the request. The payload inside the archive files changed once or twice per day.

Figure 13: Unzipped contents of the sqr-viewertr6 file downloaded with the exclude_bins=true query string, which does not include the Node executable

Finally, we observed yet another malicious component installed as part of the delivery of this malware package: A pirated copy of an RMM called NetSupport was also deployed inside the C:\ProgramData directory under the nonstandard folder Prodclear. The license key and copyright information for this RMM indicate the RMM is at least eight years old. The RMM maintains extensive log files of its activity within a subdirectory.

NetSupport's communication happens over an HTTPS connection that uses the nonstandard port 725/tcp, and this particular installation communicates with the IP address 167.148.201[.]106. The C2 traffic generated by the NetSupport Client software connects to the HTML file fakeurl.htm at the same IP address.

Figure 14: The NetSupport Client software executable was cryptographically signed eight years ago.

Stage 4: Chef Boyardon't and the Gastro Infra

As previously mentioned, the c2 and payload delivery .com domains used by the malware mostly sound like titles of a high-end magazine about cooking with charcoal: GrillRecipesPro, TheGrillJournal, EmbersAndBites, GrillMasterChef, and HomelyGrill all serve as both C2 and payload delivery domains. We found several relations between the domains, from common hosting and DNS servers to multiple payloads communicating with or being delivered from the domains.

Figure 15: Relationship map tying together C2 domains and payload delivery domain Liokida to multiple Lumma Stealer executables

Figure 16: URL, domain, and file relationships between Doina C2 domains and payload delivery domain Kiriosyka

The decidedly non-foody domains Liokida and Kiriosyka host the Lumma Stealer/Node.js payload packages, as well as several other malicious payloads that were not called during this attack.

Figure 17: Common URL patterns used to deliver payloads from Kiriosyka and Liokida domains

We also observed an IP address (167.148.201.106) used as a C2 for the NetConnect Client RMM payload. The IP address is used solely for hosting the legitimate website for a restaurant based in Detroit, but that domain has not been observed being abused. The C2 traffic connected directly to the IP address.

Figure 18: IP address linked to a restaurant domain being used for C2 communications

Figure 19: The deobfuscated Doina code calls the Lumma Stealer download and executes it

Mitigation

The best defense against ClickFix is user awareness of what it is and how it works. The attacks succeed because a large proportion of users simply don't recognize the risk of following an on-screen prompt. If you've made it this far, please tell your colleagues, family, and friends what to watch for. No legitimate CAPTCHA should ever ask anyone to paste an arbitrary line of text into an operating system command prompt. It just isn't how CAPTCHAs work.

Google's paid ad function can unwittingly host malicious links, in a technique commonly known as malvertising. Back in August, Huntress analysts reverse-engineered a MacSync Stealer sample collected from an incident that began with the user clicking on a sponsored Google result after searching for how to install Claude on a Mac.

Luckily for defenders, the way Google ad-clicks are redirected for billing the advertiser leaves some key signifiers for detection: aclk in the URL path and gclid in the resulting query strings.

Figure 20: The identifiers that Google uses to bill advertisers when users click on a sponsored result

These parameters indicate that a user reached a site through a Google-sponsored ad, even if later redirects obscure the original source. Investigators can use these markers in browser history, proxy logs, or URL telemetry to reconstruct the ad-to-malicious-site chain and connect related campaigns or domains. Reporting these identifiers to Google can kneecap attackers by cutting off their access to the ad ecosystem (at least, until they create a new account and start again).

Huntress customers and partners have an additional tool in their arsenal: A new feature called Attack Reduction is available now as part of Huntress Managed ESPM Early Access. ClickFix attacks typically prompt Windows users to open the Windows Run dialog box in order to enter a command; This feature enables admins to toggle access to the Run dialog for the majority of users who never need it. (See how it works and what it blocks.)

Figure 21: Closeup of the Attack Reduction feature that prevents users from opening the Run dialog in ESPM Early Access

It doesn't stop every form of ClickFix—notably, attackers sometimes ask users to open PowerShell, the command prompt, or even to enter commands into the address bar in Windows Explorer—but it's a very commonly abused method that most people on managed endpoints won't miss.

As reported in our newly released Tragic Quadrant, ClickFix accounted for about 2.2% of the Managed Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) detection signals Huntress has seen this year so far, but nearly 99% of those detections were high severity. Posts on social media sites still show that lots of users are getting tricked into falling for a ClickFix scam on a daily basis.

Just one malicious command pasted into a Run box can open the door to infostealers, remote access tools, ransomware, or other malicious software. The results can be devastating, leading to financial loss and, potentially, compromise of an entire enterprise. But just like we learned to look both ways before crossing the street, we'll learn not to do anything a dialog box on a web page tells us to do, just because it asks. An ounce of skepticism is worth hours of remediation.

Title: Attack Reduction in Huntress Managed ESPM: Disrupting ClickFix
Context: Introducing Attack Reduction Attack Reduction is a new capability in Huntress Managed ESPM that turns off Windows features your users never touch, but attackers rely on,...
Full Text:
Mandy was stuck at an airport with a few hours to kill. She decided to get her nails done, so she found a spa listed on the airport's website and clicked through. It looked like the spa's real website, on a normal domain with HTTPS, and Chrome showed no warnings.

Then a CAPTCHA popped up. Nothing too unusual there. It asked for a few "verification steps" to ensure she was a human user:

Press and hold Windows key + R

In the verification window, press Ctrl + V

Press Enter

An example ClickFix attack where a user is told to press "Windows Key + R" and paste a command into the Run dialog that opens.

But this simple sequence of hotkeys actually opens the Windows Run dialog, and in this case, would have pasted a malicious PowerShell command that the webpage quietly copied to the clipboard. (The Windows Run dialog is a small box that lets you type a command or program name and run it right away.)

If Mandy pressed Enter, the command would have downloaded and run a file from the internet. That file sets up persistence through a registry key, installs a remote access trojan, and steals the browser's saved passwords, cookies, and credit card details.

This is not a hypothetical example. This actually happened to a Huntress employee (name changed for privacy). Thankfully, she realized what was going on and didn't get pwned. A LOT of people aren't so lucky. So, this post is about one simple idea: what if "Windows key + R" didn't open anything at all?

What is ClickFix, and why is it everywhere?

ClickFix is a simple social engineering attack that tricks users into running malicious commands they don't understand. It often employs messaging related to fixing a problem, hence the name "ClickFix."

It also works very well. Our 2026 Cyber Threat Report linked ClickFix and fake CAPTCHA scams to over half of all malware loader activity. In our own SOC, ClickFix-style Run dialog attacks now account for 31% of EDR SOC signals.

The lures keep changing: fake Windows Update screens, fake Docker ads, compromised small-business websites, and now malicious AI chatbots. But the classic version almost always ends the same way, with Windows key + R.

Most of your users should never open the Run dialog

Here's what makes this so frustrating. The Run dialog is a power-user shortcut. IT folks love it. Most employees have never opened it on purpose and wouldn't know what to type into it if they did.

We've seen this play out in the data. Across organizations in ESPM Early Access, it's common to see 90% or more of users who never use the Run dialog at all. Which is why they don't recognize the commands they are pasting in as being a problem.

Run dialog box on Windows in which a user has pasted a malicious command, unwittingly copied from a ClickFix attack.

That's a big gap. A feature almost nobody needs is the starting point for nearly a third of what our EDR SOC investigates. Detection still matters, and Huntress Managed EDR's Attack Disruption engine can kill many ClickFix chains in under a second. But when the attack depends on a feature your users don't need, the simplest fix is to turn that feature off. If only there was an easy way to do that…Oh, wait, now there is!

Introducing Attack Reduction

Attack Reduction is a new capability in Huntress Managed ESPM that turns off Windows features your users never touch, but attackers rely on, starting with "Windows key + R". That fits what ESPM is built to do: harden your endpoints before an attack ever starts.

ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard

We're starting with the Run dialog, because that's where ClickFix starts. More controls are coming:

Available now: Blocking the Run dialog for users who don't need it to disrupt "Windows key + R" attacks.

Planned: Command Prompt restrictions for users who don't use cmd.exe.

Planned: Interactive PowerShell restrictions for users who don't use it.

Planned: Windows Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules that stop Office, script, and email apps from launching or injecting payloads.

Planned: Blocking HTML applications (mshta) for users who don't use them.

How Attack Reduction works

The hard part of turning off a Windows feature isn't flipping the switch. It's knowing who will be affected and not breaking legitimate workflows. Attack Reduction is designed with the following in mind.

1. See who actually uses the Run dialog

Once ESPM is on, Attack Reduction collects each user's Run dialog history and builds a baseline. On the Attack Reduction dashboard, you can see which users rely on the Run dialog and which never touch it, across your whole account or one organization at a time. You'll know exactly who would be affected before anything changes.

The dashboard also flags commands in a user's Run history that look like ClickFix. Windows doesn't record when those commands ran, so treat them as a reason to investigate rather than proof of an active attack.

The ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard and how many users are utilizing the Run dialog per week.

2. Turn on blocking

When you're ready, turn on blocking at the account or organization level. Attack Reduction then turns off the "Windows key + R" shortcut for users who don't need it. Users who rely on the Run dialog can keep it, and you can switch any user between allowed and blocked at any time.

3. Users get a clear message, not a mystery

If a blocked user presses Windows key + R, nothing runs. Instead, they see a pop-up explaining that the action was blocked for security reasons and asking them to contact their IT support team or take Security Awareness Training. Either way, the attack stops, and a confused user gets a quick security lesson.

4. You get a record of what they almost ran

When a blocked user presses Windows key + R, Attack Reduction also captures what was on their clipboard. If someone was about to paste a malicious command, you'll have it on record, which helps you spot users who are being targeted and follow up.

The ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard and a list of blocked attempts by users to utilize the Run dialog.

What Attack Reduction doesn't do

We want to be clear about the limits here, because ClickFix is a moving target.

Blocking the Run dialog disrupts the most common version of ClickFix. It doesn't stop every one. Attackers can, and already do, tell users to paste commands into File Explorer's address bar, Windows Terminal, Command Prompt, or PowerShell instead.

That's why the Run dialog is the first step, not the last one. Every path we close makes the attack harder to pull off, and the planned Command Prompt and PowerShell controls are aimed at exactly those next moves. Attack Reduction also works best alongside the rest of your defenses: Managed EDR to catch what gets through, and Managed SAT so users know a real CAPTCHA will never ask them to paste a command.

Get started with Attack Reduction

Attack Reduction is available now as part of Huntress Managed ESPM Early Access for existing Huntress partners and customers.

Not in ESPM Early Access yet? Click the ESPM icon in the left-hand menu of your Huntress portal to enroll. Then let Attack Reduction collect a baseline so you can see which users actually need the Run dialog before flipping on Blocking.

As Early Access partners put this capability to work, their feedback will decide which Windows features we tackle next and how we build those controls.

Have ideas or requests? Share them at feedback.huntress.com/espm. And stay tuned. There's a lot more coming to Managed ESPM.

Full Text:
Almost 3000 ransomware attacks took place between July and September 2026 and the figure marked a significant increase when compared with the same period last year.

According to an analysis by Nord Security, the 2894 ransomware attacks which took place during the quarter represents a 50% increase when compared with the same period last year.

It also represents a slight increase when compared with the previous quarter of this year, as the July to September period saw an 8.6% rise in ransomware attacks when compared with April to June.

Published on October 21, the Nord Security report suggested that the significant rise in ransomware activity is a result of the impact of law enforcement takedowns on ransomware groups.

Researchers suggested that the action against the likes of Lockbit, BlackCat and RansomHub helped to reduce ransomware activity during 2025.

“Now, the market is stabilizing, and the numbers we see today are merely the first stepping stone in ransomware’s new era,” said Vakaris Noreika, VP of product research and development at Nord Security.

Rival Ransomware Gangs Drive Attacks

During the reporting period, the two most prolific ransomware groups were The Gentlemen and Qilin. Of those ransomware incidents which could be attributed, The Gentlemen accounted for 383 ransomware attacks, while Qilin was not far behind with 363 recorded attacks.

The third most active ransomware group during the period was Inc Ransom, which accounted for 110 attacks. Other groups which showed significant activity during the quarter with almost 100 ransomware attacks each include Krybit, Akira, Deadlock and Clop Leaks.

But it is The Gentlemen and Qilin which remain by far the most active ransomware gangs. The two threat groups have traded places as the most common perpetrator of ransomware attacks throughout 2026. The Nord Security research suggested that a rivalry between the two groups is pushing them both on to develop new attack techniques for claiming more victims.

“Based on underground forum activity we observed, The Gentlemen's founder appears to have previously run one of Qilin's top affiliate crews before a dispute over an unpaid cut, which he took to an underground forum and lost,” said Mantas Sabeckis, senior threat intelligence researcher at Nord Security.

“His answer was to start a new group and lure his former colleagues away with a 90% payout, well above the usual 70% to 80%. This quarter, the breakaway The Gentlemen group edged past Qilin by 20 attacks.”

Read More: Why Ransomware Remains One of Cybersecurity’s Most Persistent and Costly Threats

One of the techniques which has been deployed by both groups to remove the encryption element of the ransomware attacks. Rather than encrypting the data and holding it hostage that way, the attackers simply steal sensitive data from their victim and threaten to publish it unless they receive a ransom payment.

“Stealing data is faster and simpler, so one group can hit many victims at once with far less effort. This shift is likely a big part of why attack volumes keep climbing,” said Sabeckis. “But that doesn’t mean encryption is going away,” he added.

While ransomware groups continue to adapt and evolve, researchers noted that when it comes to the initial entry point for attacks, they have remained broadly the same. These include attackers exploiting compromised passwords, a lack of multi-factor authentication, on accounts and unpatched security vulnerabilities.

“The names on the most prolific ransomware group list regularly change, but the way they get in doesn’t,” said Noreika. “What happens once attackers are inside may be shifting, but closing those familiar openings still removes a large share of the risk.”

Protecting Against AiTM Attacks: Is Your Microsoft Environment at Risk?

October 21, 2026

Nick Schmitz

BLOG

5 min.

The identity threat landscape has shifted considerably over the past few years. Attackers have steadily moved toward more sophisticated techniques and Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing is near the top of that list. Microsoft observed a 146% rise in AiTM attacks in 2024 and the trend has continued into 2026.

TL;DR – If your Microsoft 365 environment relies on traditional multifactor authentication (MFA) without phishing-resistant authentication and or layered Conditional Access policies, AiTM attacks can bypass your defenses and hijack active sessions in real time.

Key Takeaways:

AiTM phishing has been commoditized through Phishing-as-a-Service platforms. AI-generated lures have eliminated the visual cues that users once relied on to identify phishing attempts.

Phishing-resistant authentication methods (FIDO2, passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, certificate-based authentication) are the only category of MFA that AiTM proxies cannot relay, making them the most critical control to prioritize.

Deploying these controls in production environments with hybrid identity, legacy applications and third-party integrations requires deliberate sequencing and real-world risk assessment, not just baseline compliance.

A significant driver of AiTM growth is the Phishing-as-a-Service ecosystem. Platforms like Tycoon2FA have industrialized AiTM attacks. A threat actor with minimal technical skill can rent a fully functional proxy-based phishing kit, for as little as $120.

The result is a category of attack that was once the domain of sophisticated threat actors and is now widely accessible.

AI is accelerating this trend further. Phishing lures that used to be easy to spot, including awkward phrasing, odd formatting, generic greetings have all but vanished. Lures are increasingly generated by AI tools that produce polished, personalized and contextually convincing content at scale.

Research has found that AI-generated phishing attacks are becoming increasingly common. For organizations running Microsoft 365, this is a practical problem worth understanding.

What is AiTM and How Does It Work?

AiTM attacks build on the foundation of traditional man-in-the-middle tactics. This type of attack operates across multiple communication layers, from the network and transport layers all the way up to the application layer, relaying traffic in real time. Once positioned, the attacker actively intercepts the exchange between the victim and the legitimate service.

A user clicks a link in a phishing email and lands on an attacker-controlled reverse proxy. This proxy silently relays everything to the real login server.

The user enters their credentials and completes their multi-factor authentication (MFA) challenge, if applicable. To the user, everything looks normal, even the sign-in page will display their organization’s branding.

At the end of the authentication flow, once the server is satisfied, it issues a session cookie. The attacker’s proxy captures that token and injects it into their own browser.

They now hold a valid, active session and can navigate everywhere the user can. Traditional MFA methods like Short Message Service (SMS) codes and number matching cannot prevent this.

What Native Microsoft 365 Controls Can Help Address AiTM Risk?

Microsoft 365 includes several controls that directly address AiTM risk. The most effective are phishing-resistant authentication methods, specifically Fast Identity Online 2 (FIDO2) security keys, passkeys, Windows Hello for Business and certificate-based authentication.

These methods are cryptographically bound to the legitimate domain, meaning a proxy cannot relay them. They are the only authentication methods that can stop AiTM if setup properly.

Beyond phishing-resistant authentication methods, Conditional Access is one of the most powerful tools available for reducing AiTM risk. Requiring compliant devices, restricting access to trusted locations and enforcing risk-based policies through Entra ID Protection creates a layered defense. An attacker would need to satisfy all of these conditions at once.

Even if a session cookie is stolen, with the proper setup these controls could stop that stolen session from being used.

These controls are well-designed and, when configured correctly, meaningfully reduce AiTM risk. The operational challenge for most organizations is getting from where they are today to a state where these controls are deployed, tuned and maintained without disrupting the business in the process.

Where to Focus Your Efforts to Reduce Risk

Microsoft 365 and Entra ID environments accumulate complexity quickly. Conditional Access policies layer on top of each other. Defender configurations drift from their original intent. Permissions granted for a specific project persist long after the project ends. Staying on top of it requires deliberate, recurring attention in three areas.

Start with Strategy

Passwordless authentication, Conditional Access architecture and zero trust roadmaps each touch identity, device trust, network segmentation and application access simultaneously. The challenge is rarely understanding what the target state looks like.

It’s sequencing the work across dependencies that already exist in production, with the budget and staffing currently available, without stalling the initiatives that are already in flight. Without a solid strategy serving as a foundation, you run the risk of introducing unintended gaps where an attacker can gain entry.

Assess Against Real-world Risk, Not Just Baselines

Recommended security baselines for Microsoft 365 and Entra ID are a reasonable starting point. The more valuable exercise is mapping your current configuration against attack patterns relevant to your organization. Looking at specific business email compromise (BEC) paths, token theft scenarios and lateral movement through overprivileged service principals will give you a greater understanding of where your AiTM risk lies.

Armed with this knowledge, you can make meaningful improvements that can significantly reduce the likelihood of a successful attack.

Account for Complexity in Policy Configuration and Deployment

Deploying security controls like Conditional Access, phishing-resistant MFA and Defender policies is straightforward in a clean environment. Most environments are not clean. Hybrid identity architectures, third-party integrations, legacy applications that do not support modern authentication and user experience considerations all introduce friction that turns a textbook deployment into something more nuanced.

Accounting for that complexity upfront prevents the cycle of deploying a control, breaking something, rolling it back and losing organizational trust in the process.

How GuidePoint Security Can Help

GuidePoint Security provides credentialed, expert cloud security services, including support across the Microsoft security stack. If you need help understanding where your Microsoft environment stands against AiTM and what it would take to close the gaps, we can help start that conversation.

FAQs

Can AiTM attacks bypass phishing-resistant MFA?

Not typically. FIDO2 security keys, passkeys and Windows Hello for Business are cryptographically bound to the legitimate domain. A proxy cannot relay that handshake, which is why these are the only MFA methods that stop AiTM.However, while AiTM cannot break the cryptographic exchange of true phishing-resistant MFA, attackers bypass these deployments using secondary techniques, including MFA Downgrade Attacks, Authorization-Layer Phishing and Post-Authentication Session Theft.

How do you detect an AiTM attack in progress?

Watch for sign-ins from unfamiliar locations or devices immediately after a legitimate authentication. Entra ID Protection can flag impossible travel, anomalous token activity and risk events that indicate session hijacking.

What should you do if a session token is stolen?

Revoke the compromised session immediately and force reauthentication for the affected account. Then investigate what the attacker accessed during the active session and reset any credentials or permissions that were exposed.

How do you deploy phishing-resistant MFA without disrupting the business?

Start with a pilot group and expand in phases based on role sensitivity and application compatibility. Legacy applications that do not support modern authentication need workarounds before you enforce phishing-resistant methods organization-wide.
